Conceived directly by ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation) under the Department of Space, it proudly stands as Asia's very first premier university dedicated exclusively to the specialized study and rigorous advanced research of outer space sciences, space technology, and complex space applications. The years 1972, 1995, and 2014 are factually incorrect regarding its foundational year.

q: In which of the following year, the Department of Space was established in India?
exp: The Department of Space (DoS) was officially and decisively established by the Government of India precisely in the year 1972. This highly crucial government department is directly responsible for actively administering the heavily advanced Indian space program and strictly operates under the direct command of the Prime Minister of India. Its creation brought the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), which was formed slightly earlier in 1969, strictly under its massive institutional umbrella to efficiently drive national space research.

q: Which of the following was the first American astronaut, who set foot on moon?
exp: Neil Armstrong, the legendary American astronaut and brave commander of the historic Apollo 11 mission, became the very first human being to ever set foot on the lunar surface on July 20, 1969. His famous, immortalized words were, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." Yuri Gagarin was a pioneering Soviet cosmonaut and the first human in space, but he never landed on the Moon. Kenneth D. Cameron and Jerome Apt are much later American astronauts who flew solely on Earth-orbiting Space Shuttle missions.

q: The first gamma-ray observatory "Cos-B" was launched in ______.
exp: Cos-B was a groundbreaking, highly pioneering space mission operated by the European Space Agency (ESA). It was successfully launched into space in August 1975. As the very first satellite specifically completely dedicated to studying extraterrestrial gamma-ray sources, it profoundly revolutionized modern astrophysics by successfully mapping the Milky Way's gamma-ray emissions. The other years are factually incorrect regarding this mission: 1905 was the year of Einstein's miracle papers, 1950 predates any satellite launches (Sputnik was 1957), and 1989 saw the launch of the much later COBE satellite.

q: India's first success in launching a satellite using an indigenous vehicle came in ______.
exp: India officially achieved its historic, monumental first success in launching a satellite into orbit strictly using an indigenous launch vehicle on July 18, 1980. The Satellite Launch Vehicle-3 (SLV-3), brilliantly developed under the visionary leadership of Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, successfully deployed the Rohini (RS-1) satellite, firmly making India an exclusive member of the space-faring nations' club. The earlier years (1955, 1965, 1972) are incorrect as ISRO was only formed in 1969, and prior satellite launches (like Aryabhata in 1975) completely relied on Soviet rockets.

q: Which is the first nuclear power plant to be operational in India?
exp: The Tarapur Atomic Power Station (TAPS), strategically located in Palghar, Maharashtra, holds the monumental historical distinction of being the very first commercial nuclear power plant to become fully operational in India. Built with critical technological assistance from the United States, it officially began massive commercial operations in the year 1969. The other options represent much later additions to India's nuclear energy program: The Rajasthan Atomic Power Plant started in 1973, Narora in Uttar Pradesh started in 1991, and the massive Kudankulam plant in Tamil Nadu began in 2013.

q: GSAT-18, built by ISRO, aims at providing which type of services for the country?
exp: GSAT-18 is an incredibly advanced and massive Indian communications satellite brilliantly built by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO). It was successfully launched into space in 2016 precisely to powerfully bolster and expand the nation's critical telecommunications services. Equipped with numerous high-power Ku- band and C-band transponders, it provides essential bandwidth for television broadcasting, digital radio, and broad networking. It is definitely not a dedicated military defence satellite, an Earth-observation agriculture satellite (like RESOURCESAT), or a specialized GPS/Navigation satellite (like the NAVIC/IRNSS series).

q: Which of the following space mission of India was credited for reviving interest about presence of water on Moon?
exp: India's historic first deep-space lunar probe, Chandrayaan-I (launched brilliantly by ISRO in 2008), is globally and universally credited with the groundbreaking discovery that massively revived international scientific interest in the Moon. Using the highly advanced Moon Mineralogy Mapper instrument, it successfully provided undeniable, definitive evidence of the widespread presence of actual water molecules and hydroxyl strictly on the lunar surface. The other missions achieved different goals: Chandrayaan-III achieved a historic soft landing near the South Pole, Aditya L-1 is a solar observatory, and Mangalyaan was India's highly successful Mars orbiter.

q: Which of the following statement is correct regarding Satellite? 1. A satellite launched by man around any planet for our own purpose is called an artificial satellite. 2. The moon is an example of artificial satellite. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Statement I is absolutely scientifically correct. Any complex, man-made machine or object strategically built and launched into orbit by humans around the Earth or any other celestial body to gather critical data or provide communication is explicitly called an 'artificial satellite' (like Aryabhata or INSAT). However, Statement II is completely absurd and factually incorrect because the Moon is a naturally occurring, massive celestial body that has orbited the Earth for billions of years, making it a classic 'natural satellite', definitely not artificial. Therefore, only statement I is right.

q: What is the lift off mass of ISRO's GSLV Mk II?
exp: The Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle Mark II (GSLV Mk II), an incredibly powerful, three-stage medium-lift launch vehicle brilliantly designed and fully operated by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), prominently features a highly advanced indigenous cryogenic upper stage. Its total, massive lift-off mass is approximately 414 to 420 tonnes. It is primarily utilized to successfully deploy multi-ton communication satellites directly into Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO). The other weight options (120, 840, 1020 tonnes) are factually incorrect; for comparison, the massive LVM3 (GSLV Mk III) weighs around 640 tonnes.

q: The Vikram lander and Pragyan rover is associated with ______.
exp: The highly advanced 'Vikram' lander and the robotic 'Pragyan' rover are the iconic, heavily celebrated core components of ISRO's historically successful Chandrayaan-3 lunar mission (launched in 2023). This monumental mission achieved an unprecedented, flawless soft landing aggressively near the uncharted lunar South Pole, firmly making India the very first country to achieve this massive feat. While these identical names were also used in the partially unsuccessful Chandrayaan-2 mission, they are now globally and universally associated with the triumphant Chandrayaan-3. Aditya L-1 is a solar mission, and Mangalyaan was a Mars orbiter.

q: Which of the following is the India's first ever anti-satellite missile test?
exp: 'Mission Shakti' was an incredibly historic, highly classified, and monumentally successful strategic military operation executed flawlessly by the DRDO and ISRO on March 27, 2019. It represented India's very first successful test of an advanced Anti-Satellite (ASAT) weapon, where a kinetic kill vehicle aggressively destroyed a live Indian target satellite accurately positioned in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). This massive technological leap firmly established India as an elite space power. Mission Agni relates to standard ballistic missiles, Mission Indradhanush is a banking/health scheme, and Aditya is a solar space probe.

q: In the context of next-generation wireless communication, which of the following characteristics of Li-Fi technology distinguishes it from traditional Wi-Fi and creates both opportunities and limitations for its deployment in India's digital ecosystem?
o: Li-Fi uses millimeter waves which penetrate walls better than Wi-Fi, enhancing connectivity in remote rural areas.
Li-Fi uses visible and near-infrared light spectrum, which allows higher data transmission rates but limits operation to line-of-sight environments.
Li-Fi is based on quantum entanglement of photons, enabling secure communication even in high- interference zones like industrial corridors.
Li-Fi transmits data through ultra-low-frequency radio waves, reducing electromagnetic interference in high-density urban areas.
exp: Light Fidelity (Li-Fi) is an advanced, bidirectional wireless communication technology that uses the visible light, ultraviolet, and near- infrared spectrum to transmit data at incredibly high speeds (much faster than Wi-Fi). However, because light cannot penetrate solid opaque walls, Li-Fi is strictly limited to line-of-sight environments, functioning only within a single room or illuminated area. This provides extreme security but limits range. The other options are scientifically false. Li-Fi does not use radio waves (millimeter or ultra-low frequency) like Wi-Fi or 5G does, nor does it rely on theoretical quantum entanglement for its fundamental data transmission.

q: The PARAS Telescope, developed by the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) is located at which of the following places?
exp: The PARAS (PRL Advanced Radial-velocity Abu-sky Search) telescope is an indigenous high-resolution spectrograph developed by the Physical Research Laboratory. Located at the Mount Abu Infrared Observatory in Rajasthan, it is specifically designed to detect exoplanets around distant stars by measuring precise radial velocity shifts, marking a major milestone for Indian astronomy.

q: The scientist who was the first Director of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research was:
exp: The incredibly prestigious Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) was founded in 1945 under the visionary leadership of Dr. Homi Jehangir Bhabha, who rightfully served as its absolute first Director. Heavily supported by Sir Dorabji Tata, Dr. Bhabha meticulously built TIFR into a world-class premier institution dedicated explicitly to advanced, cutting-edge research in mathematics and theoretical physics, effectively laying the impregnable foundational bedrock for India's massive future nuclear energy program.

q: What cannot be added to the Quick Access Toolbar (QAT) in MS Office?
exp: In Microsoft Office applications (like Word or Excel), the Quick Access Toolbar (QAT) is designed to hold frequently used executable commands like 'Save', 'Undo', 'Redo', and 'Print'. However, 'Line Spacing' is a formatting option comprising a sub-menu or gallery of choices (like 1.0, 1.5, 2.0), rather than a singular one-click command. Therefore, individual formatting settings like Line Spacing cannot be directly pinned to the standard QAT like a standalone action button.

q: What is not a characteristic of a phishing email?
exp: Phishing emails are malicious cyber-attacks designed to steal sensitive data by creating a false sense of urgency (demand for immediate action), using spoofed or mismatched sender addresses, and containing deceptive links seeking passwords or OTPs. However, possessing a verified "Digital signature and an exact official domain" is the hallmark of a genuine, highly secure communication from a legitimate organization. Cybercriminals rarely possess verifiable cryptographic digital signatures for their fake domains.

q: Fill in the blank: The PSLV is mainly used to place the satellites in ______ orbits.
exp: The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) is ISRO's highly reliable third-generation launch vehicle, specifically designed and primarily used to place Earth-observation and remote-sensing satellites into Sun- Synchronous Polar Orbits (typically at an altitude of 600-900 km). While it has occasionally launched lunar (Chandrayaan-1) and interplanetary missions, its core, standardized utility is strictly for polar launches. Geostationary orbits (36,000 km) require the heavier GSLV or LVM3 rockets. Thus, 'Polar' is the most accurate defining characteristic for PSLV.

q: How often does the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) update its Prohibited List to include new performance-enhancing substances and ensure fairness in sports?
exp: The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) assumes the critical global responsibility of maintaining drug-free sports. To combat the constant emergence of new, undetectable performance-enhancing drugs, WADA strictly and comprehensively updates its global 'Prohibited List' every single year. The updated list officially comes into effect on January 1st annually. This relentless yearly review cycle ensures athletes cannot exploit loopholes. It is definitely not done every two or four years, nor restricted merely to Olympic cycles.

q: Which was the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth, marking the beginning of the space age in 1957?
exp: 'Sputnik 1' made monumental global history on October 4, 1957, when it was successfully launched by the Soviet Union, becoming the very first artificial satellite to enter Earth's orbit. This spectacular feat directly triggered the intense Space Race between the USA and the USSR. Explorer 1 was the first US satellite launched later in 1958. Luna 1 was the first spacecraft to reach the vicinity of the Moon. Therefore, Sputnik 1 is the definitive pioneer.

q: Which scientist proposed the Indian Calendar Reform Committee report, aiming to standardize Indian calendars and align them with scientific observations of solar and lunar cycles?
exp: The Calendar Reform Committee was constituted in 1952 by the Government of India under the distinguished chairmanship of the eminent astrophysicist Dr. Meghnad Saha (famous for the Saha ionization equation). The committee's monumental task was to resolve the massive discrepancies among the 30+ regional calendars used in India. Based on his rigorous scientific report, the unified 'Indian National Calendar' (Saka Samvat) was officially adopted in 1957. Sarabhai, Mahalanobis, and Raman spearheaded space, statistics, and physics respectively.

q: Who was the first Indian scientist to launch India's space program?
exp: Dr. Vikram Sarabhai is universally acknowledged as the "Father of the Indian Space Program." He was instrumental in establishing the Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR) in 1962, which later evolved into ISRO. His vision recognized the immense potential of space technology for national development. Option (a) is correct. Homi J. Bhabha (b) is celebrated as the father of the Indian Nuclear Program. Satyendra Nath Bose (c) was a pioneer in quantum mechanics (Bose-Einstein statistics). Srinivasa Ramanujan (d) was a legendary mathematician with no connection to the space program.

q: Who is known as the "Agni Putri" for her contributions to the Agni missile program?
exp: Dr. Tessy Thomas, an eminent Indian scientist at DRDO, is universally celebrated as the "Missile Woman of India" or "Agni Putri." She earned this title for her pivotal role as the Project Director for the Agni-IV and Agni-V ballistic missile systems. Option (a) is correct. Dr. Sudha Murthy (b) is an educator, author, and philanthropist. Dr. Ritu Karidhal

q: What is the primary purpose of ISRO's CMS-03 satellite?
exp: The incredibly advanced, highly sophisticated, and strategically crucial CMS (Communication Satellite) series is aggressively designed, meticulously built, and successfully launched by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO). The absolute primary, overwhelmingly essential purpose of these massive, incredibly powerful geostationary satellites, including CMS-03 (part of the heavily upgraded GSAT family series explicitly transitioning to the newer CMS naming convention), is to systematically provide absolutely robust, seamless, and highly reliable "Communication services." This aggressively includes heavily boosting massive telecommunication networks, seamlessly expanding nationwide television broadcasting, hugely supporting crucial DTH services, and flawlessly establishing incredibly vital VSAT networks across the vast, entire Indian subcontinent and its remote, sprawling islands. Option (a) precisely defines this specific satellite class's core mandate. Space observatories like Astrosat handle cosmic research (b). Cartosat specifically handles deep cartographic mapping (c), while the INSAT-3D series heavily handles vital climate and weather monitoring (d).

q: Which option accurately describes the imaging payload used in the NISAR mission?
o: Optical camera with multispectral imaging capability
Sub-millimeter radar system with a 4-meter phased array antenna
exp: The phenomenally ambitious, incredibly massive, and historically groundbreaking NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) mission is a highly prestigious, multi-billion-dollar joint space exploration project incredibly collaboratively executed by the United States (NASA) and India (ISRO). The absolute technological marvel and the core defining payload brilliantly utilized in this incredibly advanced satellite is a highly complex, phenomenally powerful "Dual-frequency (L- band and S-band) Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), which is systematically paired with an incredibly massive, unfolding 12-meter wire- mesh radar reflector antenna." This breathtaking, highly sophisticated setup allows the satellite to aggressively scan the Earth's changing surface with incredibly stunning, millimeter-level precision, easily penetrating deep, dense clouds and dark nights to monitor complex ice-sheet collapses and minute crustal deformations. Option (b) is flawlessly and highly technically correct. It strictly relies on advanced radar, absolutely not simple optical cameras (a, d).

q: The Pravasi Bharatiya Divas marks which Indian leader's return from South Africa?
exp: Pravasi Bharatiya Divas (PBD) is celebrated annually on 9th January to mark the contribution of the overseas Indian community to the development of India. The date was specifically chosen to commemorate the return of Mahatma Gandhi from South Africa to Mumbai on January 9, 1915. Gandhi's return was a watershed moment in Indian history, as he brought with him the powerful technique of *Satyagraha* (non-violent resistance), which eventually led India to independence. The convention began in 2003 and provides a platform for the government to engage with the diaspora.

q: National Women's Day in India is being celebrated on 13th February in honor of which prominent woman's legacy?
exp: National Women's Day in India is celebrated on February 13th every year to commemorate the birth anniversary of Sarojini Naidu, popularly known as the 'Nightingale of India' (Bharat Kokila). It is distinct from International Women's Day (March 8). Sarojini Naidu was a prolific poet, a fierce freedom fighter, and a champion of women's rights. She made history as the first Indian woman to become the President of the Indian National Congress (1925) and the first woman to become the Governor of an Indian state (United Provinces, now Uttar Pradesh) in 1947.

q: On October 31, India celebrates which day to mark the birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel?
exp: India celebrates National Unity Day (Rashtriya Ekta Diwas) on October 31st to honor the birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, the 'Iron Man of India'. Introduced by the government in 2014, this day pays tribute to Patel's monumental role in the political integration of India. As the first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, he successfully integrated over 560 princely states into the Indian Union through diplomacy and firmness. The 'Statue of Unity' in Gujarat, the world's tallest statue, stands as a testament to his contribution to national unity and integrity.

q: In India, 'National Science Day' is celebrated on February 28 to mark the achievement of which scientist?
exp: National Science Day is celebrated across India on February 28 to commemorate the discovery of the Raman Effect by the eminent Indian physicist Sir C.V. Raman on this day in 1928. The Raman Effect describes the scattering of light when it passes through a transparent material, leading to a change in its wavelength. For this groundbreaking discovery, C.V. Raman was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930, becoming the first Asian to receive a Nobel Prize in the sciences. The day is celebrated to promote scientific temper and innovation among the youth.

q: In India, 'National Science Day' is celebrated on February 28 to mark the achievement of which scientist?
exp: (Duplicate Question) Sir C.V. Raman is the correct answer. The celebration of National Science Day began in 1987. Every year, the Department of Science and Technology announces a specific theme for the day (e.g., "Indigenous Technologies for Viksit Bharat" in 2024). It serves as a reminder of India's scientific heritage and encourages students to pursue careers in science and technology. C.V. Raman's work remains a cornerstone in the field of spectroscopy and light scattering physics globally.

q: Who launched the National Digital Library of India in 2018?
exp: The National Digital Library of India (NDLI) was launched on June 19, 2018, by Prakash Javadekar, who was the Union Minister for Human Resource Development (now Ministry of Education) at the time. The NDLI is a project under the National Mission on Education through Information and Communication Technology (NMEICT) and is developed by IIT Kharagpur. It is a single-window platform that provides free access to a vast repository of learning resources, including textbooks, articles, videos, and theses, in multiple languages for learners of all levels.

q: Which of the following pairs is incorrectly matched?
o: Beti Bachao Beti Padhao - Ministry of Women & Child Development
PM JANMAN - Ministry of Tribal Affairs
exp: The incorrect pair is Swadesh Darshan - Ministry of Culture. The Swadesh Darshan Scheme is a Central Sector Scheme launched by the Ministry of Tourism in 2014-15 for the integrated development of theme-based tourist circuits (e.g., Ramayana Circuit, Buddhist Circuit). While it promotes culture, the nodal ministry is Tourism. The other pairs are correct: PM MITRA (Mega Integrated Textile Region and Apparel) is under the Ministry of Textiles; Beti Bachao Beti Padhao is a tri-ministerial effort led by Women & Child Development; PM JANMAN targets Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) under the Ministry of Tribal Affairs.

q: The National Youth Policy in India launched in February ________.
exp: The National Youth Policy (NYP-2014) was launched in February 2014 by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, replacing the earlier policy of 2003. The policy defines 'youth' as persons in the age group of 15-29 years. Its vision is to empower the youth of the country to achieve their full potential and enable them to contribute to the nation's development. It identifies five key objectives and eleven priority areas, including education, employment, skill development, and entrepreneurship, aiming to create a productive workforce for India's future.

q: The code on social security extends social security to ________.
exp: The Code on Social Security, 2020 is a significant labor reform that aims to extend social security benefits to employees in both the organised and unorganised sectors. This includes gig workers, platform workers (like delivery partners), and interstate migrant workers, who were previously largely excluded from such nets. It amalgamates nine central labor laws related to social security, including the Employees' Provident Fund Act and the Maternity Benefit Act. The goal is to provide universal social security coverage, including health, retirement, and insurance benefits, to the entire workforce of India.

q: Mission Parivar Vikas was initially launched in ________ high focus states.
exp: Mission Parivar Vikas was launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in 2016 for 7 high-focus states: Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, and Assam. These states were selected because they had a Total Fertility Rate (TFR) of 3.0 or above, significantly higher than the national average at the time. The mission's objective is to accelerate access to high-quality family planning choices based on information, reliable services, and supplies to reduce the TFR and stabilize the population growth in these specific regions.

q: The National Space Day of India is celebrated every year on August 23 to commemorate the ____.
o: successful launch of India's first interplanetary mission
successful launch of first satellite of India
successful soft-landing of the Vikram lander on the south pole of the moon
establishment of the Indian Space Research Organisation
exp: India officially observes August 23 as National Space Day to actively commemorate the monumental success of the Chandrayaan-3 mission. On this exact historic date in 2023, the ISRO-designed Vikram lander successfully executed a flawless soft-landing near the uncharted southern pole of the Moon. This extraordinary feat made India the first nation to conquer the lunar south pole and the fourth globally to achieve a soft lunar landing. The establishment of ISRO occurred on August 15, 1969, not August 23.

q: The Atal Pension Yojna was launched in _____.
exp: The Atal Pension Yojana (APY) is a massive, highly successful government-backed pension scheme in India explicitly aimed at providing robust, guaranteed social security primarily to workers belonging to the unorganized sector. It was officially and grandly launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on May 9, 2015, replacing the earlier Swavalamban scheme. The scheme vigorously encourages citizens to actively save for their retirement. The other years provided (2001, 2006, 2011) are factually incorrect as they drastically predate the formal inception and implementation of this specific welfare initiative.

q: National Sports Day in India commemorates which sports legend?
exp: National Sports Day in India is celebrated annually on the 29th of August to honor the birth anniversary of Major Dhyan Chand, the legendary Indian field hockey player who won three Olympic gold medals (1928, 1932, 1936) and is universally regarded as 'The Wizard' of hockey. The other options are incorrect: while Milkha Singh, Sachin Tendulkar, and Kapil Dev are all extraordinarily iconic Indian sports legends, National Sports Day is exclusively dedicated to Major Dhyan Chand's enduring legacy.

q: The Fit India Movement, promoting fitness and sports culture, was launched in which year?
exp: The Fit India Movement was launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on August 29, 2019, which is celebrated as National Sports Day in India to mark the birth anniversary of Major Dhyan Chand. The nationwide campaign encourages citizens to incorporate physical activity and sports into their daily lives.

q: The National Sports Day in India is celebrated on which date?
exp: National Sports Day in India is celebrated annually with immense enthusiasm on August 29th. This highly significant date was officially chosen to permanently honor the birth anniversary of Major Dhyan Chand, the legendary Indian hockey wizard who miraculously led India to three consecutive Olympic gold medals in 1928, 1932, and 1936.

q: The themes for World Ozone Day consistently highlight the success and future potential of which specific international treaty that governs the phase-out of ozone-depleting substances?
exp: World Ozone Day, celebrated globally every September 16th, fundamentally commemorates the historic 1987 signing of the "Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer." This incredibly vital, universally ratified international treaty is unequivocally hailed as the single most successful environmental agreement in human history, specifically dictating the mandatory global phase-out of highly destructive, ozone-depleting chemicals like Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) to effectively heal the Earth's protective atmospheric shield.

q: Which scheme was launched to provide health insurance coverage of up to 5 lakh per family per year for economically weaker sections?
o: Ayushman Bharat - Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PMJAY)
exp: Ayushman Bharat - PMJAY is the world's largest government-funded healthcare program, designed to provide a health cover of Rs. 5 lakhs per family per year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalization to vulnerable families. Option (a) is correct. Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana (b) was an older scheme providing only up to Rs. 30,000, which PMJAY later subsumed. PM Suraksha Bima Yojana (c) is an accidental death and disability insurance scheme, not general healthcare. The National Health Mission (d) is a broader framework to improve public health delivery systems.

q: How is the financial assistance under the PM-KISAN Scheme transferred to farmers?
o: Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) to bank accounts
exp: Under the Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM- KISAN) scheme, the Government of India provides income support of ₹6,000 per year in three equal installments. This financial assistance is deposited directly into the Aadhaar-seeded bank accounts of the beneficiary farmers through the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) mode to ensure transparency and eliminate middlemen. Option (c) is accurate. The government completely avoids Cash payments (a) and Cheques (b) due to the high risk of corruption and logistical delays. Post office savings (d) is not the mandated exclusive channel.

q: Which scheme aims to provide Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) connections to women from Below Poverty Line households?
exp: The Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY) is an incredibly powerful, deeply transformative flagship social welfare initiative massively launched by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. Its paramount, overriding objective is to vastly improve the severe health conditions of extremely marginalized women by actively replacing highly toxic, heavily polluting traditional cooking fuels (like firewood and dangerous cow dung) with clean, highly efficient, and incredibly safe Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG). It aggressively provides millions of entirely free initial LPG connections directly targeted to vulnerable women belonging strictly to Below Poverty Line (BPL) households. Option (c) correctly identifies this massive empowerment scheme. Saubhagya (a) specifically handles total rural electrification, while Awas Yojana (b) focuses heavily on housing.

q: What is the main purpose of the NIRBHAYA Fund?
exp: Following the incredibly horrific and deeply tragic 2012 Delhi gang-rape incident, the Government of India aggressively established the dedicated non-lapsable "Nirbhaya Fund" as an incredibly critical financial mechanism. Administered firmly by the Department of Economic Affairs, its absolute primary purpose is to forcefully channel massive financial resources toward rapidly implementing strategic initiatives precisely designed for "Ensuring women's safety and massive empowerment" across the nation. This robust fund rigorously supports vast safety projects like hyper-modern emergency response support stop crisis centers, and incredibly swift DNA analysis forensic labs. Option (a) is the definitively accurate answer.

q: The "International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer" (World Ozone Day) is observed annually on which date to commemorate the signing of the Montreal Protocol?
exp: The United Nations officially designated September 16th as the International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer. This highly specific date was chosen to eternally commemorate the signing of the landmark Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer in 1987. This immensely successful global treaty effectively phased out the production of dangerous ozone-depleting chemicals like CFCs.

q: Who hand-calligraphed the original manuscript of the Indian Constitution?
exp: The original Constitution of India was not printed but handwritten by Prem Behari Narain Raizada in a flowing italic style. He was a master calligrapher who undertook this task without charging any fee, asking only to sign his name on every page and his grandfather's name on the last page. Options (a), (c), and (d) are incorrect; B.N. Rau was the Legal Advisor, S.N. Mukherjee was the Chief Draftsman, and Gopalaswami Ayyangar was a member of the Drafting Committee. A fascinating fact is that the original pages were decorated by artists from Shantiniketan, led by Nandalal Bose.

q: In which year did the Indian Constitution come into effect?
exp: The Constitution of India officially came into effect on January 26, 1950, declaring India a sovereign democratic republic. This date was specifically chosen to commemorate the "Purna Swaraj" (Complete Independence) declaration of 1930. While it was adopted on November 26, 1949 (Constitution Day), it was enacted fully in 1950. Option (a) refers to independence, (c) to adoption, and (d) to the first general elections. This document replaced the Government of India Act 1935 as the country's fundamental governing document.

q: Who is regarded as the chief architect of the Indian Constitution?
exp: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar is universally regarded as the Chief Architect and the "Father of the Indian Constitution". As the Chairman of the Drafting Committee, he played a pivotal role in synthesizing various precedents and framing the final text that ensured social justice and equality. Option (a) was not a member of the Constituent Assembly. Options (b) and (d) played major roles (Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution, Prasad was President of the Assembly), but the architectural framework is credited to Ambedkar. He is often referred to as the "Modern Manu" for his legal contributions.

q: Who was the chairman of the drafting committee of the constituent assembly?
exp: The Drafting Committee, the most critical committee of the Constituent Assembly, was chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. Set up on August 29, 1947, it was tasked with preparing a draft constitution for India. Option (b) chaired the Union Powers Committee. Option (c) K.M. Munshi was a member of the Drafting Committee but not its chairman. Option (d) chaired the Advisory Committee. The committee consisted of seven members, and it took 2 years, 11 months, and 18 days to finalize the Constitution.

q: Which of the following is correctly matched with their leadership role in the Constituent Assembly?
o: G.V. Mavalankar - Chairman of the Committee on the Functions of the Constituent Assembly
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar - Head of the Committee on the Functions of the Assembly
N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar - Chairman of the Order of Business Committee
K.M. Munshi - Leader of the Committee on Fundamental Rights
exp: The correct match is (a), as G.V. Mavalankar chaired the Committee on the Functions of the Constituent Assembly. He later became the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha. Option (b) is incorrect as Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee. Option (c) is incorrect because K.M. Munshi chaired the Order of Business Committee. Option (d) is incorrect as Sardar Patel led the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, with J.B. Kripalani heading the specific sub- committee. Mavalankar was affectionately known as "Dadasaheb" in parliamentary circles.

q: Who headed the Credentials Committee in the Constituent Assembly?
exp: The Credentials Committee of the Constituent Assembly was headed by Alladi Krishnaswamy Aiyar. He was a distinguished lawyer and also a member of the Drafting Committee. Option (b) T.T. Krishnamachari joined the Drafting Committee later. Option (c) Nehru led the Union Constitution Committee. Option (d) Munshi led the Order of Business Committee. Aiyar was described by Ambedkar as "better than the best" legal minds, and his expertise was crucial in shaping the legal framework of the Constitution.

q: Who was the Chairman of the 'Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities, and Tribal and Excluded Areas' in the Constituent Assembly?
exp: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel was the Chairman of the massive Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities, and Tribal and Excluded Areas. This committee had several sub-committees to handle specific topics. Option (b), (c), and (d) are incorrect for this specific role. Patel's strong leadership ensured that the rights of minorities were protected while maintaining national unity, leading to the abolition of separate electorates. This committee was one of the largest, reflecting the complexity of the issues it handled.

q: Who among the following was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
exp: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar served as the Chairman of the Drafting Committee, which was appointed on August 29, 1947. This committee was responsible for scrutinizing the draft prepared by the Constitutional Advisor and preparing the final text for debate. Options (a), (c), and (d) chaired other key committees like Provincial Constitution, Rules of Procedure, and Union Powers respectively. Ambedkar defended the draft in the Assembly with great skill, earning the gratitude of the entire nation for his intellectual leadership.

q: Who was the Home Minister in the first cabinet of free India?
exp: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel held the portfolio of Home Minister (and Minister of Information & Broadcasting) in the first cabinet of independent India. He was also the first Deputy Prime Minister. Option (a) Rajendra Prasad became the first President. Option (b) Rajagopalachari was the first Indian Governor-General. Option (c) Maulana Azad was the first Education Minister. As Home Minister, Patel's greatest achievement was the political integration of over 560 princely states into the Indian Union.

q: Initially, when the 'Constitution of India' was adopted on 26th November 1949, how many Articles and Schedules did it originally contain?
exp: When the Constitution was adopted on November 26, 1949, it originally contained a Preamble, 395 Articles, and 8 Schedules. It was divided into 22 Parts. Option (a) is incorrect (284 refers to the number of members who signed it). Options (b) and (d) reflect later amendments; currently, there are 12 Schedules and over 448 Articles. The original text is arguably the longest written constitution of any sovereign country in the world.

q: Who was the constitutional advisor to the Constituent assembly of India?
exp: Sir Benegal Narsing Rau (B.N. Rau) was appointed as the Constitutional Advisor to the Constituent Assembly. He prepared the initial draft of the Constitution in October 1947, which the Drafting Committee then worked upon. Options (b), (c), and (d) were political leaders and members of the Assembly, whereas B.N. Rau was a distinguished jurist and civil servant who was not a member of the Assembly. He later served as a judge at the International Court of Justice in The Hague.

q: Which of the following was the most significant institutional innovation introduced by Pitt's India Act of 1784?
o: The introduction of an open competitive examination system for the Company's civil services.
The grant of legislative powers to the Governors-in-Council of Bombay and Madras.
Formal recognition of the undisputed sovereignty of the British Crown over the Company's territories in India.
Establishment of a clear distinction between the commercial and political functions of the East India Company.
exp: The Pitt's India Act of 1784 was a monumental piece of legislation that successfully established a critical system of 'Double Government' in British India. Its most significant institutional innovation was creating a sharp distinction between the East India Company's functions. It created a powerful new body, the 'Board of Control', appointed directly by the British Crown, to strictly oversee political, military, and revenue affairs, while leaving the existing 'Court of Directors' to manage purely commercial activities. The other options refer to different subsequent acts: open civil service exams were introduced in 1853, and absolute Crown sovereignty without the Company was established in 1858.

q: Who among the following played a critical role in drafting India's Constitution, was a social reformer, and is celebrated for his work toward the upliftment of Dalits?
exp: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was a monumental visionary, brilliant legal scholar, and the Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly, playing the most critical role in framing the Constitution of India. Beyond his unmatched legal contributions, he was a fierce social reformer who dedicated his entire life to the systematic eradication of the oppressive caste system and the socio-economic upliftment of Dalits (the depressed classes). He established the Scheduled Castes Federation to fight for their political rights. While Mahatma Gandhi, Rajendra Prasad, and Vallabhbhai Patel were monumental freedom fighters, it was specifically Ambedkar who spearheaded both the constitutional drafting and the Dalit empowerment movement.

q: Who was the Chairman of the Sub-Committee on North- East Frontier Tribal Areas and Assam Excluded & Partially Excluded Areas?
exp: The Sub-Committee on North-East Frontier Tribal Areas and Assam Excluded & Partially Excluded Areas was chaired by Gopinath Bordoloi, the first Chief Minister of Assam. This committee was formed under the Constituent Assembly to recommend administrative frameworks for the tribal regions of the Northeast, leading to the creation of the Sixth Schedule. The other options are incorrect. G.B. Pant, B.R. Ambedkar, and N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar were prominent members of the Constituent Assembly but did not chair this specific sub-committee. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, which is a frequently tested fact.

q: Who among the following is the chairman of Steering Committee in constituent assembly?
exp: Dr. Rajendra Prasad served as the Chairman of the critical Steering Committee in the Constituent Assembly, guiding its proceedings. Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru headed the Union Powers and Union Constitution Committees. Sardar Patel chaired the Provincial Constitution Committee and the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights. K.M. Munshi was a vital member of the Drafting Committee. Hence, Dr. Rajendra Prasad correctly held the Steering Committee post.

q: Which British mission in 1946 proposed the formation of a 'Constituent Assembly' and an 'Interim Government'?
exp: The Cabinet Mission (1946), sent by the British Prime Minister Clement Attlee, was highly successful in laying down the definitive blueprint for the transfer of power. It explicitly proposed the formation of a Constituent Assembly to draft India's constitution and an Interim Government comprising Indian leaders. The Simon Commission (1927) and Cripps Mission (1942) had previously failed. The Wavell Plan (1945) also failed at the Shimla Conference. Therefore, the Cabinet Mission is correct.

q: How many members initially constituted the Indian Constituent Assembly formed to draft the Constitution before membership reduced after the partition?
exp: The Indian Constituent Assembly, formed in 1946 under the precise framework of the Cabinet Mission Plan, initially possessed exactly 389 members representing undivided India. This included 296 seats from British Indian provinces and 93 from Princely States. Following the partition of India in 1947, the members representing territories that went to Pakistan withdrew, drastically reducing the effective assembly strength to 299. Therefore, 389 is the correct initial composition.

q: Who chaired the Constituent Assembly of India, overseeing the drafting of the Constitution, and later became the first President of independent India?
exp: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was unanimously elected as the permanent President (Chairman) of the Constituent Assembly of India on December 11, 1946. He masterfully guided and presided over the complex deliberations of the assembly that drafted the Indian Constitution over nearly three years. Upon the Constitution's adoption, he became the first President of the Republic of India in 1950. B.R. Ambedkar merely chaired the Drafting Committee. Nehru and Patel headed other specific sub-committees.

q: Who served as the chairman of the Constituent Assembly's Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee, responsible for drafting key civil liberties?
exp: Acharya J.B. Kripalani, a veteran freedom fighter, served efficiently as the Chairman of the Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee within the Constituent Assembly. His committee was instrumental in deliberating and structuring the core civil liberties embedded in Part III of the Constitution. Sardar Patel was the chairman of the broader Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal Areas, under which Kripalani's sub-committee operated. H.C. Mookherjee headed the Minorities Sub-Committee. G.V. Mavalankar was the first Lok Sabha Speaker.

q: On which date did the Constituent Assembly of undivided India hold its first official meeting to begin drafting the Constitution?
exp: Formed under the strict provisions of the Cabinet Mission Plan, the Constituent Assembly of undivided India convened for its historic, inaugural session exactly on 'December 9, 1946', at the Central Hall of Parliament in New Delhi. Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha temporarily presided over this foundational meeting as the oldest member, before Dr. Rajendra Prasad was officially elected President. November 26, 1949, marks the momentous day the finalized Constitution was formally adopted, not the starting date.

q: Who among the following was NOT a member of the Constituent Assembly?
exp: The incredibly monumental Constituent Assembly of India, rigorously tasked with the unimaginably complex and deeply historic responsibility of meticulously drafting the supreme Constitution for a newly liberated nation, comprised some of the absolute greatest legal, political, and intellectual minds of that tumultuous era. While iconic, globally recognized stalwarts like Dr. B.R. Ambedkar (who brilliantly chaired the pivotal Drafting Committee), the iron-willed Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, and the visionary Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru were extremely active, deeply instrumental leading figures within the assembly, the universally revered "Father of the Nation," Mahatma Gandhi, deliberately and consciously chose to remain completely outside of it. He fundamentally believed in grassroots village-level empowerment rather than formal, centralized institutional power structures, making option (c) the absolute correct historical answer.

q: On what date was the Constitution of India put into force?
exp: The incredibly monumental and historically unparalleled Constitution of India, which stands proudly today as the absolute longest meticulously written national constitution in the entire world, was officially formally adopted by the dedicated Constituent Assembly on November 26, 1949 (a date now highly celebrated as national Constitution Day). However, in order to deeply honor and fiercely commemorate the legendary 1930 historic declaration of 'Purna Swaraj' (Complete Independence) boldly made by the brave Indian National Congress in Lahore, the founding fathers deliberately waited. They officially and powerfully put the massive document into full legal force exactly two months later, on the grand, deeply auspicious date of January 26, 1950, permanently transforming India into a fully sovereign, vibrant Democratic Republic. Option (d) is definitively the accurate historical date.

q: Who was the first and temporary president of the Constitutional Assembly formed to draft the Constitution of India?
exp: During the incredibly historic and monumental inaugural session of the prestigious Constituent Assembly of India held firmly on December 9, 1946, there was an immediate administrative need for a presiding officer. Following a deeply respected French practice of formally honoring the most senior member present, the incredibly eminent, highly educated, and veteran parliamentarian Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha was respectfully elected as the absolute first and temporary (interim) President of the august Assembly. Option (c) is definitively the exact historical answer. Just two days later, Dr. Rajendra Prasad was officially and permanently elected to the presidential position. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar (b) famously chaired the separate, vital Drafting Committee. Sir B.N. Rau (a) served exceptionally as the Constitutional Advisor, while H.V.R. Iyengar (d) worked effectively as the Secretary of the Constituent Assembly.

q: The Constitution of India was adopted on:
exp: The Constitution of India was formally adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26th November 1949, a historic day now celebrated annually as Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas). However, it officially came into full legal force two months later on 26th January 1950 (Republic Day). 15th August 1947 marks India's Independence, and 9th December 1946 was the very first meeting of the Constituent Assembly. Differentiating between the "adoption" and "enforcement" dates is a classic tricky polity question.

q: The Objectives Resolution was moved in the Constituent Assembly by:
exp: The Objectives Resolution was introduced by Jawaharlal Nehru on December 13, 1946, during the first session of the Constituent Assembly. It laid down the fundamental philosophy and guiding principles for framing the Indian Constitution, emphasizing justice, equality, and freedom. This historic resolution eventually became the basis for the Preamble of the Indian Constitution. B.R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee, Vallabhbhai Patel led the Provincial Constitution Committee, and Rajendra Prasad was the President of the Assembly.

q: Who was the temporary chairman of the Constituent Assembly?
exp: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, the oldest member of the Constituent Assembly, was elected as its temporary (interim) Chairman on December 9, 1946, following the French practice. Just two days later, on December 11, 1946, Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected as the permanent President. B.N. Rau served as the Constitutional Advisor, while H.C. Mukherjee was the Vice-President of the Assembly. Knowing these specific roles is crucial for SSC polity questions.

q: As of July 2025, how many articles and parts does the Indian Constitution comprise (excluding repealed sections)?
exp: The Indian Constitution originally had 395 articles and 22 parts. With amendments over the years, the number of articles has increased to approximately 448, and the parts have increased to 25. While the last article is still numbered 395, new articles have been inserted as sub-sections (like 21A, 51A, etc.), making the total count 448.

q: Identify the correct option based on given statements: 1. Schedule VI applies to tribal areas in Assam and Tripura. 2. Autonomous Councils under Schedule VI can make laws on forest management. 3. Schedule VI is applicable to Jharkhand. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: The Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution contains provisions for the administration of Tribal Areas in the states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram (often remembered by the acronym ATM-M). Therefore, Statement 1 is correct, and Statement 3 is incorrect (Jharkhand is covered under the Fifth Schedule). The Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) created under this schedule have legislative powers on specific subjects, including forest management, land, and inheritance. Thus, Statement 2 is correct.

q: Identify the correct option based on given statements: Assertion (A): The Union Government alone can legislate on matters related to the deployment and jurisdiction of armed forces within Indian states. Reason (R): The Constitution includes the deployment of Union forces in aid of civil power, regulation of cantonments, and control over arms and atomic energy in the Union List. Select the correct option:
o: A and R are correct, and R is the correct reason for A
A and R both true, but R is not the appropriate explanation for A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
exp: Assertion (A) is correct because the deployment of armed forces of the Union is an exclusive subject of the Central Government. Reason (R) is also correct and explains the assertion: Entry 2A of the Union List (inserted by the 42nd Amendment) specifically empowers the Union to deploy its armed forces in any state in aid of civil power. Additionally, Entry 2, 4, and 5 cover naval/military forces, cantonments, and arms, granting the Union exclusive legislative competence over these areas.

q: How many schedules are there in the Indian Constitution?
exp: The Indian Constitution currently has 12 Schedules. Originally, when adopted in 1949, it contained only 8 Schedules. The 9th Schedule was added by the 1st Amendment (1951), the 10th by the 52nd Amendment (1985 - Anti-Defection), and the 11th and 12th by the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992 - Panchayats and Municipalities) respectively. Schedules serve as appendices to the Constitution, detailing lists and administrative provisions.

q: The division of powers between the Union (Central) Government and State Governments in India is a key feature of its constitutional structure. What term describes this system?
exp: The division of powers between the Union and States via the Seventh Schedule is a hallmark of a Federal system. In a federal setup, there are two levels of government, each drawing authority directly from the Constitution. While India is often described as "Quasi-federal" due to its strong centralizing tendency, the structural division of legislative, administrative, and financial powers is fundamentally a federal feature. Option (a) is incorrect because a unitary system concentrates all power in the center.

q: Which of the following statements about federalism in India is true?
o: States have the right to secede from the Union
There is rigid division of powers
exp: In the Indian federal system, the Union has overriding authority in many areas, earning it the label "Federal in form, Unitary in spirit". For example, in the Concurrent List, Union law prevails over State law in case of conflict. Additionally, residuary powers lie with the Centre, and the Parliament can alter state boundaries. Options (a) and (d) are incorrect because Indian states have no right to secede, and they are not sovereign entities (sovereignty lies with the people of India as a whole).

q: Which law prevails in case of a conflict between Union and State laws on a subject in the Concurrent List?
exp: According to Article 254 of the Constitution, if there is a confiict/repugnancy between a Union law and a State law on a subject in the Concurrent List, the Union law prevails, and the State law becomes void to the extent of the repugnancy. The only exception (Option b) is if the State law has been reserved for the President's consideration and has received his assent, in which case it prevails in that State (though Parliament can still override it later).

q: Which of the following topics falls under the State List as per the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India?
exp: Police and Public Order are subjects enumerated in the State List (List II) of the Seventh Schedule. This means state legislatures have the exclusive power to make laws regarding the police forces and maintenance of law and order within their territories. Options (a), (b), and (c) (Defense, Foreign Affairs, Currency) are core subjects of the Union List (List I), ensuring a uniform policy across the nation for security and economy.

q: What is the supreme law of India?
exp: The Indian Constitution is the supreme law of the land (Lex Loci). All other laws, executive orders, and government actions must conform to the Constitution; otherwise, they can be declared void by the judiciary. It defines the powers and limitations of the Parliament, Executive, and Judiciary. Option (b) is incorrect because Parliament is a creature of the Constitution and is not sovereign in the British sense; its laws are subject to judicial review.

q: Which of the following subjects are included in the 'Union List/Center List' in the Indian Constitution?
exp: National Defense and Foreign Affairs are quintessential Union List subjects. These matters require a unified national policy and cannot be left to individual states. Option (a) Police is in the State List. Option (c) Education is in the Concurrent List (transferred from State List by the 42nd Amendment), and Local Government is in the State List. Option (d) Agriculture is generally a State subject. The Union List contains 100 items (originally 97) of national importance.

q: Which Schedule of the Constitution contains the distribution of powers between Union and States?
exp: The Seventh Schedule of the Constitution contains the three legislative lists: the Union List, State List, and Concurrent List, which distribute legislative powers between the Union and the States. This schedule works in conjunction with Article 246. Option (a) Sixth Schedule deals with Tribal Areas. Option (c) Eighth Schedule lists official languages. Option (d) Tenth Schedule deals with the Anti-Defection Law.

q: When there is a disagreement between Union and State laws on a matter listed in the Concurrent List, which law takes precedence?
exp: Under the doctrine of repugnancy enshrined in Article 254, Union Law takes precedence over State Law on matters in the Concurrent List. This ensures uniformity in basic legal principles across the country while allowing states some flexibility. As noted in previous explanations, the State law can only prevail if it has received the President's assent, but even then, Parliament retains the power to enact a law adding to, amending, varying, or repealing the law so made by the State.

q: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with respect to the Schedules of the Indian Constitution?
o: Eleventh Schedule - Powers and responsibilities of Panchayats
Twelfth Schedule - Election of President and Vice-President
Tenth Schedule - Languages recognised by the Constitution
Ninth Schedule - Allocation of powers between Union and States
exp: The correct match is (a). The Eleventh Schedule, added by the 73rd Amendment Act (1992), specifies the 29 functional items placed within the purview of Panchayats. Option (b) is incorrect; the 12th Schedule deals with Municipalities. Option (c) is incorrect; the 10th Schedule is the Anti-Defection Law (Languages are in the 8th). Option (d) is incorrect; the 9th Schedule protects acts from judicial scrutiny (Allocation of powers is in the 7th).

q: Which of these is not a feature of Indian federalism?
exp: Dual Citizenship is not a feature of Indian federalism. Unlike the USA, where a person is a citizen of both the country and their specific state, the Indian Constitution provides for single citizenship for the entire country. Options (a), (b), and (d) are essential features of federalism present in India: an independent judiciary to interpret the constitution, a written constitution defining powers, and the division of powers between the Centre and States.

q: Which of the following statements based on the Union List entries is/are correct? conducted by both the Central and State governments. 2. Matters related to the incorporation and regulation of cooperative societies are included in the Union List. 3. The Reserve Bank of India, foreign exchange, and currency are all under the legislative domain of the Union. 4. Parliament can make laws regarding corporations whose activities are not limited to one State, excluding universities. Select the correct option:
o: All four statements 1, 2, 3 and 4 are correct
exp: Statements 1, 3, and 4 are correct. Lotteries organized by the Govt of India or a State are Entry 40 of the Union List. RBI and Currency are Entries 36 and 38. Regulation of corporations with multi-state objects is Entry 44. Statement 2 is incorrect because "Cooperative Societies" generally fall under the State List (Entry 32), except for Multi-State Co- operative Societies, which are Union.

q: Read the statements given below: Statement 1: The Constitution of India divides the legislative subjects into 3 lists, namely the Centre, State and Concurrent List. Statement 2: The subject of 'Protection of wild animals and birds' is transferred to the Concurrent list from the State list by the 42nd Amendment Act. Statement 3: Only the Parliament of India can make laws on the subjects under the Concurrent List. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
o: All three statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct
exp: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Constitution divides powers into three lists (Statement 1). The 42nd Amendment Act (1976) transferred five subjects, including 'Protection of wild animals and birds', from the State List to the Concurrent List (Statement 2). Statement 3 is incorrect because the Concurrent List allows both the Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws.

q: Which of the following North-Eastern states has areas governed under the Sixth Schedule?
exp: The Sixth Schedule applies to the Tribal Areas in four specific North-Eastern states: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram. Therefore, Tripura is the correct answer. Manipur, Nagaland, and Arunachal Pradesh are not covered under the Sixth Schedule (though Manipur has some Hill Councils, they are under different acts, and Nagaland has special provisions under Art 371A).

q: Consider the following statements: Statement I: Land and agriculture fall under the State List. Statement II: Marriage laws and adoption fall under the Concurrent List. Select the correct option:
o: Both statements I and II are correct
Neither statement I nor II is correct
exp: Both statements are correct. Land (Entry 18) and Agriculture (Entry 14) are prominent subjects in the State List, giving states control over land tenure and farming. Marriage, Divorce, and Adoption (Entry 5) fall under the Concurrent List, allowing for a unified personal law code (like the Hindu Marriage Act) while permitting state- specific variations.

q: Which body has the power to amend the Union and State power distribution under the Indian Constitution?
exp: The Parliament of India has the power to amend the Constitution, including the distribution of powers between the Union and States. However, such an amendment (affecting the 7th Schedule or federal provisions) requires a special majority in Parliament and ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures under Article 368. The Supreme Court cannot amend the Constitution; it can only interpret it.

q: Which of the following statements is correct in the context of constitutional interpretation and judicial doctrine?
o: The Constitution of India clearly defines the term 'basic structure' under Article 368.
The Judiciary rejected the idea of spirit-based interpretation and strictly follows the written text.
The 'basic structure' doctrine was brought into existence by the Supreme Court to protect the fundamental features of the Constitution
The Parliament can propose amendments that repeal judicial principles without limitation.
exp: The 'Basic Structure' doctrine was judicially innovated by the Supreme Court in the landmark Kesavananda Bharati case (1973). It holds that Parliament cannot alter the fundamental features (basic structure) of the Constitution, such as democracy, secularism, and federalism. Option (a) is incorrect as the term is not found in the text of the Constitution. Option (d) is incorrect because the doctrine specifically limits Parliament's amending power.

q: Match the following Schedules of the Indian Constitution with their respective features: Schedule Feature 1. First Schedule a. Allocation of powers and responsibilities between Union and States 2. Third Schedule b. Forms of Oaths or Affirmations 3. Fifth Schedule c. Administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Tribes... 4. Seventh Schedule d. Names of the States and Union Territories...
exp: The correct matching is 1-d, 2-b, 3-c, 4-a. First Schedule: Lists the States and UTs and their territories. Third Schedule: Contains the forms of Oaths and Affirmations for officeholders. Fifth Schedule: Provisions for the administration of Scheduled Areas (other than the 4 NE states). Seventh Schedule: Division of powers (Union, State, Concurrent Lists).

q: The 'emoluments, allowances, and privileges of constitutional officeholders' are governed under which Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
exp: The Second Schedule of the Indian Constitution deals with the emoluments, allowances, privileges, and so on of Constitutional dignitaries. This includes the President, Governors, Speaker/Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha and State Assemblies, Chairman/Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils, Judges of SC/HC, and the CAG.

q: Which list allows both Centre and State to legislate on the same subject?
exp: The Concurrent List (List III) contains subjects on which both the Parliament and State Legislatures have the power to make laws. This list includes items like criminal law, education, forests, and marriage. It acts as a "twilight zone" to ensure uniformity while respecting diversity. If there is a conflict, the Central law generally prevails.

q: Read the below statements related to Concurrent List laws: 1. Union law overrides state law in conflict. 2. State law can prevail if reserved and assented by President. Select the correct option:
exp: Both statements are correct. The general rule under Article 254(1) is that Union law overrides conflicting State law on a Concurrent List subject. However, Article 254(2) provides an exception: if the State law has been reserved for the President's consideration and has received his assent, it will prevail in that State over the earlier Union law.

q: The Indian Constitution is often described as 'quasi-federal' or 'federal in form, unitary in spirit' primarily due to which characteristic?
o: The equal representation of states in the Rajya Sabha.
The presence of a written constitution.
Strong centralizing tendencies and powers of the Union Government.
exp: India is described as 'Quasi-federal' because of its strong centralizing tendencies. While it has federal features like division of powers, the Centre has dominant powers: it appoints Governors, can change state boundaries, has residuary powers, and can convert the system into a unitary one during emergencies. Also, unlike the US Senate, Rajya Sabha does not have equal representation for all states.

q: The system of federalism in India divides power between:
exp: Federalism is defined by the vertical division of power between the Centre (Union) and the States. This ensures that both levels of government have their own sphere of authority derived from the Constitution. Option (b) is division within the legislature (bicameralism). Option (d) is horizontal separation of powers.

q: The power to legislate on 'Residuary Subjects' (matters not enumerated in any of the three Lists) rests exclusively with:
exp: The power to legislate on Residuary Subjects (subjects not mentioned in the Union, State, or Concurrent Lists) vests exclusively with the Parliament under Article 248. Examples include cyber laws and space exploration. This is a departure from the American or Australian model and follows the Canadian model, reflecting the Indian Constitution's bias towards a strong Centre.

q: The provision for 'Oath or Affirmation' by members of the legislature is mentioned in which Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
exp: The Third Schedule of the Constitution contains the Forms of Oaths or Affirmations for various constitutional offices, including Union Ministers, MPs, Judges, and State Legislators. Option (a) Second allocates seats in the Rajya Sabha. Option (c) Fifth Schedule deals with Scheduled Areas.

q: Education is now placed under which list after the 42nd Amendment?
exp: Education was transferred from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1976. This change empowered the Central Government to legislate on education to ensure uniform standards and national integration, while still allowing states to have a role. Other subjects transferred included forests, weights and measures, and protection of wild animals.

q: Which of the following statements regarding Article 270 are correct? 1. Governs sharing of taxes including GST. 2. Includes provisions for revenue distribution after 101st Amendment. 3. GST Compensation Cess is shared under Article 270. Select the correct option:
exp: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Article 270 governs the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and States. After the 101st Amendment, it explicitly includes the Union's share of GST. Statement 3 is incorrect because cesses levied for a specific purpose (like the GST Compensation Cess) are excluded from the divisible pool of taxes under Article 270(1) and are not shared with states in the general sense.

q: Schedule VII of the Constitution contains:
exp: Schedule VII contains the three legislative lists: Union List (List I), State List (List II), and Concurrent List (List III). This schedule is the backbone of the federal distribution of legislative powers in India. It enumerates the specific subjects on which the Parliament and State Legislatures can make laws.

q: Which reflects the legal implication of Article 255 regarding assent to bills?
o: Omission of prior recommendation cured by assent
exp: Article 255 provides that no Act of Parliament or a State Legislature shall be invalid strictly because a required prior recommendation or sanction (e.g., from the President or Governor) was omitted, provided that the Act eventually received the necessary assent. Essentially, the final assent cures the procedural defect of missing the prior recommendation.

q: Article 246A gives power to both Parliament and State to make laws on:
exp: Article 246A, introduced by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, grants special powers to both the Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws with respect to the Goods and Services Tax (GST) imposed by the Union or by such State. This overrides the traditional division where Centre taxed manufacture/services and States taxed sales. It is a unique concurrent power for GST.

q: Which statement regarding legislative power distribution is correct?
o: State can legislate on Union List
Union needs State approval for Concurrent
Union can issue directions to States (Art 256)
Union/States have equal power on Union List
exp: The correct statement is (c). Under Article 256, the executive power of every State must be exercised so as to ensure compliance with laws made by Parliament, and the Union executive can issue directions to a State to ensure this. Options (a) and (d) are false; the Union List is exclusive to Parliament. Option (b) is false; Parliament does not need State approval to legislate on the Concurrent List.

q: Under Article 262, what is Parliament's authority regarding inter-State water disputes?
o: Set up tribunals and bar SC review
exp: Article 262 empowers Parliament to adjudicate disputes relating to waters of inter-state rivers. Crucially, Article 262(2) allows Parliament to provide that neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in respect of any such dispute. Parliament enacted the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956, setting up tribunals for this purpose.

q: Under which Article is Hindi in Devanagari declared official language?
exp: Article 343(1) of the Indian Constitution declares that the official language of the Union shall be Hindi in Devanagari script. It also stated that English would continue to be used for official purposes for 15 years (later extended indefinitely by the Official Languages Act). Article 351 deals with the directive to promote Hindi, while Article 348 deals with language in the Supreme Court and High Courts.

q: Which of the following is correct regarding State law on Concurrent List? 1. State law with President's assent overrides Union law 2. Parliament cannot nullify such law Select the correct option:
o: State law with President's assent overrides Union law
exp: Statement 1 is correct: Under Article 254(2), a State law on a Concurrent subject, if reserved for and assented to by the President, prevails over an earlier conflicting Union law in that State. Statement 2 is incorrect because the proviso to Article 254(2) explicitly states that Parliament can still enact a law adding to, amending, varying, or repealing such a State law.

q: Consider the following: 1. Indian federalism is biased towards the Centre. 2. Constitution uses the word 'federal' explicitly. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Only Statement 1 is correct. Indian federalism is structurally biased towards the Centre (e.g., appointment of Governors, emergency powers, single citizenship). Statement 2 is incorrect because the word 'Federal' is nowhere used in the Constitution. Article 1 describes India as a "Union of States," a deliberate choice by Dr. Ambedkar to emphasize that the Union is indestructible.

q: What does Article 268 primarily deal with?
o: Service tax by Union, collected by State
Stamp duties by Union, collected by State
exp: Article 268 deals with Stamp Duties (and duties of excise on medicinal/toilet preparations) which are levied by the Union but collected and appropriated by the States. The proceeds of these duties do not form part of the Consolidated Fund of India but are assigned to the State where they are collected.

q: Consider the following: 1. Sixth Schedule is applicable to Nagaland and Arunachal. 2. Empowers autonomous district councils. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Only Statement 2 is correct. The Sixth Schedule empowers the creation of Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) with legislative and judicial powers. Statement 1 is incorrect because the Sixth Schedule applies only to Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram. Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh are not covered under the Sixth Schedule.

q: Consider the following: 1. Article 262 empowers Parliament to set up tribunals for river disputes. 2. SC has appellate jurisdiction in such disputes. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Only Statement 1 is correct. Article 262(1) empowers Parliament to adjudicate inter-state river water disputes (often done via tribunals). Statement 2 is incorrect because Article 262(2) explicitly allows Parliament to exclude the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and other courts in these disputes. The Inter-State Water Disputes Act bars the SC's jurisdiction.

q: Under Article 258A, what power is granted to States?
o: States need Presidential assent to assign functions
Governor entrusts State functions to the Union
State Govt assign Union functions to officers
exp: Article 258A (inserted by the 7th Constitutional Amendment, 1956) provides that the Governor of a State may, with the consent of the Government of India, entrust — either conditionally or unconditionally — to the Union Government or to its officers, functions relating to any matter to which the executive power of the State extends. It is the mirror provision of Article 258, under which the President entrusts Union functions to a State. So under 258A the direction is State → Union: the Governor entrusts State functions to the Union.

q: Consider the following: 1. Article 300 allows legal suits against State Govts. 2. 'Government of India' is a legal entity under Art 300. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Both statements are correct. Article 300 declares that the Government of India may sue or be sued by the name of the Union of India and the Government of a State may sue or be sued by the name of the State. It establishes their juristic personality (Statement 2) and allows for legal suits against them (Statement 1) regarding their respective affairs.

q: Taxes on interstate trade are restricted by Article ______ unless Parliament provides otherwise.
exp: Article 286 restricts the power of a State to impose a tax on the supply of goods or services where such supply takes place outside the State or in the course of inter-state trade or commerce. States cannot tax inter-state trade; that power (IGST) lies with the Parliament (Article 269A). Before GST, Art 286 specifically barred sales tax on inter-state sales.

q: What is the role of Article 263?
exp: Article 263 empowers the President to establish an Inter- State Council to inquire into and advise upon disputes between states, and to investigate and discuss subjects of common interest. It provides the constitutional framework for coordination between States and the Centre. Option (b) is incorrect; Zonal Councils are statutory bodies, not constitutional ones.

q: The ______ List in Schedule VII deals with defence and foreign affairs.
exp: The Union List (List I) deals with subjects of national importance such as Defence, Foreign Affairs, Atomic Energy, and Railways. Legislative power over these subjects is exclusively vested in the Parliament to ensure the sovereignty and security of the nation are maintained through a single, unified policy.

q: Grants-in-Aid to States are provided under Article ______.
exp: Article 275 empowers the Parliament to make Grants-in-Aid from the Consolidated Fund of India to such States as Parliament may determine to be in need of assistance. These are statutory grants, distinct from discretionary grants (Article 282). Option (b) Article 280 constitutes the Finance Commission, which recommends these grants.

q: Consider the following: 1. Art 263 empowers Parliament to establish ISC. 2. Council can investigate disputes. 3. Composition includes PM. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. The Inter-State Council (ISC) can investigate and discuss subjects of common interest (Statement 2), and its composition includes the Prime Minister as Chairman (Statement 3). Statement 1 is incorrect because Article 263 empowers the President, not the Parliament, to establish the council. The ISC was set up by a Presidential Order in 1990.

q: Consider the following on State borrowing: 1. State requires Centre consent if debt exists. 2. No external loans without Union approval. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Both statements are correct. Under Article 293(3), a State may not raise any loan without the consent of the Government of India if there is any outstanding loan owed to the GOI. Furthermore, States have no independent power to raise loans from external (foreign) sources; they must do so through the Union.

q: Consider the following: 1. Art 246A gives exclusive power to Parliament on GST. 2. States have no power on intra-state GST. 3. GST Council is under Art 279A. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Only Statement 3 is correct. The GST Council is constituted by the President under Article 279A. Statement 1 is incorrect because Article 246A confers simultaneous (concurrent) power on both Parliament and State Legislatures to levy GST.
