exp: According to the strict provisions of Article 61 of the Indian Constitution, the President of India can solely and exclusively be impeached by the Parliament, and strictly on the singular ground of "violation of the Constitution." The rigorous impeachment motion can be actively initiated by either house of the Parliament (the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha) after meeting a heavy majority requirement. The Prime Minister, the Supreme Court, and the Election Commission possess absolutely no constitutional power or legal authority to directly impeach the President.

q: Who serves as the nominal (titular) head of the executive in the Union Government of India?
exp: In the Union Government of India, the President serves as the nominal (titular) or constitutional head of the executive, in accordance with Article 53 of the Constitution. All executive actions are formally taken in the name of the President. The Prime Minister, however, is the real executive authority (de facto head). The other options are incorrect. The Chief Justice of India heads the judiciary, not the executive. Understanding the difference between the nominal head (President) and the real executive head (Prime Minister) is a fundamental concept in Indian polity.

q: Who is the constitutional head of the Union Government of India?
exp: Under the robust framework of the Indian Constitution, the President is designated as the supreme constitutional and formal executive head of the Union Government. According to Article 53, the executive power of the Union is strictly vested in the President. However, the President is a nominal or 'de jure' head, executing these vast powers on the binding aid and advice of the Council of Ministers. The other options occupy different roles. The Prime Minister is the 'de facto' or real executive head who actively drives the government. The Cabinet Secretary is the topmost civil servant in the nation.

q: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes between the clemency powers of the President of India and the President of the United States as per their respective constitutional frameworks and judicial interpretations?
o: The President of India can grant clemency only in cases involving sentences of death, whereas the President of the USA has unlimited power to pardon any federal offense including civil cases.

The President of India's clemency powers under Article 72 are subject to judicial review regarding the procedure followed, while the President of the USA's pardon power under Article II, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution is absolute and not reviewable by courts.
Both Presidents can grant pardons only on the advice of the Council of Ministers or Cabinet, ensuring executive accountability.
The President of India's clemency powers are limited to cases where convictions occur under central laws, while the President of the USA can grant clemency only in cases tried by state courts.
exp: The key distinction lies in the scope and judicial oversight of their powers. Under Article 72 of the Indian Constitution, the President grants clemency on the advice of the Council of Ministers, and the Supreme Court has ruled (e.g., Epuru Sudhakar case) that this power is subject to limited judicial review to prevent arbitrariness or procedural lapses. Conversely, the U.S. President's pardon power under Article II is virtually absolute for federal offenses and cannot be reviewed or overturned by the courts or Congress. The other options are factually incorrect regarding the scope of their respective powers.

q: Consider the following statements regarding the current Vice President of India: 1. Chandrapuram Ponnusami (CP) Radhakrishnan is the Vice President of India, took charge on 12th September 2025. 2. Unlike the Presidential election, the electoral college for the Vice President includes nominated members of both Houses of Parliament. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Both statements are correct. C.P. Radhakrishnan assumed office as the 15th Vice President of India on 12th September 2025, succeeding Jagdeep Dhankhar. Constitutionally, the electoral college for the Vice President differs from the President’s; it includes all members of the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, specifically including nominated members. As the Vice President, he also serves as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, presiding over the upper house’s legislative proceedings and maintaining parliamentary decorum.

q: The ordinance-making power of the President is equivalent to
o: Judicial Power of the Supreme Court
Executive Power of the Prime Minister
exp: Enshrined meticulously in Article 123 of the Indian Constitution, the extraordinary power of the President to urgently promulgate Ordinances (during parliamentary recess) is absolutely and legally co-extensive with the "Legislative Power of the Parliament." This means any validly issued presidential ordinance fiercely carries the exact same supreme legal force, profound effect, and rigid constitutional limitations as a regular, fully debated Act aggressively passed by both sovereign houses of the Indian Parliament.

q: When the office of the president remain vacant, what is the deadline to conduct new election and appoint new president?
exp: According to Article 62(2) of the Indian Constitution, if the highest office of the President falls prematurely vacant due to sudden death, resignation, or formal impeachment, an election to fill that crucial vacancy must be conducted as soon as possible, and strictly in no case later than six months from the date of the vacancy occurring. During this six- month interim period, the Vice-President acts as the acting President.

q: Which Article grants the President the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions, or commute sentences in certain cases?
exp: Article 72 of the Indian Constitution empowers the President of India with pardoning powers, including reprieves, respites, remissions, and commuting sentences, especially for court-martials and death sentences. Article 73 deals with the executive power of the Union. Article 76 provides for the Attorney General of India. Article 161 gives similar pardoning powers to the Governor of a state, but not for death sentences or military courts. Thus, Article 72 is correct.

q: The final authority to decide disputes related to the election of the President of India lies with:
exp: According to Article 71 of the Indian Constitution, all doubts and disputes arising out of or in connection with the election of a President or Vice-President shall be inquired into and decided exclusively by the Supreme Court, whose decision shall be final. The Election Commission conducts the elections but cannot adjudicate election disputes for these top offices. The Vice President and Parliament have no judicial authority over this matter.

q: Commutation, remission, reprieve and other forms of clemency granted to convicted individuals fall under which category of constitutional powers exercised by the President?
exp: Under Article 72 of the Indian Constitution, the President possesses the exclusive, sovereign 'Pardoning Power' which legally entitles them to grant pardons, reprieves (delay in execution), respites (lesser sentence), remissions (reducing period), or commutations (substituting penalty type) to individuals convicted of offenses, especially death sentences. This acts as an ultimate executive check to correct judicial errors. Emergency, legislative (ordinances), and administrative powers deal with separate, distinct constitutional governance mechanisms.

q: Which of the following is not a discretionary power of the President?
exp: The President of India lacks discretionary power when it comes to Money Bills. A Money Bill requires the prior recommendation of the President before introduction, making it mandatory for them to give assent when it is passed; they cannot return it. Option (d) is correct. Returning an ordinary bill for reconsideration (a) is a suspensive veto. Sending messages to Parliament (b) is a constitutional right. The Appointment of PM (c) becomes fully discretionary only when no party secures a clear majority in the Lok Sabha.

q: Which authority decides on doubts and disputes relating to the election of the president?
exp: Under the strict legal framework established by Article 71 of the Indian Constitution, all complex doubts and heated disputes arising out of or directly connected with the critical election of the President or Vice-President are exclusively inquired into and decisively settled solely by the Supreme Court of India. Its final sweeping judgment on such presidential election matters is absolutely final and binding on all parties. Option (a) is the accurate constitutional answer. The overarching Parliament (b), the organizing Election Commission (c), and the presiding Speaker of Lok Sabha (d) hold absolutely zero jurisdictional authority to adjudicate these specific high-level constitutional disputes.

q: The president submits resignation to:
exp: Under the rigid, highly formalized, and meticulously structured framework of the Indian Constitution, the President of India occupies the absolute highest ceremonial office in the nation. However, if the President deliberately chooses to prematurely voluntarily vacate this supreme position before the completion of their standard five-year term, Article 56 explicitly dictates the precise legal procedure. The President must formally address and systematically submit their official, hand- written letter of resignation directly to the Vice-President of India. Upon receiving this critical document, the Vice-President is constitutionally obligated to immediately communicate this highly significant development to the Speaker of the Lok Sabha. Option (b) is correct.

q: Under Article 77 of the Constitution, the executive actions of the Government of India shall be expressed to be taken in the name of:
exp: Under the incredibly rigid, highly formalized, and deeply ceremonial constitutional framework governing India's massive administrative apparatus, Article 77 establishes a strict, absolute protocol for executing supreme national authority. It explicitly, powerfully mandates that absolutely every single formal executive action, massive powerful Central Government of India must legally and officially be expressed as being taken exclusively in the solemn name of the President of India. While the remarkably powerful Prime Minister and their robust Council of Ministers indisputably wield the actual, tangible, day-to-day political executive power, the President remains the absolute supreme, official constitutional head of state. Option (b) perfectly describes this profound constitutional requirement, thoroughly overriding the operational roles of the PM (d) or Cabinet Secretary (a).

q: Who appoints the governor of a state?
exp: As mandated by Article 155 of the Indian Constitution, the Governor of a State is officially appointed directly by the President of India by warrant under his hand and seal. The Governor acts as the central government's representative and holds office strictly during the pleasure of the President. The Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor. Neither the Parliament nor the Prime Minister possesses the direct constitutional authority to appoint state governors.

q: Under which circumstances the President can promulgate an ordinance under Article 123?
o: Both houses are prorogued or adjourned sine die.
exp: Article 123 explicitly grants the President of India the powerful legislative capability to promulgate an ordinance solely when either one or both Houses of Parliament are not in session, and immediate action is deemed urgently necessary. An ordinance has the exact same force as an Act of Parliament. If the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the government cannot pass ordinances arbitrarily without parliamentary oversight capability. "Parliament is not in session" accurately covers the constitutional prerequisite.

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution specifies the procedure for impeaching the President?
exp: Article 61 of the Indian Constitution outlines the strict procedure for the impeachment of the President, strictly on the grounds of "violation of the Constitution." The charge can be initiated by either house of Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha) with a special majority (two-thirds of the total membership). The provided options (70, 72, 68) were factually incorrect.

q: The President of India is elected by which method?
exp: Article 54 of the Indian Constitution specifies that the President is elected by an Electoral College. This college consists of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States, including Delhi and Puducherry. Option (c) is correct. The President is not chosen through Direct election (a) by citizens, nor solely by Nomination (b) without voting. A Lottery system (d) is entirely unconstitutional and irrelevant to India's democratic framework.

q: Which statement regarding Council of Ministers (COM) is correct?
o: Union COM is collectively accountable to LS
State COM is accountable to Legislative Council
exp: Statement (a) is correct because Article 75(3) of the Indian Constitution explicitly states that the Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People (Lok Sabha). This means they swim or sink together. Statement (b) is incorrect because the State Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha), not the Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad), as per Article 164(2). Therefore, option (c) and (d) are also invalid. A key fact is that "collective responsibility" implies that a vote of no confidence against a single minister leads to the resignation of the entire council.

q: Consider the following: 1. PM and CM can advise dissolution of respective Lower House. 2. Only PM can recommend President's Rule. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
exp: Only Statement 1 is correct. The Prime Minister advises the President to dissolve the Lok Sabha (Article 85), and the Chief Minister advises the Governor to dissolve the State Assembly (Article 174), provided they enjoy a majority. Statement 2 is incorrect because the recommendation for imposing President's Rule (Article 356) usually comes from the Governor of the state via a report to the President, not the Prime Minister alone (though the Union Cabinet advises the President to act on it). The Governor's report is the constitutional basis for satisfaction.

q: Who served as the Prime Minister of India from 1991 to 1996?
exp: P.V. Narasimha Rao served as the Prime Minister of India from 1991 to 1996. His tenure is historically significant for dismantling the License Raj and introducing major economic liberalization policies. Option (a) Charan Singh served briefly in 1979-80. Option (b) Rajiv Gandhi served from 1984 to 1989. Option (c) Gulzarilal Nanda served as acting PM twice (1964, 1966). A notable fact is that Rao was the first Prime Minister from South India and was fluent in over 17 languages.

q: For how long a person can serve as a minister without being a member of either House of Parliament of India?
exp: According to Article 75(5) of the Constitution, a person can remain a minister for a maximum period of six consecutive months without being a member of either House of Parliament. If they are not elected to either the Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha within this period, they cease to be a minister. Options (b), (c), and (d) are incorrect durations. This provision allows the Prime Minister to induct experts or non-political figures into the cabinet, such as Dr. Manmohan Singh or S. Jaishankar, who were later elected to the Rajya Sabha.

q: What subject does Article 77 of the Indian Constitution pertain to?
o: Conduct of business of the Government of India
Council of Ministers to aid and advise President
exp: Article 77 deals with the Conduct of Business of the Government of India. It states that all executive action of the Government of India shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the President. Option (a) refers to Article 88. Option (b) refers to Article 78 (Duties of PM). Option (d) refers to Article 74 (Council of Ministers to aid and advise). Under Article 77(3), the President makes rules for the convenient transaction of government business (Allocation of Business Rules).

q: Which of the following statements best explains the dual role of the Prime Minister of India as both the leader of the Council of Ministers and the chief coordinator between the executive and the President, highlighting the extent and limits of his/her constitutional powers?
o: The Prime Minister can independently appoint and dismiss ministers without consulting the President or the Cabinet

The Prime Minister acts as the principal advisor to the President, heading the Council of Ministers, and exercises real executive authority, but all decisions require formal approval from the President who can refuse the Prime Minister's advice.

The Prime Minister leads the Council of Ministers, advises the President on appointment and dismissal of ministers, and directs policy, but formally exercises power only through the President, who generally acts on the Prime Minister's advice except in exceptional circumstances
The Prime Minister has absolute authority to make all executive decisions and can override the President's constitutional powers at will.
exp: Under Article 74 of the Indian Constitution, the Prime Minister heads the Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President. While the Prime Minister holds the real executive power (de facto), all executive actions are formally taken in the name of the President (de jure head). The President generally acts on the advice of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers, making the Prime Minister the most powerful figure, though formally operating through the President. The Prime Minister cannot independently appoint ministers without the President's formal assent, nor can the President arbitrarily refuse advice except under specific constitutional situations.

q: In the Union Government of India, who is considered the real executive authority and head of the Council of Ministers?
exp: In the deeply rooted parliamentary system of the Indian Union Government, the Prime Minister functions as the 'de facto' or real executive authority, actively heading the Council of Ministers and driving national policy. According to Article 74 of the Constitution, the Council of Ministers, with the Prime Minister at the helm, exists to aid and forcefully advise the President. The other options hold different constitutional roles. The President is merely the 'de jure' (nominal) head of state. The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The Cabinet Secretary is the highest-ranking civil servant, not a political executive.

q: Which of the following statements regarding Cabinet Committees in India is incorrect?
o: Cabinet Committees are extra- constitutional bodies established for administrative convenience.
The Prime Minister has the authority to constitute Cabinet Committees and alter their composition.
The Cabinet Committee on Security is always chaired by the Home Minister.
Cabinet Committees can include non-Cabinet Ministers as special invitees.
exp: The statement that the Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) is always chaired by the Home Minister is completely incorrect. The Prime Minister of India explicitly chairs the immensely powerful Cabinet Committee on Security, which makes all final statutory decisions on India's defense expenditure, national security apparatus, and strategic foreign policy matters. The Home Minister is a key member, not the chair. The other statements are correct: Cabinet Committees are indeed extra- constitutional bodies created under the Transaction of Business Rules to reduce the massive workload of the Cabinet, and the Prime Minister has full authority to configure them.

q: Which Article deals with the extent of executive power of the Union, defining the scope and limitations of the Union Government's authority in administration?
exp: Note: Fourth option added for completeness. Article 73 of the Indian Constitution strictly outlines the absolute extent of the executive power vested in the Union Government. It explicitly states that the central executive power extends powerfully to all complex matters with respect to which the Parliament has the supreme power to make laws, effectively ensuring that the Union's administrative authority perfectly mirrors its immense legislative jurisdiction.

q: Which of the following constitutional amendments made the Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha?
o: Not by amendment; it's already in the constitution
exp: The fundamental democratic principle that the Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible strictly to the House of the People (Lok Sabha) was not added by any later amendment. It has been an absolute, bedrock provision deeply ingrained in the original, unamended Indian Constitution since its inception in 1950, specifically enshrined under Article 75(3). This ensures the executive remains perpetually accountable to the directly elected legislature.

q: Which Article enshrines the the principle of collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha, making them accountable as a group for policy decisions?
exp: Article 75(3) of the Indian Constitution is the bedrock of the parliamentary system in India, explicitly stating that "The Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People (Lok Sabha)." This ensures that the government acts as a unified body and must maintain the confidence of the lower house. Article 74(1) deals with advising the President. Articles 73 and 77 deal with the executive power and conduct of business of the Union.

q: Who is the first woman Prime Minister of India?
exp: Indira Gandhi was the first and, to date, the only female Prime Minister of India, serving from 1966 to 1977 and again from 1980 until her assassination in 1984. She played a pivotal role in historical events like the 1971 Indo-Pak war and the Green Revolution. Pratibha Patil was the first female President of India. Sarojini Naidu was the first female Governor of an Indian state (UP). Rajkumari Amrit Kaur was the first Health Minister in independent India's cabinet.

q: What is the minimum age to become the Prime Minister of India?
exp: To become the Prime Minister of India, a person must strictly be a citizen of India and a member of either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha. Since the minimum age to become a Lok Sabha member is 25 years, this practically translates to the absolute minimum age required to become the Prime Minister. Option (a) is correct. The age of 30 years is required for the Rajya Sabha. The age of 35 years is the minimum requirement for the President and Vice-President. 18 is the voting age.

q: Who was the first finance minister of independent India?
exp: Sir R. K. Shanmukham Chetty, a brilliant Indian lawyer, industrialist, and highly capable economist, historically served as the absolute first Finance Minister of an independent India from 1947 to 1948. He achieved the monumental task of presenting the newly liberated nation's very first Union Budget on November 26, 1947. Option (d) is definitively the correct answer. Jawaharlal Nehru (a) was the first Prime Minister, handling External Affairs. John Mathai (not C.D. Deshmukh who was RBI governor) soon succeeded Chetty. Morarji Desai (c) holds the record for presenting the maximum number of budgets but came much later.

q: The Constitution prescribes that Union Ministers are collectively responsible to:
exp: In the incredibly complex, rigidly structured, and highly robust democratic framework of the Indian parliamentary system, the absolute bedrock, fundamental defining principle is the massive, unshakeable doctrine of "collective responsibility." According to the strict, explicitly clear legal mandate embedded deeply within Article 75(3) of the Indian Constitution, the entire Council of Ministers (the powerful central Union Cabinet) is exclusively, continuously, and collectively responsible directly to the Lok Sabha (the powerful Lower House of the People), and absolutely not to the broader, generalized Parliament or the ceremonial President. This essentially implies that the sitting government can only legally survive and wield immense executive power as long as it successfully maintains the total, unbroken confidence and massive majority support specifically of the directly elected Lok Sabha. Option (c) is perfectly correct.

q: Under which constitutional provision is the principle of Collective Responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha contained?
exp: Article 75(3) of the Indian Constitution explicitly states that the Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People (Lok Sabha). This means the entire ministry acts as a single team; if a no-confidence motion is passed against one minister, the entire council must resign. Article 74(1) deals with the Council aiding and advising the President, while Article 77 deals with the conduct of government business.

q: Under what circumstances can the Parliament legislate on a subject in the State List?
o: When Rajya Sabha passes a resolution
exp: Parliament can legislate on a subject in the State List if the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) passes a resolution by a two-thirds majority declaring it necessary in the national interest, under Article 249. This resolution remains in force for one year. Option (a) and (d) do not grant such legislative power. Option (b) allows the Centre to give financial directions but does not automatically transfer legislative power over the State List (unlike National Emergency under Art 352). This provision highlights the Rajya Sabha's role as the protector of federal/state rights.

q: If someone becomes a minister or the Prime Minister without being a Member of Parliament, they must get elected to the Parliament within ______ months or they will have to vacate the office.
exp: A person can be appointed as a Minister (or PM) even if they are not a member of either House, but they must become a member (via election or nomination to either House) within six consecutive months. Failure to do so results in them ceasing to be a minister. Options (a), (c), and (d) are incorrect timeframes. This constitutional provision (Article 75(5)) ensures accountability while allowing talent from outside to be inducted quickly.

q: Under which of the following circumstances the Parliament of India can legislate on the matters listed in the State List?
o: If there is a need to regulate local government elections
If there is a need to impose state- level taxes
If there is a need to appoint new state ministers
If there is a need to implement an international treaty
exp: Under Article 253, the Parliament has the power to make any law for the whole or any part of the territory of India for implementing any international treaty, agreement, or convention, even if the subject falls under the State List. Options (a), (b), and (c) are typically state prerogatives unless specific emergencies apply. This provision ensures the Union government can fulfill its international obligations without being hindered by state jurisdiction.

q: Which of the following sportspersons has been a nominated Rajya Sabha member since 2022?
exp: Legendary athlete P.T. Usha was nominated to the Rajya Sabha in July 2022. She is often called the "Payyoli Express" and has served as the president of the Indian Olympic Association. Option (b) Mary Kom was nominated earlier (2016). Option (d) Sachin Tendulkar was nominated in 2012. Option (c) Abhinav Bindra has not been a nominated MP. The President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha for their contributions to art, literature, science, and social service.

q: What is the total number of houses that make up the Indian Parliament?
exp: The Indian Parliament is bicameral, consisting of two houses: the Rajya Sabha (Council of States or Upper House) and the Lok Sabha (House of the People or Lower House). While the Parliament technically comprises the President and the two houses (Article 79), the question specifically asks for the number of "houses". Option (a), (c), and (d) are incorrect. The bicameral system is inspired by the British Parliament (House of Lords and House of Commons).

q: What is the basis for the allocation of seats to states in the Lok Sabha?
exp: The allocation of seats to the states in the Lok Sabha is based on population. Article 81 states that the ratio between the number of seats allocated to a state and its population should be, as far as practicable, the same for all states. The population data used is currently frozen at the 1971 Census levels (until the first census after 2026) by the 84th Amendment to encourage population control measures. Options (a), (c), and (d) are not the constitutional basis for seat allocation.

q: Who acts as the chairperson during a joint meeting of both houses of Parliament?
exp: A Joint Sitting of both houses of Parliament (Article 108) is presided over by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha. If the Speaker is absent, the Deputy Speaker presides. If he is also absent, the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha presides. The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Vice President) never presides over a joint sitting because he is not a member of either house. Option (a) summons the session but does not preside.

q: Who holds the power to dissolve the Lok Sabha prior to the completion of its tenure?
exp: The President of India has the power to dissolve the Lok Sabha before the completion of its five-year term, usually on the advice of the Prime Minister/Council of Ministers (Article 85). The Rajya Sabha is a permanent house and cannot be dissolved. Option (c) Speaker can adjourn the house sine die but not dissolve it. Option (a) PM advises but the formal act is by the President. Dissolution ends the life of the House, necessitating general elections.

q: How many members are nominated by the President of India for the Rajya Sabha?
exp: The President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha under Article 80. These members are chosen for their special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, and social service. Option (a) 2 refers to the now-abolished provision for Anglo-Indians in the Lok Sabha. Options (b) and (d) are incorrect numbers. This nomination ensures that seasoned experts who may shy away from electoral politics can still contribute to legislative debates.

q: Which schedule of the Constitution contains provisions for the disqualification of legislators under the anti-defection law?
exp: The Tenth Schedule, popularly known as the Anti- Defection Law, contains provisions for the disqualification of MPs and MLAs on grounds of defection. It was added by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1985. Option (a) protects laws from judicial review. Option (b) deals with Panchayats. Option (d) lists official languages. Decisions on disqualification under this schedule are made by the presiding officer of the House (Speaker/Chairman).

q: According to the Constitution of India, what is the quorum required to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament?
o: One-third of the total number of members of the House.
Fifty members in the Lok Sabha and twenty-five members in the Rajya Sabha.
One-tenth of the total number of members of the House.
One-fourth of the total number of members of the House.
exp: The Quorum to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament is one-tenth of the total number of members of the House (Article 100). This includes the presiding officer. For the Lok Sabha (543 members), the quorum is 55, and for the Rajya Sabha (245 members), it is 25. If the quorum is not present, the presiding officer must adjourn or suspend the meeting until a quorum is met.

q: The maximum strength of the Lok Sabha (House of the People) as stipulated by the Constitution is:
exp: The maximum strength of the Lok Sabha was fixed at 552 (530 from States, 20 from UTs, and 2 nominated Anglo-Indians). However, the 104th Constitutional Amendment Act (2019) abolished the nomination of Anglo-Indians, effectively making the maximum strength 550. Since SSC exams often refer to the traditional number or the text before the amendment in older question banks, (b) 552 is often the expected answer in such contexts. Currently, the actual strength is 543.

q: What is the role of the Speaker in case of a tied vote in the Lok Sabha election?
o: Refers the decision to the President
exp: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha does not vote in the first instance. However, in the case of an equality of votes (a tie), the Speaker exercises a Casting Vote to break the tie and resolve the deadlock (Article 100). This ensures that the business of the House continues. Option (a), (c), and (d) are incorrect. This practice upholds the Speaker's impartiality while providing a mechanism for decision-making.

q: Which Indian state does S. Jaishankar represent in the Rajya Sabha?
exp: External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar was elected to the Rajya Sabha from the state of Gujarat. He was first elected in 2019 and re- elected in 2023. Although he is a bureaucrat-turned-politician originally from Tamil Nadu, Rajya Sabha members are elected by the MLAs of the state legislature, and he was fielded by the BJP from Gujarat.

q: The Parliament can create a new All-India Service by a resolution in the:
exp: The power to initiate the creation of a new All-India Service lies exclusively with the Rajya Sabha under Article 312. The Rajya Sabha must pass a resolution supported by a two-thirds majority of members the interests of states, as All-India Service officers serve both the Union and States.

q: Arrange the steps for passage of a Money Bill: A. Introduction in Lok Sabha B. Passage in Lok Sabha C. Transmission to Rajya Sabha D. Presentation for Assent Which of the above sequences is correct?
exp: The correct procedure for a Money Bill is: Introduction in Lok Sabha (A) -> Passage in Lok Sabha (B) -> Transmission to Rajya Sabha (C) -> Presentation for Assent (D). A Money Bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha (not Rajya Sabha). The Rajya Sabha has limited powers (can only recommend amendments within 14 days). Finally, the President must give assent (cannot return it for reconsideration). Thus, sequence (a) is correct.

q: Which authority decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill?
exp: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha has the final authority to certify whether a bill is a Money Bill or not under Article 110(3). His decision is final and cannot be challenged in any court of law or by the President. Option (a), (b), and (d) do not have this constitutional power. This certification is crucial because Money Bills have a special procedure that bypasses the Rajya Sabha's veto power.

q: Consider the following: 1. Every Money Bill is a Financial Bill. 2. Every Financial Bill is a Money Bill. Which is/are correct?
exp: Statement 1 is correct: A Money Bill (Article 110) is a specific type of Financial Bill that deals exclusively with taxation, borrowing, etc. Therefore, every Money Bill is a Financial Bill. Statement 2 is incorrect: Financial Bills (Article 117) are a broader category containing fiscal matters plus other legal provisions. Not all Financial Bills meet the strict criteria of Article 110 to be called Money Bills. Thus, Option (a) is correct.

q: Consider the following: 1. Parliament can create All India Services with RS approval. 2. Article 312 mentions 'Security Services'. Which is/are correct?
exp: Statement 1 is correct: Parliament can create new All-India Services only after the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution under Article 312. Statement 2 is incorrect: Article 312 specifically mentions the Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS), and allows for an All-India Judicial Service. It does not use the term "Security Services" as a category. Therefore, option (a) is the correct answer.

q: Consider the following about delegated legislation: 1. Made by administrative authorities. 2. Cannot be challenged in court. Which is/are correct?
exp: Statement 1 is correct: Delegated (or subordinate) legislation refers to laws (rules, regulations, bye-laws) made by administrative authorities (executive) under powers delegated by the legislature. Statement 2 is incorrect: Delegated legislation can be challenged in court on grounds of being ultra vires (beyond the scope) of the parent act or the Constitution. Judicial review is a key check on delegated legislation.

q: Which Article empowers Parliament to create laws on State List under national interest?
exp: Article 249 empowers the Parliament to legislate on a matter in the State List if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution declaring it necessary in the national interest. Option (b) Art 253 is for international treaties. Option (c) Art 248 is for residuary powers. Option (d) Art 254 handles repugnancy between Union and State laws. This article exemplifies the "quasi-federal" nature of the Indian Constitution.

q: Article 312 provides for creation of new ______ by Parliament.
exp: Article 312 of the Constitution provides for the creation of new All-India Services common to the Union and the States. This can be done by Parliament only if the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) has declared by resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest to do so.

q: Consider the following: 1. Consolidated Fund of State defined under Art 266. 2. Contingency Fund operated by Governor. Which is/are correct?
exp: Both statements are correct. Article 266 defines the Consolidated Fund for both the Union and the States (Statement 1). Article 267 establishes the Contingency Fund, which for a State is placed at the disposal of the Governor to meet unforeseen expenditure pending authorization by the State Legislature (Statement 2). The Governor issues advances from this fund by executive order.

q: Rajya Sabha's power under Art 249 allows legislation on ______ List.
exp: Article 249 explicitly empowers the Rajya Sabha to authorize Parliament to make laws on a matter enumerated in the State List (List II). This is a special federal power of the Rajya Sabha. It cannot authorize legislation on Union (already Parliament's domain) or Concurrent lists via this specific article. This power is temporary, valid for one year at a time.

q: A Bill that "imposes a new tax" is categorised as a ______ Bill.
exp: A Bill that contains provisions dealing with the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration, or regulation of any tax is strictly categorized as a Money Bill under Article 110(1)(a). Such bills can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha with the President's recommendation. Option (b) Ordinary bills do not deal exclusively with taxes. Option (c) refers to the introducer (non-minister), not content.

q: Consider the following: 1. Art 249 resolution valid for one year. 2. Parliament extends President's Rule with RS concurrence. Which is/are correct?
exp: Both statements are correct. A resolution passed under Article 249 (legislation on State List) remains in force for a period not exceeding one year (Statement 1). Regarding President's Rule, if the Lok Sabha is dissolved when the proclamation needs approval or extension, the proclamation survives if it is approved by the Rajya Sabha (Statement 2), provided the new Lok Sabha approves it within 30 days of its reconstitution.

q: Practice of putting demands to vote without discussion is called:
exp: The practice of putting all the undiscussed clauses of a bill or demands for grants to vote at once due to paucity of time is called the Guillotine. This usually happens on the last day allotted for the discussion of the budget. Option (b) Cut motions are to reduce the grant amount. Option (d) Point of order is raised on procedural rules.

q: There is a constitutional requirement in India to present the annual financial statement before the ______ every year.
exp: Article 112 mandates that the President shall cause to be laid before both the Houses of Parliament an Annual Financial Statement (Budget) regarding the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for that year. While the President causes it to be laid, the requirement is for it to be presented to the Parliament for approval.

q: Which article of the Indian Constitution deals with sessions of Parliament?
exp: Article 85 of the Constitution deals with the Sessions of Parliament, prorogation, and dissolution. It states that the President shall summon each House to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit, ensuring that six months do not intervene between two sessions. Option (a) deals with Council of Ministers. Option (c) deals with the Speaker/Deputy Speaker. Option (d) deals with Voting and Quorum.

q: What is the minimum age to become a member of Rajya Sabha?
exp: The minimum age required to become a member of the Rajya Sabha is 30 years (Article 84). For the Lok Sabha, the minimum age is 25 years. For President, Vice-President, and Governor, it is 35 years. For Panchayat elections, it is 21 years. This higher age limit for the Upper House reflects its role as a "House of Elders."

q: The Parliament of India can legislate on a state subject if:
o: Council of state passes a resolution by 2/3 majority of the members present
Lok Sabha passes a resolution by simple majority
Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by simple majority
exp: Parliament can legislate on a State subject if the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) passes a resolution supported by not less than two- thirds of the members present and voting, declaring that it is necessary in the national interest (Article 249). Option (b) is the correct answer. Simple majority (d) is insufficient. This provision is a unique federal feature empowering the Upper House.

q: Who decides whether a bill is a Money Bill or not?
o: Speaker of the House of the People
exp: The Speaker of the House of the People (Lok Sabha) has the final authority to decide whether a bill is a Money Bill or not under Article 110(3). If any question arises, the Speaker's decision is final. When a Money Bill is transmitted to the Rajya Sabha or presented to the President, it must be endorsed by the Speaker's certificate.

q: Which of the following bill provides details on the imposition, abolition, or regulation of taxes proposed in the budget?
exp: The Finance Bill is introduced every year to give effect to the financial proposals of the Government of India for the following financial year, including the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration, or regulation of taxes. It is a Money Bill. It is distinct from the Appropriation Bill, which deals with expenditure (withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund).

q: The estimates of revenue receipts take into account the effects of tax proposals made in the:
exp: The estimates of revenue receipts in the Budget are based on the existing tax regime and the effects of new tax proposals contained in the Finance Bill. Since the Finance Bill legalizes the tax changes, the revenue projections are directly dependent on its passage. Option (b) Appropriation Bill authorizes expenditure, not revenue collection.

q: President shall from time to time summon each House of Parliament to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit, but ______ months shall not intervene between its last sitting in one session and the date appointed for its first sitting in the next session.
exp: According to Article 85(1), the maximum gap allowed between two sessions of Parliament cannot exceed six months. This implies that Parliament must meet at least twice a year. In practice, India typically follows a three-session calendar: Budget, Monsoon, and Winter sessions.

q: Rajya Sabha is required to return a Money Bill passed and transmitted by Lok Sabha within a period of ______ days from the date of its receipt.
exp: The Rajya Sabha has very limited powers regarding a Money Bill. It must return the bill to the Lok Sabha within 14 days, with or without recommendations. The Lok Sabha is free to accept or reject these recommendations. If the Rajya Sabha fails to return the bill within 14 days, it is deemed to have been passed by both Houses.

q: What is the first hour of Lok Sabha proceedings called?
exp: The first hour of every parliamentary sitting is generally reserved for the asking and answering of questions and is known as the Question Hour. During this time, members ask questions to ministers about the administration. The Zero Hour follows immediately after the Question Hour (around 12 noon) and is an Indian innovation for raising urgent matters without notice.

q: The members of Rajya Sabha are elected for a term of:
exp: Members of the Rajya Sabha are elected for a term of 6 years. Unlike the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha is not subject to dissolution; it is a permanent body. However, one-third of its members retire every second year, ensuring continuity. Vacancies are filled by fresh elections and nominations.

q: In the context of the Indian Parliament, the ______ Reading refers to the discussion on the motion that the Bill or the Bill, as amended, be passed.
exp: The Third Reading of a bill is the final stage where the debate is confined to the acceptance or rejection of the bill as a whole. No amendments are allowed at this stage (except formal/verbal ones). The motion moved is "that the Bill be passed." The First Reading is introduction; the Second Reading involves detailed clause-by-clause scrutiny and amendment.

q: Which of the following article of Indian constitution deals with the definition of money bill?
exp: Article 110 of the Indian Constitution defines a Money Bill. It lists specific provisions (taxes, borrowing, Consolidated Fund custody, etc.) that qualify a bill as a Money Bill. Option (a) Article 109 provides the special procedure for Money Bills. Option (c) Article 112 deals with the Annual Financial Statement (Budget). Option (d) Article 117 deals with Financial Bills.

q: Which of the following statement is correct regarding the article 253 of Indian Constitution? 1. It is found in Part XI of the Constitution. 2. It relates to the Legislation for giving effect to international agreements. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Both statements are correct. Article 253 empowers Parliament to make laws to implement international treaties, agreements, or conventions. This article is located in Part XI (Relations between the Union and the States), Chapter I (Legislative Relations). This provision ensures the Centre can fulfill global commitments even if they impinge on State List subjects.

q: Who presides over the Lok Sabha sessions?
exp: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is the presiding officer of the lower house of the Parliament of India. Under Article 93, the members elect the Speaker from among themselves. The Speaker maintains discipline, interprets rules, and guides the proceedings of the house. Option (c) is correct. The Chief Justice of India (a) heads the Judiciary and has no role in parliamentary sessions. The Prime Minister (b) is the leader of the executive branch. The President of India (d) addresses both houses during special sessions but does not preside over routine Lok Sabha meetings.

q: Which of the following articles of the Indian Constitution provides Provisions as to Introduction and passing of Bills in parliament?
exp: Article 107 of the Indian Constitution explicitly details the foundational provisions regarding the introduction and passing of ordinary bills in the Parliament. It outlines that an ordinary bill can originate in either House and must be passed by both to become a law. Article 101 strictly deals with the vacation of seats by Members of Parliament. Article 103 pertains to decisions on questions as to disqualifications of members. Article 105 covers the specific powers, privileges, and immunities of Parliament Houses and their members.

q: In Lok Sabha, how many seats are reserved for Scheduled castes?
exp: In the Lok Sabha (the powerful lower house of the Indian Parliament), exactly 84 seats are constitutionally reserved for elected representatives from the Scheduled Castes (SC). Additionally, 47 seats are strictly reserved for the Scheduled Tribes (ST), making a grand total of 131 reserved seats out of the current maximum strength of 543 elected members. The arbitrary figures 54, 56, and 92 do not correspond to any official constitutional reservation numbers. Memorizing exact parliamentary demographic seat distribution is highly crucial for Polity.

q: A 'Cut Motion' in Indian parliament is related to _____.
exp: In the intricate parliamentary procedures of India, a 'Cut Motion' is a special legislative power officially granted to the members of the Lok Sabha to strongly oppose and actively seek a reduction in the budget demands for grants presented by the government. It strictly has three specific types: Disapproval of Policy Cut, Economy Cut, and Token Cut. It is completely unrelated to amending the Constitution, removing a sitting judge, or dissolving the lower house. Understanding crucial budgetary tools is a highly favored topic in SSC Polity.

q: Which of the following article of Indian constitution deals with the special provisions as to financial bills?
exp: Article 117 of the deeply detailed Indian Constitution specifically and strictly deals with the crucial special provisions relating to Financial Bills. It clearly mandates that any bill deeply involving taxation or massive government expenditure cannot be formally introduced in the parliament without the prior explicit recommendation of the President. Article 123 boldly grants the President the extreme power to strictly promulgate ordinances. Article 121 firmly restricts parliamentary discussion regarding the conduct of Supreme Court judges.

q: In the Rajya Sabha, the total number of women members in 1952 was _______.
exp: In the very first historically constituted Rajya Sabha (the Council of States) of independent India in 1952, the total number of elected women members was exactly 15. This was a highly significant, pioneering milestone for women's political representation and empowerment in the early Indian parliamentary democracy, featuring prominent female leaders like Rukmini Devi Arundale and Violet Alva. The other numerical options provided (22, 41, 52) are statistically incorrect for the specific 1952 inaugural session of the Upper House.

q: In Lok Sabha, how many seats were reserved for Scheduled Tribes?
exp: In the Lok Sabha (the powerful Lower House of the Indian Parliament), exactly 47 seats are strictly and constitutionally reserved for the representatives of the Scheduled Tribes (ST) to ensure their adequate political voice. Simultaneously, exactly 84 seats are permanently reserved for the Scheduled Castes (SC). These crucial reservations are made according to the Delimitation Commission's extensive demographic calculations based on population ratios. Therefore, 47 is the only correct answer for STs, while 84 is meant for SCs, and 54/56 have no constitutional significance here.

q: Match the Constitutional provision with its effect on Parliament's power over State List subjects: Column A (Provision) Column B (Effect) 1. Art. 249 P. During national emergency 2. Art. 250 Q. By international agreement 3. Art. 252 R. On request of 2+ states 4. Art. 253 S. For national interest
exp: The correct combination is 1-S, 2-P, 3-R, 4-Q. Under the Indian Constitution, the Parliament can exceptionally legislate on State List subjects under specific conditions. Article 249 empowers Parliament if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution in the 'National Interest'. Article 250 allows it universally 'During a National Emergency'. Article 252 enables legislation if 'two or more States request' it through resolutions. Lastly, Article 253 grants power to implement any 'International Agreement' or treaty, overriding state powers. Any other combination fundamentally misaligns these critical federal provisions.

q: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes a Money Bill from a Finance Bill in the Indian Parliamentary system, in light of constitutional provisions and judicial interpretations?
o: All Finance Bills are Money Bills, but not all Money Bills are Finance Bills.
A Money Bill can be introduced in either House of Parliament, whereas a Finance Bill must be introduced only in the Lok Sabha
The Speaker's decision on whether a bill is a Money Bill is subject to judicial review after the K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2018) verdict.
A Finance Bill deals exclusively with taxation matters listed under Article 110 of the Constitution.
exp: In the landmark Aadhaar case (K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, 2018), the Supreme Court ruled that the Speaker's decision to certify a bill as a Money Bill is not entirely immune from judicial review if there is a constitutional violation. The other options are factually incorrect. All Money Bills are Finance Bills, but not all Finance Bills are Money Bills. Furthermore, Money Bills can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha, not in either house. Lastly, it is the Money Bill that deals exclusively with matters listed under Article 110, not the Finance Bill.

q: Who is the 2024-2025 Lok Sabha Speaker (as of July 2025)?
exp: Om Birla, a prominent Member of Parliament representing the Kota-Bundi constituency in Rajasthan, serves as the highly esteemed Speaker of the Lok Sabha. He was re-elected to this profoundly powerful constitutional post following the constitution of the 18th Lok Sabha in 2024, continuing his tenure into 2025. As Speaker, he strictly presides over the lower house, firmly maintaining discipline and deciding critical matters like the certification of Money Bills. The other politicians listed are regular Members of Parliament but definitely do not hold the supreme presiding office of the Speaker.

q: When deadlock arises the President has to summon joint sitting of two houses of parliament comes under which article?
exp: Under Article 108 of the Indian Constitution, the President is granted the specific constitutional authority to summon a joint sitting of both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. This extraordinary mechanism is utilized strictly to ruthlessly break legislative deadlocks (when one House rejects a non-financial bill passed by the other, or disagreements on amendments persist for six months). The Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over this joint session.

q: Which Article defines a Money Bill and lists matters such as taxation, Consolidated Fund, and public expenditure pertaining exclusively to the Lok Sabha's legislative authority?
exp: Article 110 of the Indian Constitution provides a strict, comprehensive legal definition of a "Money Bill." It clearly states a bill is deemed a Money Bill only if it exclusively deals with matters like the imposition/abolition of taxes, government borrowing, or massive expenditures from the Consolidated Fund of India. Crucially, a Money Bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha, where the Speaker holds the final certification authority.

q: Which of the following areas does the Rajya Sabha hold equal powers with the Lok Sabha?
exp: In the Indian parliamentary system, the Rajya Sabha strictly enjoys absolutely equal legislative powers and status with the Lok Sabha concerning the critical passage of Constitutional Amendment Bills (under Article 368). Both houses must independently pass the amendment with a special majority; no joint sitting is allowed. Conversely, only the Lok Sabha can remove the government (No-Confidence Motion), while only the Rajya Sabha can exclusively create new All-India Services (Article 312).

q: 'Consolidated Fund of India', into which all government revenues (taxes, loans) flow, is constituted under which Article?
exp: Article 266(1) of the Indian Constitution unequivocally establishes the monumental "Consolidated Fund of India." This serves as the absolute primary, supreme treasury account of the Government of India. Every single rupee earned through direct/indirect taxes, massive treasury bills, and repayment of huge national loans flows strictly into this fund. Furthermore, the constitution rigidly mandates that absolutely no money can be withdrawn from it without explicit, formal parliamentary approval.

q: 12 members having knowledge in the literature, science, art & social service are elected directly by the president to which of the following house?
exp: Article 80 of the Indian Constitution grants the President the explicit power to nominate 12 members to the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) from among persons possessing special knowledge or practical experience in fields like literature, science, art, and social service. This ensures the presence of eminent non-political figures in parliamentary debates. The Lok Sabha (House of the People) historically had two Anglo- Indian nominations, which are now abolished. The President does not nominate to State Legislatures.

q: Article 102 of the Indian Constitution is related to?
exp: Article 102 of the Indian Constitution specifically deals with the grounds for the "Disqualification for membership of either House of Parliament". It outlines conditions such as holding an office of profit, being of unsound mind, being an undischarged insolvent, or losing Indian citizenship. The powers of the President are detailed in Article 53. Speaker is guided by Article 93. Thus, disqualification is the correct subject.

q: The qualifications for Members of Parliament (MPs) are described in which article?
exp: Article 84 of the Indian Constitution strictly lays down the qualifications required for membership of Parliament, mandating that the person must be a citizen of India, make an oath, and meet age requirements (25 for Lok Sabha, 30 for Rajya Sabha). Article 79 describes the constitution of Parliament. Article 80 details the composition of the Rajya Sabha. Article 102 lists the disqualifications for members. Thus, Article 84 is the precise provision for qualifications.

q: When the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution under Article 249, the power of Parliament to legislate remains valid for:
exp: Under Article 249 of the Indian Constitution, if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by a two-thirds majority stating that it is necessary in the national interest, Parliament gains the power to legislate on a subject enumerated in the State List. Such a resolution remains forcefully valid for a maximum period of exactly one year. However, it can be renewed any number of times for one year each.

q: Rahul Gandhi was recognized as the Leader of the Opposition (LOP). This post was vacant for 10 years (2014-2024) because no opposition party had?
o: A leader from a national party
exp: To be officially recognized as the Leader of the Opposition (LoP) in the Lok Sabha, the leader's party must secure at least 10% of the total strength of the House (i.e., a minimum of 55 seats out of 543). From 2014 to 2024, no single opposition party, including the Congress, reached this 10% numerical threshold, leaving the constitutional post vacant. In 2024, Congress won 99 seats, crossing the 10% mark, allowing Rahul Gandhi to officially assume the LoP post.

q: The Speaker has a special power to certify a bill, declaring it cannot be blocked by the Rajya Sabha. What is this bill called?
exp: Under Article 110 of the Indian Constitution, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha holds the exclusive and final authority to certify a bill as a 'Money Bill'. Once certified, the Rajya Sabha (Upper House) has highly restricted powers regarding it; they cannot amend or reject it, and can only delay its passage for a maximum of 14 days. Ordinary bills and Constitutional Amendment bills require the approval of both houses equally.

q: According to the Constitution, what is the maximum permissible gap between two sessions of Parliament to ensure regular legislative functioning?
exp: Article 85 of the Indian Constitution strictly mandates the President to summon each House of Parliament to meet at such time and place as they think fit, but stipulates that exactly "six months shall not intervene between its last sitting in one session and the date appointed for its first sitting in the next session." This essentially forces the Parliament to meet robustly at least twice a year. Limits like 3, 4, or 12 months are unconstitutional.

q: Which parliamentary period begins around noon, following the Question Hour, enabling members to raise urgent matters without prior notice?
exp: In the daily proceedings of both houses of the Indian Parliament, the 'Zero Hour' is an innovative, indigenous parliamentary device that begins exactly at 12:00 noon, immediately following the mandated Question Hour. It provides a highly critical, unstructured time slot explicitly allowing Members of Parliament to urgently raise matters of immense, pressing public importance without requiring the usual 10-day prior notice. "Debating hour" and "Complain hour" are completely fictitious and unrecognized terms in standard parliamentary lexicon.

q: Which house of Parliament is called the Upper House?
exp: In India's bicameral parliamentary system, the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) functions as the Upper House. It represents the states and union territories of the nation and is a permanent body not subject to dissolution. Option (b) is correct. The Lok Sabha (a) is the directly elected Lower House representing the people. The Vidhan Sabha (c) is the lower house of a state legislature. The Gram Sabha (d) is a local village governing body at the grassroots level.

q: Which article empowers the president to dissolve the Rajya Sabha?
exp: According to Article 83(1) of the Indian Constitution, the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) is a permanent legislative body and is strictly not subject to dissolution. One-third of its members retire every second year. Thus, no article empowers the President to dissolve it. Option (d) is correct. Article 83 details the duration of Houses, Article 84 outlines qualifications for membership, and Article 85 empowers the President to prorogue the houses or dissolve only the Lok Sabha, not the Rajya Sabha.

q: What is the minimum age required to become a Member of Lok Sabha?
exp: According to Article 84(b) of the Indian Constitution, a candidate must be a citizen of India and not less than 25 years of age to be qualified to become a member of the Lok Sabha (House of the People). Therefore, option (c) is the correct answer. The age of 18 years is the minimum voting age for adult suffrage. 21 years is the minimum age to contest in local Panchayat elections. Finally, 30 years is the minimum age requirement for becoming a member of the Rajya Sabha.

q: Which of the following statements is correct about All India Services?
o: Their creation requires a 2/3 majority resolution of the Rajya Sabha
Their creation is based on an Inter-State Council recommendation
Their creation requires a simple majority of Lok Sabha
Their creation requires a Constitutional Amendment
exp: According to Article 312 of the Indian Constitution, the Parliament can create a new All India Service only if the Rajya Sabha first passes a resolution declaring it is necessary in the national interest. Crucially, this resolution must be supported by a special majority, meaning not less than two-thirds (2/3) of the members present and voting. Option (a) is completely correct. It does not require a Constitutional Amendment, nor is it based on the Lok Sabha's simple majority or Inter-State Council recommendations.

q: Which body is responsible for approving India's Union Budget before it can be implemented?
exp: The Union Budget of India, constitutionally referred to as the Annual Financial Statement under Article 112, fundamentally represents a Money Bill. According to the strict democratic protocols of the Indian Constitution, a Money Bill can only be formally introduced and decisively approved by the Lok Sabha (the Lower House of Parliament), which holds exclusive supreme authority over financial legislation. Therefore, option (a) is completely correct. While the Rajya Sabha (b) can discuss the budget and suggest non-binding recommendations within 14 days, it possesses zero power to reject or amend it. The Finance Ministry (c) is merely the administrative body that prepares the budget, and NITI Aayog (d) holds no legislative powers.

q: Who presides over the joint sitting of Parliament?
exp: In the highly dramatic event of a massive legislative deadlock or severe disagreement between the two houses of the Indian Parliament regarding an ordinary bill, the President holds the explicit constitutional power to formally summon a joint sitting. However, according to the strict protocols defined in Article 118 of the Constitution, it is exclusively the Speaker of the Lok Sabha who possesses the supreme authority to actively preside over this massive joint session and maintain parliamentary decorum. Option (c) is completely correct. The President (b) merely calls the meeting but never presides. The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (a) and the Prime Minister (d) are constitutionally barred from presiding over this specific joint legislative gathering.

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution governs the allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha (Council of States)?
exp: Article 80 of the Indian Constitution explicitly dictates the maximum composition of the Rajya Sabha (250 members) and governs the exact allocation of seats to the various States and Union Territories based on their population (detailed heavily in the Fourth Schedule). Article 81 deals with the composition of the Lok Sabha. Article 88 relates to the rights of Ministers. Article 102 deals with disqualifications. The structural articles of Parliament are always tested.

q: Under which provision of the Indian Constitution can the President dissolve the Lok Sabha?
exp: Under the specific provisions heavily laid out in Article 85(2)(b) of the Indian Constitution, the President of India retains the explicit constitutional authority to prorogue either House and to definitively dissolve the Lok Sabha (House of the People), usually on the advice of the Prime Minister. Article 123 distinctly handles the ordinance- making power. Article 60 handles the President's oath, and Article 82 deals with demographic readjustment after a census.

q: Which House can authorize Parliament to legislate on a State List subject in national interest?
o: Both Houses jointly by simple majority
exp: Under Article 249 of the Constitution, the Rajya Sabha laws concerning matters enumerated in the State List. This requires the Rajya Sabha to pass a resolution by a special majority—specifically, not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting—declaring it necessary in the broader national interest.

q: In case of a conflict between Central and State law on a Concurrent List subject, the State law prevails only if:
o: It is passed by a two-thirds majority
It is supported by a Supreme Court ruling
exp: Under Article 254(2) of the Constitution, if a State law on a Concurrent List subject is repugnant (contradictory) to an earlier Central law, the State law can still prevail in that specific state if it has been reserved for the consideration of the President and has received his assent. However, the Parliament retains the power to enact a law later that adds to, amends, or repeals such a state law. Option (b) is the correct constitutional mechanism for this exception.

q: Which constitutional authority decides on the disqualification of a Member of State Legislature under the Anti- Defection Law?
exp: Under the Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law), the question of disqualification on the grounds of defection is decided by the Chairman or Speaker of the House (in the case of the Legislative Assembly, the Speaker). Their decision is subject to judicial review (Supreme Court judgment in Kihoto Hollohan case). Option (d) Governor decides on disqualifications related to other matters (like holding office of profit) under Article 192, after consulting the Election Commission.

q: What is the maximum number of members in a State Legislative Assembly as per the Constitution?
exp: Article 170 of the Indian Constitution stipulates that the Legislative Assembly of each State shall consist of not more than 500 and not less than 60 members chosen by direct election. However, exceptions regarding the minimum strength exist for smaller states like Sikkim (32), Goa (40), and Mizoram (40) via special provisions (Article 371 series) or parliamentary acts. The maximum cap remains 500.

q: Consider the following statements: 1. President can dissolve Lok Sabha on his own discretion. 2. Governor appoints Chief Minister in a hung assembly. 3. Governor has no role in Money Bills. Which of the above is/are correct?
exp: Statement 2 is correct: In the case of a hung assembly (no clear majority), the Governor has the discretionary power to appoint a Chief Minister who he believes can prove a majority. Statement 1 is incorrect: The President dissolves the Lok Sabha usually on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 85); discretion is only available if the government has lost its majority. Statement 3 is incorrect: A Money Bill can only be introduced in the state legislature with the prior recommendation of the Governor (Article 207), giving him a crucial role.

q: Which state has a bicameral legislature?
exp: Maharashtra is one of the few Indian states with a bicameral legislature, consisting of both the Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) and the Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad). As of now, only six states have bicameral legislatures: Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, and Uttar Pradesh. Tamil Nadu abolished its Council in 1986, and West Bengal did so in 1969.

q: Who is the first woman to become the Chief Minister of an Indian state?
exp: Sucheta Kripalani was the first woman to become the Chief Minister of an Indian state. She served as the Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh from 1963 to 1967. She was a prominent freedom fighter and a member of the Constituent Assembly. Option (d) Nandini Satpathy (Odisha) and (a) Anwara Taimur (Assam) became CMs later. Option (c) Shashikala Kakodkar was CM of Goa (then a UT) in the 1970s.

q: Who acts as the link between the Governor and the State Council of Ministers?
exp: The Chief Minister acts as the main channel of communication (link) between the Governor and the Council of Ministers. Under Article 167, it is the duty of the Chief Minister to communicate to the Governor all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to the administration of the affairs of the State and proposals for legislation.

q: Who has the power to appoint the Chief Minister (CM) of a state in India?
exp: The Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor of the State under Article 164(1). By convention, the Governor appoints the leader of the majority party (or coalition) in the State Legislative Assembly as the Chief Minister. Other ministers are appointed by the Governor on the advice of the Chief Minister.

q: What is the tenure of a Governor in an Indian state?
exp: According to Article 156(3), a Governor holds office for a term of 5 years from the date on which he enters upon his office. However, this term is subject to the pleasure of the President (Article 156(1)), meaning he can be removed by the President at any time before the completion of the 5-year term without any specific grounds mentioned in the Constitution.

q: Which of the following is a subject under the State List?
exp: Public Order (Entry 1) and Police (Entry 2) are subjects under the State List (List II) of the Seventh Schedule. This gives State governments the primary responsibility for maintaining law and order. Option (a) Banking and (c) Defence are in the Union List. Option (d) Education is in the Concurrent List (transferred from State List by the 42nd Amendment).

q: How does Article 356 impact the federal structure of India?
o: It allows Centre to dismiss State governments
exp: Article 356 (President's Rule) allows the Centre to dismiss a State government and assume its executive and legislative powers if the constitutional machinery in the state fails. This provision significantly tilts the balance of power towards the Centre, impacting the federal structure by suspending state autonomy. Critics often describe it as a threat to federalism if misused for political gains.

q: Which article provides for the appointment of Governors in India?
exp: Article 155 states that the Governor of a State shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. Option (b) Article 154 vests the executive power of the State in the Governor. Option (d) Article 168 constitutes state legislatures. The method of appointment (rather than election) was chosen to maintain national unity and prevent friction between an elected Governor and an elected CM.

q: Which discretionary power allows a Governor to reserve a bill passed by the state legislature for the consideration of the President?
o: To send a report to the President for the imposition of President's Rule.
To reserve a bill for the President's consideration.
To grant pardon in certain cases.
To summon, prorogue, and dissolve the state legislative assembly.
exp: Under Article 200, the Governor has the discretionary power to reserve a bill for the consideration of the President. This is mandatory if the bill endangers the position of the state High Court, but the Governor can also use discretion for other bills (e.g., if it conflicts with national policy or the Constitution). Option (b) describes this specific legislative discretion.

q: Statement 1: Governor is state's constitutional head. Statement 2: He acts solely on Council's advice. Which of the above statements holds true regarding Governor's executive powers?
exp: Only Statement 1 is correct. The Governor is indeed the constitutional head of the state. Statement 2 is incorrect because, unlike the President (who is bound by advice under Art 74), the Governor acts on advice except when the Constitution requires him to exercise his functions in his discretion (Article 163), such as in reserving bills, recommending President's Rule, or appointing a CM in a hung assembly.

q: The President is elected by an electoral college, while the Governor is:
exp: The Governor is appointed by the President of India (Article 155). This implies he is a nominee of the Central Government. The Constituent Assembly rejected the proposal of a direct election (American model) to avoid creating a rival center of power to the Chief Minister and to ensure the Governor remains a neutral constitutional head representing the Centre.

q: How are Money Bills handled in bicameral State Legislatures?
o: Council can only recommend within 14 days
exp: In a bicameral state legislature, a Money Bill can only originate in the Legislative Assembly. The Legislative Council has very limited powers; it can only make recommendations and must return the bill within 14 days. It cannot amend or reject the bill. If it fails to return it, the bill is deemed passed. This mirrors the Rajya Sabha's position at the Centre.

q: Which statements are correct? 1. Governor's power to recommend President's Rule is in Art 356. 2. 41st Amendment curtailed Governor's term. 3. Sarkaria Commission advised on Governor's tenure. Choose the correct option:
exp: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The Governor recommends President's Rule under Article 356 (Statement 1). The Sarkaria Commission (1983) made significant recommendations to secure the Governor's tenure and independence (Statement 3). Statement 2 is incorrect; the 41st Amendment (1976) raised the retirement age of State Public Service Commission members, unrelated to the Governor's term.

q: Collective responsibility of State CoMs appears in Article ______ .
exp: Article 164(2) of the Constitution states that the Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly of the State. This is the bedrock of the parliamentary system in the states. Option (b) Article 163 deals with the Council of Ministers to aid and advise the Governor. Option (c) Article 154 vests executive power in the Governor.

q: After Bill is passed by State, Governor may forward it to:
exp: When a Bill passed by the State Legislature is presented to the Governor, Article 200 gives him four options: give assent, withhold assent, return the bill (if not a Money Bill), or reserve the Bill for the consideration of the President. Thus, he forwards it to the President. This is a key tool for Central control over State legislation.

q: In India, Socio-Economic and Caste Census (SECC) 2011 was conducted by which of the following? 1. Ministry of Rural Development 2. Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs Choose the correct option:
exp: The SECC 2011 was a massive exercise conducted by the Government of India. The rural component was conducted by the Ministry of Rural Development (I), and the urban component was conducted by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation (now Housing and Urban Affairs) (II). The census data is used to identify beneficiaries for government schemes. Therefore, option (c) is correct.

q: The Contingency Fund of an Indian State is held by:
exp: Article 267(2) establishes a Contingency Fund for each State, which is placed at the disposal of the Governor of the State. It enables the Governor to make advances for meeting unforeseen expenditure pending authorization by the State Legislature. This parallels the President's role for the Union Contingency Fund.

q: Who can dissolve the Indian state Legislative Assembly before its term ends?
exp: The Governor has the power to dissolve the Legislative Assembly under Article 174(2)(b). This is usually done on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister, provided they enjoy a majority. Dissolution ends the life of the House, leading to fresh elections.

q: Which article of the Indian constitution is related with the Special address by the Governor?
exp: Article 176 deals with the Special Address by the Governor. At the commencement of the first session after each general election and at the commencement of the first session of each year, the Governor addresses the Legislative Assembly (or both Houses in bicameral states) and informs the Legislature of the causes of its summons. Option (a) Article 175 is the right to address and send messages.

q: A Bill passed by the Indian State Legislature is sent to the Governor under:
exp: Article 200 outlines the process when a Bill passed by the State Legislature is presented to the Governor. It lists his powers: assent, withhold assent, return, or reserve for the President. Option (b) Article 201 deals with the procedure after a bill is reserved for the President. Option (c) Article 202 deals with the Annual Financial Statement (State Budget).

q: Which of the following can recommend the creation of a Legislative Council in an Indian state?
