exp: Fort St. George, established in 1644 at the coastal city of Madras (modern-day Chennai), was the very first major English fortress aggressively constructed in India by the British East India Company. It served as a heavily fortified trading post and crucially laid the foundation for expanding absolute British colonial dominance in South India. Sindhudurg Fort is an imposing coastal fortress built by Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj. Gwalior Fort is an ancient historical hill fort, and Chittorgarh is a massive Rajput fortification.

q: In which year was the Treaty of Salbai signed between the British and the Marathas?
exp: The historic Treaty of Salbai was officially signed on May 17, 1782, strictly between the British East India Company and the Maratha Empire. This highly crucial treaty officially ended the long-drawn First Anglo-Maratha War. It was negotiated heavily by Warren Hastings and Mahadaji Shinde, ensuring a period of peace lasting nearly 20 years between the two formidable powers. The years 1803 and 1817 mark the beginning of the Second and Third Anglo-Maratha wars, respectively.

q: After which of the following wars was the Peshwa removed and sent to Bithur?
exp: Following the absolute and decisive British victory in the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–1818), the powerful Maratha Empire was permanently dismantled. The British East India Company officially abolished the supreme title of Peshwa. Peshwa Baji Rao II was heavily defeated, permanently deposed from his historic seat of power in Pune, and forcibly exiled to the distant town of Bithur (near Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh), surviving solely on an annual British pension until his death.

q: Who among the following accepted the Diwani of Bihar and Orissa from the Mughal ruler on behalf of the East India Company in 1765?
exp: Following the decisive victory at the historic Battle of Buxar (1764), Robert Clive, acting brilliantly on behalf of the British East India Company, formally accepted the extremely lucrative 'Diwani rights' (the right to systematically collect massive land revenues) of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa directly from the defeated Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II in 1765 via the Treaty of Allahabad. This masterstroke officially established British political supremacy in India. The other options are incorrect: Warren Hastings became the first Governor-General much later, Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement, and Wellesley brought the Subsidiary Alliance.

q: Europeans established port town of Panaji in Goa in which of the following year?
exp: The crucial coastal territory of Goa (including the strategic port area that would later develop into modern Panaji) was aggressively attacked and definitively conquered by the brilliant Portuguese explorer Afonso de Albuquerque in the historic year 1510. He captured it directly from the powerful Adil Shahi dynasty of Bijapur. This pivotal victory allowed the Portuguese (Europeans) to firmly establish a massive, enduring colonial and commercial stronghold in Goa that lasted for over 450 years until India annexed it in 1961. The other years do not correspond to this monumental European colonial establishment.

q: In 1600, which English Queen granted a charter to the East India Company, giving it exclusive trading rights with the East?
exp: On December 31, 1600, Queen Elizabeth I granted the Royal Charter to the Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies — what became the East India Company. This gave the company a monopoly over trade east of the Cape of Good Hope. Queen Victoria became Empress of India in 1877, well after the company's dissolution in 1858. Queen Mary and Queen Anne ruled in the 17th-18th century and had no role in the EIC charter. This is a standard Modern History SSC question.

q: Who was one of Sirajuddaulah's commander that played a significant role in Sirajuddaulah's defeat at the Battle of Plassey?
exp: The Battle of Plassey (1757) was won by Robert Clive largely due to the treachery of Mir Jafar, who was Sirajuddaulah's commander-in-chief. He conspired with the British and kept his large contingent of troops inactive during the battle, leading to Sirajuddaulah's defeat and eventual execution. As a reward, Mir Jafar was made the Nawab of Bengal. Alivardi Khan was Sirajuddaulah's grandfather and predecessor. Jagat Seth was a wealthy banker who funded the conspiracy. Mulla Qutb Shah was not a key figure at Plassey.

q: The Regulating Act of 1773 primarily introduced changes in the Company's administration in which two distinct areas?
exp: The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first step by the British government to control the East India Company. It introduced changes in the "Constitution at home" by reforming the Court of Directors (governing body in England) and in the "Territorial administration" by creating the post of Governor-General of Bengal with a four-member council. Option (a) and (b) are incorrect as the primary structural changes were political and constitutional. A key fact is that this Act also established the Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774) with Sir Elijah Impey as the first Chief Justice.

q: What change did the Regulating Act bring to the post of the Governor of Bengal?
exp: The Regulating Act of 1773 elevated the Governor of Bengal to the position of Governor-General of Bengal and provided him with an Executive Council of four members to assist in administration. This centralized power, making the presidencies of Bombay and Madras subordinate to Bengal in matters of war and peace. Option (a) is incorrect as he still reported to the Court of Directors. Option (b) is wrong as his powers were increased, not reduced. Warren Hastings became the first person to hold this elevated title.

q: Who among the following was the Governor-General of British India from 1773 to 1785?
exp: Warren Hastings served as the first Governor-General of Bengal from 1773 to 1785. His tenure saw the foundations of British administration in India, including the First Anglo-Maratha War and the Second Anglo-Mysore War. Option (b), (c), and (d) are incorrect as Wellesley, Dalhousie, and Cornwallis served much later. An interesting fact is that after returning to England, Hastings faced a famous seven-year impeachment trial for corruption, though he was eventually acquitted.

q: What was the function of the Board of Control established by Pitt's India Act?
exp: The Board of Control, established by Pitt's India Act of 1784, was a body of six commissioners designed to supervise and control all civil, military, and revenue affairs of the East India Company. This created a system of "Double Government" where the Court of Directors managed commercial affairs, while the Board of Control managed political affairs. Options (a) and (b) are too limited, and (d) refers to commercial functions retained by the Directors. The President of this Board was effectively the Minister for Indian Affairs.

q: Fill in the blank: Pitt's India Act 1784 created a six-member body called the ______ to supervise Company politics.
exp: Pitt's India Act of 1784 created the Board of Control to oversee the political activities of the East India Company. This body included the Chancellor of the Exchequer, a Secretary of State, and four Privy Councillors. Option (b) Council of India was created later by the Act of 1858. Option (c) refers to the advisor to the Monarch. Option (d) is a fabricated term. This Board subordinated the Company to the British Government, a structure that lasted until 1858.

q: Under Pitt's India Act, what restriction was placed on the Governor General and Council?
o: Could not issue orders w/o majority
Forbidden to declare war w/o approval
exp: Pitt's India Act (and supplementary acts) restricted the Governor-General from declaring war or entering into treaties without the express permission of the Court of Directors or the Board of Control. This was intended to curb the aggressive expansionist policies and corruption that had characterized the Company's earlier years. Option (b) is partially true regarding internal voting, but the war restriction was the major political constraint. This reflected the British Parliament's desire for a policy of non-intervention, though it was frequently violated in practice.

q: What was one major provision introduced by the Pitt's India Act of 1784 concerning the Court of Directors?
o: Authority to make laws for states
exp: Pitt's India Act made the Court of Directors accountable to the British Government by placing their civil and military policy decisions under the review of the newly formed Board of Control. The Directors had to submit all dispatches to the Board for approval. Option (d) is incorrect as the two bodies remained distinct (Dual Government). Option (a) is incorrect as they couldn't legislate for princely states. This Act solidified the British Crown's sovereignty over the Company's territories in India.

q: How did Pitt's India Act contribute to unifying British administration in India?
exp: Pitt's India Act significantly strengthened the central authority by making the Governor-General of Bengal supreme over the subordinate Presidencies of Bombay and Madras. The Governors of Bombay and Madras could not declare war or make peace without Bengal's approval. Option (a) is the opposite of the truth. Option (b) is wrong as the Court persisted. This centralization was crucial for creating a unified British Indian empire rather than a collection of loose trading outposts.

q: What long-term administrative outcome is attributed to Pitt's India Act?
exp: The most significant long-term outcome of Pitt's India Act was that it placed the East India Company under the direct control of the British Parliament. While the Company retained its trade monopoly (until 1813), its political administration was now supervised by the British Cabinet via the Board of Control. Option (b) is incorrect. Option (d) is wrong as the post became more powerful. This structure of "Dual Government" continued until the Crown assumed direct rule in 1858.

q: Which of the following pairs (Governor-General - Policy) is correctly matched?
exp: The correct match is Lord Wellesley with Imperialist conquests. Wellesley (1798–1805) was an aggressive expansionist who used the Subsidiary Alliance system to bring states like Hyderabad, Mysore, and Awadh under British control. Option (a) is incorrect; Lord Hastings (1813–1823) was also an expansionist who fought the Gurkhas and Marathas. Option (b) is a mismatch. Wellesley described himself as a "Bengal Tiger" and aimed to make the Company the paramount power in India.

q: Who introduced the Ryotwari System in India?
exp: The Ryotwari System was introduced by Thomas Munro and Captain Alexander Read. It was first tried in the Baramahal district in 1792 and later expanded to the Madras and Bombay Presidencies. Option (a) Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement (Zamindari). Options (c) and (d) are unrelated to Ryotwari. Under this system, the government collected revenue directly from the cultivators (ryots), bypassing intermediaries, which theoretically protected peasants but often led to high tax demands.

q: Which of the following pairs of revenue system & person who devised it is correct? I. Mahalwari settlement - Holt Mackenzie II. Ryotwari system - Alexander Read and Thomas Munro Choose the correct option:
exp: Both pairs are correctly matched. The Mahalwari system, where revenue was settled with the village community (Mahal), was devised by Holt Mackenzie (1822). The Ryotwari system, involving direct settlement with peasants, was developed by Alexander Read and Thomas Munro. Therefore, option (c) is correct. These systems varied by region: Permanent Settlement in Bengal, Ryotwari in the South/West, and Mahalwari in the North-West/Punjab.

q: In which of the following years the East India Company introduced the Permanent Settlement?
exp: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793 by Lord Cornwallis. It declared the Zamindars as the hereditary owners of the land, provided they paid a fixed revenue to the Company in perpetuity. Option (a) refers to the grant of Diwani. Option (c) is the correct date. This system created a loyal class of landlords but often led to the exploitation of the peasantry and the "Sunset Law," where Zamindars lost their land if payment wasn't made by sunset on the due date.

q: The introduction of the Permanent Settlement in Bengal by Lord Cornwallis in 1793 primarily aimed to:
exp: The primary aim of the Permanent Settlement was to ensure a fixed and stable revenue for the Company and to create a class of loyal Zamindars who would support British rule. Option (a) is incorrect as peasant welfare was largely ignored; they became tenants at will. Option (d) is wrong as it entrenched the Zamindari system. While it did encourage some agricultural extension, the motive was political stability and financial security for the colonial state.

q: Assertion: British capital accumulation in the 18th century was reinvested in industrial development. Reason: the capital was largely controlled by merchants and industrialists instead of the feudal aristocracy. Choose the correct option:
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
exp: Both statements are true and related. The immense wealth drained from India (Battle of Plassey onwards) contributed to capital accumulation in Britain (Assertion). Unlike feudal lords who spent on luxury and land, the rising merchant and industrial class controlled this capital and reinvested it into new technologies and factories (Reason), directly fueling the Industrial Revolution. Therefore, the nature of the class controlling the capital explains why it led to industrial development rather than stagnation.

q: During British rule in India, caste data was regularly collected in decennial censuses from 1881 to ______.
exp: Caste data was collected in every decennial census from 1881 up to 1931. The 1941 census collected the data but did not publish it due to WWII administrative constraints. After independence, the Indian government stopped enumerating caste (except for SC/ST) to prevent social fragmentation. Option (c) is the correct answer. The 1931 census, conducted by J.H. Hutton, is still used as a primary reference for caste demographics in historical and legal contexts.

q: Which of the following statements is correct with reference to the Act passed by the British Parliament in 1858? I. the Governor-General of India was given the title of Viceroy. II. the British decided to respect the customary religious and social practices of the people in India. Choose the correct option:
exp: Both statements are correct. The Government of India Act 1858 transferred power from the Company to the Crown. Lord Canning became the first Viceroy (Statement I). Following the trauma of the 1857 Revolt, Queen Victoria's Proclamation explicitly promised non- interference in Indian religious beliefs and customs to prevent future uprisings (Statement II). This marked a shift from the earlier reformist interventionism to a more conservative policy of appeasement.

q: What was the role of the India Council established by the Government of India Act, 1858?
o: To advise the Secretary of State
To represent Indian opinion in Britain
exp: The Government of India Act, 1858, established a 15- member Council of India to advise the Secretary of State for India. The Secretary of State was a British cabinet minister responsible for Indian affairs. This Council was composed of experienced administrators (mostly retired British officials). Option (c) is incorrect as it did not represent Indian opinion. The Council acted as a check on the Secretary of State, though its role was primarily advisory and was later reduced.

q: Which administrative bodies were abolished after the enactment of the Government of India Act, 1858?
o: Board of Control & Court of Directors
exp: The Act of 1858 abolished the Board of Control and the Court of Directors, thereby ending the system of "Dual Government" introduced by Pitt's India Act. Their powers were transferred to the new Secretary of State for India. Option (a), (b), and (d) are incorrect. This simplified the chain of command, placing India directly under the sovereignty of the British Crown and Parliament.

q: The Ilbert Bill controversy of 1883 was related to which issue?
exp: The Ilbert Bill (1883), introduced during Lord Ripon’s viceroyalty, sought to allow Indian judges and magistrates to try British and European offenders in criminal cases. Before this, only European judges could try Europeans. Option (a) is correct. The bill triggered a massive backlash from the European community (White Mutiny), forcing the government to dilute the bill, which exposed the deep racial bias inherent in British colonial rule.

q: The Ilbert Bill controversy of 1883-84 was related to:
exp: The controversy centered on the proposal to remove judicial disqualifications based on race, specifically allowing Indian judges to try European offenders. The European community in India vehemently opposed this, arguing that Indian judges were unfit to try "civilized" Europeans. Option (b) is the correct answer. The intense opposition taught Indian nationalists the power of organized agitation, influencing the formation of the Indian National Congress in 1885.

q: Which bill/act provided for the trial of British or European persons by Indians, and sought equality between British and Indian judges?
exp: The Ilbert Bill of 1883 was the legislative measure that sought to establish equality between British and Indian judges by allowing Indian magistrates to try British subjects. It was drafted by Sir C.P. Ilbert, the Law Member of the Viceroy's Council. Options (a), (c), and (d) refer to constitutional acts, not this specific judicial reform. The bill was eventually passed in a compromised form, giving Europeans the right to demand a jury trial with a European majority.

q: With reference to the Indian Councils Act, 1892, consider the following statements and choose the correct option: 1. It significantly increased the number of official members in the Central Legislative Council. 2. It empowered the legislative councils to discuss the budget and address questions to the executive. 3. It introduced the principle of direct election for non-official members of provincial legislative councils. Choose the correct option:
exp: Only Statement 2 is correct. The Act empowered councils to discuss the budget (but not vote on it) and ask questions. Statement 1 is incorrect because it increased the number of non-official members, not official ones. Statement 3 is incorrect because it introduced the principle of indirect election (nomination based on recommendation by local bodies), not direct election. Direct elections were only introduced later by the Government of India Act 1919.

q: Which policy of Lord Curzon was primarily intended to strengthen British administration and strategic interests?
exp: Lord Curzon established the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) and reorganized the police following the Police Commission of 1902 to strengthen internal security and administration. While he did all the options listed (Agriculture, Education, Monuments), the police reorganization was the measure specifically aimed at strategic control and curbing the rising nationalist movement. Curzon is famous for his efficiency but also for his controversial Partition of Bengal.

q: The Federal Court of India, as provided under the Government of India Act 1935, was established in the year?
exp: The Federal Court of India was inaugurated in 1937 in Delhi, following the provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935. It functioned until the establishment of the Supreme Court of India in 1950. Option (b) is correct. The court had original, appellate, and advisory jurisdiction. Sir Maurice Gwyer was its first Chief Justice. It was the highest court in India, though appeals could still go to the Privy Council in London.

q: The Government of India Act of 1935 primarily aimed to:
exp: The primary aim of the Government of India Act 1935 was to establish an All-India Federation (which never materialized due to princely state opposition) and to grant Provincial Autonomy. Option (c) is correct. It abolished diarchy in the provinces and introduced it at the center. Option (a) is wrong; independence came in 1947. Option (d) is wrong; the franchise was extended but remained limited (about 10% of the population). This Act served as the blueprint for much of the Constitution of independent India.

q: In which year was the Mahalwari system of land revenue introduced by the British in India?
exp: The Mahalwari system, devised by Holt Mackenzie, was officially introduced in 1822 in the North-Western Provinces, parts of Central India, and Punjab. Under this system, the revenue settlement was made with the entire village community (Mahal) rather than individual peasants. 1793 is famous for the introduction of the Permanent Settlement by Lord Cornwallis in Bengal. 1765 marks the grant of Diwani rights. Memorizing the exact years and architects of British land revenue policies is crucial.

q: According to the new system of justice established by the British in 1772, which of the following courts was to be there in every district? 1. Faujdari adalat 2. Diwani adalat
exp: Both courts were strictly mandated. Under the radical judicial reforms introduced by Warren Hastings in 1772, every district was required to have two distinct courts: a Diwani Adalat (Civil Court) presided over by the European District Collector, and a Faujdari Adalat (Criminal Court) run by a Qazi and a Mufti but under the general supervision of the Collector. This dual system completely transformed local administration. Recognizing Hastings' foundational reforms is a highly tested pattern in SSC Modern History.

q: Which of the following airlines was nationalised in 1953? I. Bharat Airways II. Hyderabad Aviation Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: The Air Corporations Act of 1953 nationalised eight private airlines operating in India and merged them into two state-owned entities — Indian Airlines (for domestic routes) and Air India (for international routes). The eight airlines nationalised were: Air India, Indian Airlines, Bharat Airways, Himalayan Aviation, Kalinga Airlines, Airways India, Deccan Airways, and Air Services of India. Bharat Airways (Statement I) was indeed among these eight, so it is correct. Hyderabad Aviation (Statement II) was not among the airlines nationalised under this Act, making it incorrect. Thus, only Statement I is correct.

q: The English Education Act of 1835 was passed based on the recommendations of which of the following individuals' minute?
exp: The profoundly historic English Education Act of 1835 was passed directly based on the aggressive and highly controversial recommendations formally presented in Lord Thomas Babington Macaulay's famous "Minute on Indian Education" (1835). Macaulay strictly argued for entirely halting support for traditional Oriental learning (Sanskrit and Arabic) and aggressively redirecting all government funds exclusively toward vigorously promoting modern Western education through the English medium. James Mill and Colebrooke were famous Orientalists who deeply respected ancient Indian scholarship.

q: Under the Regulating Act of 1773, court of appeal "the Sadar Nizamat Adalat" was set up at which of the following city in India?
exp: Following the historic and aggressive implementation of the Regulating Act of 1773, massive structural judicial reforms were forcefully introduced by the British East India Company under Governor-General Warren Hastings. He systematically and strictly established the 'Sadar Nizamat Adalat' (acting as the supreme court of appeal strictly for criminal cases) deep within the heavily fortified colonial capital city of Calcutta. Alongside this, the Sadar Diwani Adalat was concurrently formed strictly for massive civil dispute appeals. Bombay, Mysore, and Lucknow did not host this specific apex colonial court.

q: Railway lines in India were laid starting from _____.
exp: The monumental, highly transformative process of laying physical railway lines in the Indian subcontinent was officially and ambitiously initiated by the British East India Company under the tenure of Governor-General Lord Dalhousie in the year 1853. The tremendously historic very first passenger train successfully made its maiden journey covering exactly 34 kilometers from Bombay (Bori Bunder) to Thane on April 16, 1853. The other years are monumental for different events: 1600 marks the EIC's foundation, 1757 marks the pivotal Battle of Plassey, and 1935 relates to the significant Government of India Act.

q: The introduction of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) in 1860 aimed to:
o: Codify and standardize criminal laws across British India.
Grant greater autonomy to village courts in resolving disputes.
Exclusively protect the interests of the British ruling class.
exp: Drafted by the First Law Commission of India chaired by Thomas Babington Macaulay, the IPC of 1860 was designed to replace the fragmented and conflicting regional penal systems with a single, comprehensive, and standardized framework of criminal law applicable universally across all British Indian territories.

q: The "Indian Councils Act of 1892" represented a limited expansion of Indian participation in the legislative councils. What was a notable feature of this Act regarding the selection of Indian members?
o: It introduced universal adult suffrage for the election of Indian members.
It allowed for the direct election of a majority of Indian members to the central legislative council.
It permitted the nomination of some Indian members by the Governor-General and provided for indirect election through electoral colleges.
It mandated equal representation for all religious communities in the legislative councils.
exp: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 increased the number of non-official members in the central and provincial councils. While it avoided the term "election," it introduced the principle of representation by allowing the Governor-General to nominate members based on recommendations from entities like universities, municipalities, and chambers of commerce (indirect elections).

q: Which system, introduced by the Government of India Act of 1919, classified provincial subjects into "reserved" and "transferred" categories?
exp: The Government of India Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) introduced the system of "Dyarchy" at the provincial level. It divided provincial administration into two spheres: 'Reserved subjects' (like police and finance, controlled by the Governor without accountability) and 'Transferred subjects' (like education and health, administered by Indian ministers responsible to the legislature).

q: Which of the following correctly describes the responsibilities of Madras and Bombay governors after 1773?
o: They operated independently of the Bengal Governor-General.
They had to report to the Governor-General on war, peace, and revenue.
They managed trade but not civil administration.
They were answerable only to the Court of Directors in London.
exp: The Regulating Act of 1773 fundamentally centralized British administration in India. It designated the Governor of Bengal as the 'Governor-General of Bengal' and subordinated the presidencies of Madras and Bombay to Bengal. The governors of Madras and Bombay were required to report to the Governor-General, especially on matters of war, peace, and alliances.

q: What was the primary focus of the 1812 House of Commons Committee before the renewal of the East India Company's Charter in 1813?
o: Judicial and police administration in India
exp: The 1812 Select Committee of the House of Commons was tasked with reviewing the East India Company’s governance before the Charter Act of 1813. While the public debate was about trade monopoly, the committee's primary investigation focused on the administrative and legal systems. Its findings, published in the famous Fifth Report (1812), critically examined the effectiveness of the judicial and police systems in Bengal and Madras, highlighting the corruption and delays that plagued the Company’s rule in India.

q: The main purpose of the introduction of the railway network in India by the British was to:
o: Facilitate the movement of Indian pilgrims across the country.
Promote tourism and cultural exchange among different regions of India.
Enhance the efficient transportation of raw materials and finished goods for British economic interests and to facilitate troop movement.
Connect remote rural areas to urban centers for the benefit of local trade.
exp: The British systematically introduced the massive railway network in India during the 1850s primarily to serve their own imperial interests. The core objectives were to rapidly transport cheap raw materials from India's interior to ports for export to Britain, flood Indian markets with British manufactured goods, and swiftly mobilize military troops.

q: The "Wood's Despatch" of 1854 recommended several significant changes in the Indian education system. Which of the following was a key recommendation of this despatch?
o: The immediate vernacularization of all levels of education.
The establishment of a comprehensive system of education from the primary to the university level, with English as the medium of instruction at higher levels.
The complete privatization of the education sector in India.
The exclusive focus on the training of religious leaders and scholars.
exp: Popularly celebrated as the "Magna Carta of English Education in India," Charles Wood's Despatch (1854) proposed a structured educational hierarchy. It formally recommended vernacular languages for primary schools, Anglo-vernacular for high schools, and specifically mandated English as the exclusive medium of instruction for comprehensive university-level higher education.

q: Fill in the blank: The Indian Councils Act 1892 for the first time permitted legislative councils to _______
exp: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 was a highly significant constitutional milestone. Prompted by early demands from the Indian National Congress, the Act substantially expanded the functions of the Legislative Councils, officially permitting the Indian members, for the very first time, to critically discuss the annual financial budget and address questions to the executive.

q: How did the Bombay and Madras governments respond to the proposal of the 1839 Draft Act on slavery?
o: Both supported the Act without reservations
Bombay supported it, Madras opposed it
Bombay saw no need for a law; Madras questioned its expediency
Both governments demanded full enforcement of the Act
exp: When the British drafted the 1839 Act aiming to systematically abolish slavery in India, they faced sharp regional pushback. The Bombay government brazenly argued there was absolutely no need for such legislation in their presidency, while the Madras government cynically questioned the immediate political and economic expediency of abruptly abolishing the entrenched system.

q: The "Charter Act of 1833" made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of:
exp: The historically significant Charter Act of 1833 was a pivotal moment in centralizing British administration. It officially elevated the title of the 'Governor-General of Bengal' to the prestigious 'Governor- General of India', investing him with absolute, sweeping civil and military authority across all British territories. Lord William Bentinck proudly became the very first Governor-General of India.

q: The "Subsidiary Alliance" system, pioneered by Lord Wellesley, had a significant impact on the political map of India. What was a primary consequence for the Indian states that entered into this alliance?
o: They gained greater military strength and autonomy in their external relations.
They were effectively brought under British political influence and control, losing their independent foreign policy and often their military capacity.
They experienced rapid economic growth due to British investment and administrative reforms.
They formed a strong unified front against the expansion of British power in India.
exp: The Subsidiary Alliance was a highly coercive diplomatic strategy engineered by Lord Wellesley. When Indian rulers accepted this alliance, they were completely stripped of their fundamental right to form foreign alliances or wage war independently. They were forced to maintain British troops at their own massive expense, completely surrendering their sovereignty to overwhelming British control.

q: The "Indian Forest Act" of 1878 categorized forests into reserved and protected areas. What was a key difference in the treatment and rights of local communities between these two categories?
o: Both categories granted complete autonomy to local communities in forest management.
In reserved forests, all traditional rights of local communities were extinguished, while some limited rights were permitted in protected forests.
Protected forests were exclusively for commercial exploitation by the British, while reserved forests were for local use.
There was no significant difference in the restrictions imposed on local communities between the two categories.
exp: The oppressive 1878 Forest Act heavily restricted indigenous access to resources. "Reserved Forests" were absolute state property where local communities were strictly banned from grazing or timber collection. Conversely, in "Protected Forests," locals retained very fragile, limited customary rights, which the British could arbitrarily revoke at any time.

q: Which Act formally ended the East India Company's trade monopoly over the Indian market, reflecting the shift in British economic policy toward "Free Trade"?
exp: The Charter Act of 1813 officially abolished the East India Company's strict trade monopoly over India, finally opening the massive Indian market to all British merchants under the doctrine of "Free Trade". However, the Company temporarily retained its highly lucrative monopoly over the tea trade and exclusive commercial trading rights with China.

q: Regarding the 'Subsidiary Alliance' system introduced by Lord Wellesley (1798-1805), which of the following statements is INCORRECT?
o: The ruler was free to employ any European (French, Portuguese, etc.) as long as they were not in active conflict with the British
If the ruler failed to make payments for the maintenance of the British force, a portion of his territory was ceded as a penalty.
The Indian ruler was required to disband his own military and maintain a permanent British contingent within his territory.
The British promised not to interfere in the internal administrative affairs of the allied state.
exp: The first statement is blatantly incorrect. Under the intensely coercive conditions of the Subsidiary Alliance, Indian rulers were absolutely forbidden from employing any Europeans (especially French rivals) in their service without the prior explicit, written consent of the British East India Company, systematically eliminating all foreign competition from the subcontinent.

q: What was the primary change introduced by the Charter Act of 1833 regarding the Governor-General's position?
o: The Governor-General's position was abolished, and the Viceroy of India was appointed.
The Governor-General of Bengal was elevated to the position of Governor-General of India.
The Governor-General of Bengal lost all powers in favor of the British
The position of the Governor- General of Bengal was decentralized to regional governors.
exp: The Charter Act of 1833 represents the absolute, final step towards rigid administrative centralization in British India. The act explicitly and officially elevated the "Governor-General of Bengal" to the supremely powerful new title of "Governor-General of India," vesting in him the exclusive civil and military powers for the entire British Indian territory. Lord William Bentinck became the very first Governor-General of India under this act.

q: What was the impact of the Charter Act of 1853 on the recruitment of civil servants in India?
o: It limited civil servant recruitment to British nationals and excluded Indians entirely.
It abolished the covenanted civil service, leaving no administrative body.
It replaced the competition system with appointments based on seniority alone.
It introduced an open competition system for civil servants, allowing Indians to compete.
exp: The highly historic Charter Act of 1853 brought a massive, fundamentally transformative structural change to the incredibly elitist British Indian administration. Crucially, it completely abolished the corrupt patronage system aggressively operated by the Court of Directors of the East India Company. Instead, it explicitly and officially introduced the "system of open competitive examination" for heavily recruiting elite 'covenanted' civil servants, officially (though restrictively) throwing open the highly prestigious doors of the massive Indian Civil Service to educated Indians for the very first time.

q: Which of the following was a key feature introduced by the Indian Councils Act of 1861?
o: The establishment of a unicameral legislative system in India.
The complete independence of provincial legislatures.
The appointment of a British monarch as the head of the Indian government.
The introduction of the portfolio system and decentralization of power.
exp: Following the devastating aftermath of the 1857 Revolt, the British Parliament urgently enacted the Indian Councils Act of 1861. This monumental, highly consequential legislation explicitly introduced two massive administrative changes. First, it gave full statutory recognition to the highly efficient "Portfolio System" (allocating specific departments to Viceroy's council members). Second, it aggressively initiated the "decentralization of power" by rapidly restoring absolute legislative powers back to the Bombay and Madras Presidencies, completely reversing the previous harsh centralizing trends of the 1833 Act.

q: Who relaxed the laws imposed by the Press Act of 1799 and removed pre-censorship of the press in 1818?
exp: The extremely draconian Censorship of Press Act was violently imposed by Lord Wellesley in 1799, essentially gagging Indian newspapers facing French threats. However, it was the comparatively progressive Governor-General Lord Hastings (Marquess of Hastings) who officially and drastically relaxed these severe restrictions in 1818. He permanently abolished the stifling "pre-censorship" requirement, momentarily granting a brief, encouraging period of relative freedom to the burgeoning Indian press.

q: The 'Permanent Settlement' (1793), a land revenue system, was introduced by Lord Cornwallis in which region?
exp: The 'Permanent Settlement' (Zamindari System) was a deeply exploitative, historic land revenue policy officially introduced by Governor-General Lord Cornwallis in 1793. It was ruthlessly implemented primarily across the fertile provinces of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. Under this rigid system, prominent Zamindars were recognized as absolute, permanent owners of the land, heavily tasked with aggressively collecting fixed revenue for the East India Company, permanently stripping poor peasants of their customary land rights.

q: Which system was introduced by the Indian Councils Act of 1861, assigning members to specific government departments?
exp: The Indian Councils Act of 1861 fundamentally revolutionized the executive functioning of the British Indian government by giving strict statutory recognition to the "Portfolio System" (originally introduced informally by Lord Canning in 1859). Under this highly efficient, modern system, ordinary members of the Viceroy's Executive Council were officially placed in absolute charge of specific, individual government departments (like Finance, Home, or Military) and authorized to issue binding final orders on behalf of the entire council.

q: What was the purpose of the Vernacular Press Act of 1878?
o: To allow free criticism of the British government
To foster a free and independent press in Indis
To restrict criticism by seizing newspaper assets
exp: The intensely draconian Vernacular Press Act of 1878, ruthlessly enacted by the unpopular Viceroy Lord Lytton, was deliberately designed to violently suppress and heavily silence the rapidly growing anti- British sentiment spreading through native Indian-language (vernacular) newspapers. The oppressive act explicitly granted magistrates massive dictatorial powers to mercilessly confiscate printing presses, assets, and properties of any regional newspaper that dared to publish anything remotely critical or "seditious" against the brutal colonial government.

q: Which reform first introduced the principle of 'separate electorates' (for Muslims), also known as communal representation?
exp: The deeply divisive Indian Councils Act of 1909, famously known throughout history as the "Morley-Minto Reforms," marked a deeply damaging turning point in India's political trajectory. It notoriously and officially introduced the dangerous principle of "separate electorates" specifically for Muslims. Under this highly controversial, toxic system of communal representation, Muslim candidates could only be exclusively voted for by Muslim voters, a deliberate British 'divide and rule' tactic that tragically planted the earliest seeds of India's bloody partition.

q: Which provinces were granted legislative councils under the Indian Councils Act of 1861?
exp: Note: Added Madras as a 4th option. The landmark Indian Councils Act of 1861 completely reversed the massive, rigid centralization thrust of the 1833 Charter Act. It aggressively restored legislative powers to the Bombay and Madras Presidencies. More importantly, it explicitly mandated the establishment of entirely new Legislative Councils for the vast provinces of Bengal (formed in 1862), the North-Western Provinces (formed in 1886), and 'Punjab' (formed subsequently in 1897), marking the absolute genesis of provincial legislative devolution in British India.

q: How did the Regulating Act of 1773 change the administrative structure of British India?
o: It made the governors of Bombay and Madras independent of the Governor-General of Bengal.
It removed the powers of the Governor-General of Bengal in the administration.
It introduced multiple governors for each presidency without central auth
It created a central administration under the Governor-General of Bengal with a new Executive Council.
exp: The Regulating Act of 1773 is monumental because it was the British Parliament's very first aggressive attempt to strictly control the wildly corrupt East India Company. It totally radically altered the entire administrative structure by aggressively elevating the Governor of Bengal (Warren Hastings) to the supremely powerful position of "Governor- General of Bengal." It heavily established a central administration, subordinating the previously independent Bombay and Madras Presidencies entirely to Bengal, and created a formidable four-member Executive Council to assist him.

q: The first railway line in India (Bombay to Thane) was opened in 1853 during the time of which Governor-General?
exp: The very first passenger railway line in the Indian subcontinent, smoothly connecting Bombay (Bori Bunder) to Thane over a distance of 34 kilometers, was inaugurated strictly on April 16, 1853. This historic technological milestone occurred during the highly expansive tenure of Governor-General Lord Dalhousie. Because of his aggressive push to rapidly build railways, telegraph lines, and postal networks, Dalhousie is universally hailed as the definitive "Maker of Modern India."

q: The first synchronous (regular) census, which began the 10- year cycle, was conducted in 1881 under which Viceroy?
exp: While the very first, localized, and non-synchronous census attempts in India occurred around 1872 under Lord Mayo, the first absolute, complete, and perfectly synchronous pan-India Census was meticulously conducted in the year 1881. This monumental bureaucratic achievement took place under the progressive administration of Viceroy Lord Ripon. This crucial 1881 census permanently established the rigid, uninterrupted decennial (10-year) cycle of demographic enumeration that India strictly follows even today.

q: What was the reason for the Partition of Bengal (1905) given by Lord Curzon?
exp: When Viceroy Lord Curzon violently executed the highly controversial Partition of Bengal in 1905, his official, publicly stated justification was purely "administrative efficiency." He argued that the Bengal Presidency, with its massive 78 million population, was far too enormous and unwieldy to govern effectively. However, the sinister, actual underlying political motive was to ruthlessly divide the fiercely united Bengali nationalists along religious lines to actively weaken the raging Indian freedom struggle.

q: Why was the Vernacular Press Act of 1878, often referred to as the "Gagging Act," enacted?
o: Facilitate translation of English literature into regional languages.
Suppress Indian-language newspapers that criticized colonial policies.
exp: The notoriously draconian Vernacular Press Act of 1878, aggressively enacted by the unpopular Viceroy Lord Lytton, was deliberately designed to violently "suppress Indian-language newspapers that criticized colonial policies." Fearing the rapid rise of fierce, anti-British nationalist sentiments spread by regional papers, this 'Gagging Act' granted magistrates sweeping dictatorial powers to ruthlessly confiscate the printing presses of native publishers without any right to judicial appeal. It notably exempted English-language newspapers completely.

q: The Hunter Commission of 1882 was primarily related to what?
exp: The Hunter Education Commission of 1882 was established by Lord Ripon (headed by Sir William Wilson Hunter) explicitly to review and recommend crucial reforms in the primary and secondary education sectors in British India, advocating for local body control over primary education. The 1919 Hunter Committee (Disorders Inquiry Committee) investigated the Jallianwala Bagh massacre. Famine commissions were led by Strachey or MacDonnell. Police reforms were handled by the Fraser Commission (1902). Therefore, education is the precise context here.

q: Who was the Viceroy of India in 1904?
exp: Lord Curzon served as the powerful and controversial Viceroy of India from 1899 to 1905, placing him directly in power during the year 1904. In 1904, he notably passed the Indian Universities Act and the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act. Lord Minto succeeded him (1905-1910). Lord Hardinge served later (1910-1916). Lord Chelmsford governed during the passage of the Rowlatt Act (1916-1921). Thus, Lord Curzon is the historically correct Viceroy for the specified year.

q: The Hunter Commission (1882) was appointed primarily to review the progress of what?
exp: The Indian Education Commission of 1882, popularly known as the Hunter Commission, was appointed by Lord Ripon to rigorously review the educational progress made since Charles Wood's Despatch of 1854. Its primary mandate and resulting recommendations overwhelmingly focused on improving and expanding primary and secondary education across British India, rather than university or specialized technical education. Higher education was later targeted by the Raleigh Commission (1902) and Sadler Commission (1917).

q: Who among the following was the first Indian to join the ICS (Indian Civil Service)?
exp: Satyendranath Tagore, the elder brother of Rabindranath Tagore, made history in 1863 by becoming the very first Indian to qualify for and join the highly prestigious Indian Civil Service (ICS), navigating through the rigorous examination held in England. Surendranath Banerjee and Romesh Chandra Dutt also qualified for the ICS, but they achieved this feat in later years (1869). Subramania Iyer was a prominent jurist. Thus, Satyendranath Tagore holds the inaugurating distinction.

q: Which of the following pioneering English-language publications, founded in the late 18th century by James Augustus Hicky, is recognized as India's first newspaper?
exp: 'Hicky's Bengal Gazette', bravely founded by the eccentric Irishman James Augustus Hicky in Calcutta in 1780, holds the monumental historical distinction of being the very first printed newspaper published in both India and the entire Asian continent. It was highly critical of Governor-General Warren Hastings, leading to its eventual suppression. The Times of India and Amrita Bazar Patrika were highly influential but were established much later in the 19th century.

q: The 'Ryotwari System' of land revenue, introduced in South India, was mainly associated with?
exp: The 'Ryotwari System' was a prominent land revenue model designed by Captain Alexander Read and extensively implemented by Sir Thomas Munro in 1820 across the Madras and Bombay Presidencies. Under this system, revenue settlements were directly made with the individual cultivators (ryots), entirely bypassing intermediaries like Zamindars. Lord Cornwallis is associated with the Permanent Settlement in Bengal. Therefore, Thomas Munro is the historically accurate architect of the Ryotwari framework.

q: Under the Regulating Act of 1773, who became the first Governor-General of Bengal?
exp: Under the provisions of the pivotal Regulating Act of 1773, the administration of the East India Company was centralized, elevating the Governor of Bengal to the newly created position of the 'Governor- General of Bengal'. Warren Hastings, who was serving as the Governor, officially became the very first Governor-General. Robert Clive was an earlier Governor who won Plassey. Cornwallis and Wellesley assumed this apex office much later in history.

q: What was the Ilbert Bill controversy?
o: Recruitment of Indians in Indian Civil Services
Equality of judicial powers for Indian judges
exp: The Ilbert Bill, introduced in 1883 during the viceroyalty of Lord Ripon by Sir Courtenay Ilbert, aimed to grant equal judicial powers to Indian magistrates, allowing them to preside over cases involving British or European offenders in rural areas. This sparked a massive, racist backlash and organized protests from the European community in India, eventually forcing the government to severely dilute the bill. It was not related to vernacular education, civil services recruitment, or land tax increments.

q: Why was the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 enacted during the late 19th century under British India?
o: Standardizing land revenue procedures in Punjab
Expanding the powers and revenue claims of zamindars
Protecting tenant farmers from arbitrary eviction by landlords
exp: The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 was enacted explicitly to protect the rights of the tenant farmers (ryots) against the severe exploitation, exorbitant rent demands, and arbitrary evictions carried out by the powerful Zamindars under the Permanent Settlement system. It recognized occupancy rights for tenants who had held land for over 12 years. It aimed to curtail Zamindar powers, not expand them, and had nothing to do with Punjab's revenue or specifically promoting indigo cultivation.

q: The 'Delhi Durbar' of 1911 was held to commemorate the coronation of which British monarch?
exp: The spectacular Delhi Durbar of 1911 was held to officially commemorate the coronation of King George V and Queen Mary as the Emperor and Empress of India. It was the only Durbar that a reigning British sovereign attended in person. During this event, he historically announced the shifting of India's capital from Calcutta to Delhi and annulled the Partition of Bengal. Queen Victoria was proclaimed Empress in the 1877 Durbar, while Edward VII was honored in 1903.

q: What was the primary purpose of the Regulating Act of 1773?
o: To establish a new administrative system for the East India Company
To grant complete independence to the East India Company.
To control and regulate the affairs of the East India Company.
To eliminate the British government's influence in India.
exp: The incredibly monumental and historically unprecedented Regulating Act of 1773 stands firmly as the absolute very first massive legislative intervention deliberately executed by the supreme British Parliament concerning Indian territories. Prompted forcefully by massive reports of severe, rampant financial corruption, extreme administrative mismanagement, and a shocking, massive impending bankruptcy within the massive commercial corporation, its absolute primary, overarching constitutional objective was forcefully "To systematically control, strictly oversee, and tightly regulate the chaotic, highly unregulated affairs of the incredibly powerful East India Company in India." The crucial act explicitly subordinated the incredibly wealthy Company to intense, strict British parliamentary supervision, creating the powerful office of the Governor-General of Bengal to aggressively centralize administrative authority. Therefore, option (c) is flawlessly the correct historical answer. It definitely did not grant them complete independence (b) or establish a totally brand-new system (a).

q: What was the primary purpose of the Government of India Act of 1858?
o: To establish a system of self-rule for the Indian population.
To introduce local Indian representation in the governance system.
To grant full independence to the Indian subcontinent.
To transfer governance from the East India Company to the British Crown.
exp: Immediately following the massive Revolt of 1857, the British Parliament enacted the Government of India Act 1858 to entirely liquidate the British East India Company. Its sole primary purpose was to formally and completely transfer the administrative governance, territories, and revenues of India directly to the British Crown, establishing the British Raj under a Secretary of State. It absolutely did not grant independence or self-rule; those came a century later.

q: Why was there a furore over the Ilbert Bill in 1883?
o: It suggested the removal of Indian judges from the courts, replacing them with British judges.
It proposed equal rights for British and Indian judges, opposed by the British.
It allowed Indians to hold positions in the British army, giving them opportunities for higher- ranking roles.
It introduced new taxes on Indian businesses, increasing their financial burden.
exp: Introduced during Lord Ripon's viceroyalty in 1883, the Ilbert Bill sought to abolish racial discrimination in the judiciary by allowing senior Indian magistrates to preside over cases involving European subjects. This sparked massive outrage and organized protests among the European community in India (the "White Mutiny"), ultimately forcing the British government to severely dilute the bill.

q: Which case is recognized as the first sedition case in India under Section 124A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC)?
o: Queen Empress vs. Bal Gangadhar Tilak
Queen Empress vs. Jogendra Chunder Bose
Queen Empress vs. Lala Lajpat Rai
exp: The case of Queen Empress vs. Jogendra Chunder Bose (1891) is historically recognized as the first registered sedition case under Section 124A of the IPC. Bose, the editor of the Bengali magazine 'Bangobasi', was charged for writing articles heavily criticizing the British government's Age of Consent Act. Cases against prominent leaders like Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Mahatma Gandhi happened much later in 1897 and 1922, respectively.

q: Who was responsible for drafting the Indian Penal Code (IPC) in 1837?
exp: The comprehensive Indian Penal Code (IPC) was meticulously drafted by the First Law Commission of India in 1834 under the strict chairmanship of Lord Thomas Babington Macaulay. The highly detailed draft was completed and submitted to the Governor-General of India in 1837. Macaulay’s brilliant legal framework systematically codified all criminal offences, replacing arbitrary local laws, and officially came into force much later in 1862.

q: Which legendary martyr's attack on British officers in 1857, is considered the first major incident of the Sepoy Mutiny?
exp: Mangal Pandey is the legendary martyr whose attack on his British superiors at Barrackpore on March 29, 1857, is widely considered the first major incident triggering the Sepoy Mutiny. He injured Lieutenant Baugh and Sergeant-Major Hewson before being overpowered. Options (a), (c), and (d) are incorrect as these leaders belonged to later phases of the freedom struggle (Moderate and Gandhian eras). An interesting fact is that the British were so panicked by his actions that they executed him ten days before the scheduled date to prevent further unrest.

q: At which of the following places Mangal Pandey was hanged till death for attacking his officers?
exp: Mangal Pandey was hanged at Barrackpore (in present-day West Bengal) on April 8, 1857. The execution took place before the garrison to set an example for other sepoys. Options (a), (c), and (d) are incorrect; while Delhi and Lucknow were major centers of the subsequent revolt, the initial incident and execution occurred at the Barrackpore cantonment. A key fact is that the regiment to which he belonged, the 34th Bengal Native Infantry, was disbanded in disgrace shortly after his execution.

q: The revolt of 1857 was started by the sepoys from which of the following places?
exp: The formal outbreak of the Revolt of 1857 began in Meerut on May 10, 1857. The sepoys broke open the prisons, released their comrades who had been jailed for refusing the Enfield cartridges, and marched towards Delhi. While Mangal Pandey's incident in Bengal (Barrackpore) preceded this, the actual organized rebellion started in Meerut. Options (a) and (b) saw fighting later, and (d) Madras remained largely peaceful. The rebels marched to Delhi and proclaimed the aging Bahadur Shah Zafar as the Emperor of Hindustan.

q: At which of the following places Nana Saheb gathered the armed forces and expelled the British garrison from the city?
exp: Nana Saheb, the adopted son of the exiled Peshwa Baji Rao II, led the revolt in Kanpur. He expelled the British garrison and declared himself the Peshwa, acknowledging the sovereignty of the Mughal Emperor. Options (a), (b), and (c) are incorrect locations for his specific leadership; Delhi was led by General Bakht Khan, and Nagpur was largely quiet. A notable fact is that the Siege of Cawnpore (Kanpur) became infamous for the Satichaura Ghat massacre, which severely hardened British attitudes against the rebels.

q: Tantia Tope was the general of whom among the following?
exp: Tantia Tope was the commander-in-chief and most capable general of Nana Saheb. He played a pivotal role in capturing Kanpur and later, after Nana Saheb’s defeat, he joined forces with the Rani of Jhansi to capture Gwalior. Option (b) Begum Hazrat Mahal led the revolt in Lucknow. Option (c) Bahadur Shah Zafar was the symbolic head in Delhi. Option (d) is incorrect as Baji Rao II was Nana Saheb's father. Tantia Tope was a master of guerrilla warfare and evaded the British for nearly two years before being betrayed and executed in 1859.

q: Rani Laxmi Bai was defeated and killed in:
exp: Rani Laxmi Bai of Jhansi attained martyrdom on June 18, 1858, during the battle for Gwalior. She died fighting bravely against the British forces led by Sir Hugh Rose at Kotah-ki-Serai. Options (a), (b), and (d) are incorrect dates. Her death effectively marked the end of the most active phase of the rebellion. Sir Hugh Rose famously described her as "the most dangerous of all Indian leaders" and "the only man among the rebels."

q: Peer Ali Khan organized rebels and challenged British rule in which major city of Bihar?
exp: Peer Ali Khan was a humble bookbinder who organized the rebellion in Patna, Bihar. He distributed secret leaflets and mobilized the local population against the British. He was captured and hanged by Commissioner William Taylor in July 1857. Options (a), (c), and (d) are incorrect as his activities were centered in Patna. An inspiring fact is that when offered a pardon in exchange for names of co-conspirators, he refused, stating, "You may hang me... but you cannot kill our ideal."

q: What happened to Bahadur Shah Zafar after the revolt of 1857 was put down by the British East India Company?
o: He was forced to leave the kingdom.
He was made a puppet ruler.
He was made the emperor again.
exp: Following the brutal suppression of the 1857 Sepoy Mutiny, the British East India Company arrested the 82-year-old last Mughal Emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar. He was tried for treason, stripped of all titles, and forced to leave the kingdom, being exiled to Rangoon (Yangon, Myanmar) where he eventually died in 1862. He was neither made a puppet ruler nor restored as emperor. The rebellion's aftermath, specifically the harsh fate of the Mughal dynasty, is heavily tested by SSC.

q: Who among the following raised and led an army of four thousand against the British in the Mandla region of Madhya Pradesh?
exp: Rani Avantibai Lodhi was a remarkably brave and prominent warrior queen of the princely state of Ramgarh (in present-day Madhya Pradesh). During the historic Indian Rebellion of 1857, she aggressively raised and courageously led a massive army of four thousand soldiers directly against the oppressive British East India Company forces in the Mandla region. She fought valiantly but ultimately embraced martyrdom rather than surrendering. Bahadur Shah Zafar was the symbolic head in Delhi, Begum Hazrat Mahal led the revolt in Awadh, and Tantia Tope fought primarily in the Kanpur/Gwalior regions.

q: Read the following statements and mark the correct option: Assertion (A): Peer Ali Khan was executed during the 1857 Revolt. Reason (R): He was a British informant who switched sides during the uprising.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
exp: Peer Ali Khan was a courageous bookseller and a prominent leader of the 1857 rebellion in Patna. He successfully mobilized masses against the East India Company. He was never a British informant; instead, he was arrested by Commissioner William Tayler and publicly hanged for his fierce anti-colonial resistance.

q: Bhima Nayak, a prominent tribal leader during the 1857 rebellion, is known for which of the following contributions?
o: Leading tribal uprisings in the Satpura region of Madhya Pradesh and coordinating guerrilla tactics against the British.
Negotiating a peace treaty between British authorities and rebel leaders in Central India.
Serving as a close aide to Rani Lakshmibai and leading regular army battalions in open warfare.
Establishing a provisional government in Jhansi during the rebellion.
exp: Bhima Nayak (often called the Robin Hood of Nimar) was a fierce Bhil warrior. During the 1857 Mutiny, he organized the tribal populations of the Satpura-Nimar region in Madhya Pradesh, unleashing successful guerrilla warfare against the British, disrupting their crucial supply lines, and fighting alongside prominent rebel leader Tatya Tope.

q: Which region did Kunwar Singh primarily organize resistance against the British?
exp: The legendary, fiercely heroic Babu Veer Kunwar Singh, famously a powerful Zamindar of the expansive Jagdishpur estate, emerged as the absolute most prominent and formidable leader during the massive Great Revolt of 1857 in the state of "Bihar." Despite being nearly 80 years old, he brilliantly orchestrated relentless, highly tactical armed resistance. Waging brilliant guerrilla warfare, he ruthlessly repeatedly defeated massive British forces across Arrah and central Bihar, permanently becoming a grand icon of anti-colonial valor.

q: How did Raja Rammohan Roy contribute to the movement against the practice of Sati?
exp: Raja Rammohan Roy led a relentless crusade against Sati primarily by campaigning using newspapers, writing tracts, and organizing public debates to prove that the practice had no sanction in ancient Hindu scriptures. He used his journal Sambad Kaumudi to mold public opinion. Option (a) is incorrect as he was a pacifist reformer. Option (b) is wrong as only the Governor-General could issue ordinances. Option (d) is incorrect; while he knew missionaries, his arguments were rooted in rationalism and Hindu texts. His efforts directly led to the 1829 ban.

q: Who introduced the law that abolished the practice of Sati in British India in 1829?
exp: The practice of Sati was legally abolished in 1829 by Lord William Bentinck, the then Governor-General of Bengal. He passed Regulation XVII, which declared Sati illegal and punishable by courts. Option (a), (b), and (d) are incorrect; Dalhousie and Canning came later, and Curzon ruled in the early 20th century. Bentinck is often regarded as the "Father of Modern Western Education in India" (alongside Macaulay) and was known for his liberal social reforms, unlike many of his predecessors who feared interfering in Indian customs.

q: Prime Minister Narendra Modi paid tribute to Mahatma Jyotiba Phule on his birth anniversary. Phule is best known for his contributions to which of the following?
exp: Mahatma Jyotiba Phule is best known for his pioneering work in Social Reform and the Anti-Caste Movement in Maharashtra. He founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (Truth Seekers' Society) in 1873 to secure human rights and social justice for the marginalized lower castes. Options (a), (b), and (c) are not his primary fields of contribution. He also wrote the famous book Gulamgiri (Slavery), dedicating it to the American movement to abolish slavery, linking the condition of the "black slaves" in America with the "lower castes" in India.

q: Who was the first female teacher of India who founded the first girls' school?
exp: Savitribai Jyotiba Phule is honored as India's first female teacher. Along with her husband Jyotiba Phule, she established the first school for girls in Pune at Bhide Wada in 1848. Options (a), (b), and (c) are incorrect; while they were prominent figures, they came much later in history. Savitribai faced immense social opposition, with people often throwing mud and stones at her as she walked to school, yet she persisted in her mission to educate women and the oppressed.

q: Who set up a Dayanand Anglo Vedic school in Lahore?
exp: The Dayanand Anglo Vedic (DAV) schools were established to honor Swami Dayanand Saraswati after his death. The first DAV School was set up in Lahore in 1886 by Mahatma Hansraj, with the active support and leadership of Lala Lajpat Rai. Among the given options, Lala Lajpat Rai is the correct answer as he was a key figure in the Arya Samaj's educational movement in Punjab. Option (c) is incorrect as Dayanand had already passed away. Options (b) and (d) were not associated with this specific initiative in Lahore.

q: Which of the following pairs (Educational Event - Key Outcome) is correctly matched?
exp: The Charter Act of 1813 is the correct match as it sanctioned a sum of one lakh rupees annually for the promotion of education in India, marking the first time the British government accepted responsibility for education. Option (b) is incorrect because Macaulay's Minute (1835) strongly advocated for English education, not Sanskrit. Option (c) is wrong as Serampore missionaries focused on vernacular education and printing. Option (d) is a mismatch in context. This Act opened the door for English education and missionary activities in India.

q: Which education-related document, issued in 1854, laid the foundation for modern education in India?
exp: Wood's Despatch of 1854, issued by Charles Wood (President of the Board of Control), is often called the "Magna Carta of English Education in India." It laid the comprehensive foundation for the modern educational structure, recommending a hierarchy of schools from primary to university level. Option (a) came earlier (1835). Option (b) came later (1882). Option (d) is a generic term. A key outcome of this despatch was the establishment of the Universities of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras in 1857.

q: Thakkar Bapa was a dedicated social worker known for efforts towards the upliftment of:
exp: Amritlal Vithaldas Thakkar, popularly known as Thakkar Bapa, dedicated his life to the upliftment of Tribal (Adivasi) communities and Harijans. He served as the General Secretary of the Harijan Sevak Sangh founded by Gandhi and also established the Bhil Seva Mandal in 1922. Option (a), (b), and (d) were not his primary focus. He actually coined the term "Adivasi" to refer to the indigenous tribes and played a crucial role in drafting the constitutional provisions for Scheduled Tribes in India.

q: In 1930, _____ established the Depressed Classes Association.
exp: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar established the Depressed Classes Association in 1930. The primary motive was to politically organize the Dalit community and strongly demand separate electorates for them, a demand he famously presented during the Second Round Table Conference. Mahatma Gandhi founded the Harijan Sevak Sangh later in 1932. Jyotiba Phule formed the Satyashodhak Samaj in 1873. M.G. Ranade was associated with the Prarthana Samaj. SSC frequently tests the distinction between organizations founded by Ambedkar and Gandhi.

q: Veda Samaj, established in Chennai, was inspired by which of the following?
exp: The Veda Samaj, actively founded in Madras (Chennai) in 1864 by Keshab Chandra Sen and K. Sridharalu Naidu, was profoundly inspired by the progressive reformist ideals of the Brahmo Samaj of Bengal. It aggressively campaigned to eradicate rigid caste distinctions, promote widow remarriage, and champion women's education, while strictly condemning orthodox superstitions. The Arya Samaj was founded much later in 1875 by Swami Dayananda Saraswati. The Ramakrishna Mission was established in 1897. Understanding the ideological lineage of socio- religious movements is heavily tested.

q: Which of the following institutions was established by Rabindranath Tagore?
exp: In 1901, the visionary poet Rabindranath Tagore officially established an experimental, open-air school at Santiniketan (Abode of Peace) in rural Bengal, aiming to heavily blend the ancient Indian Gurukul system with modern progressive education. This highly prestigious institution eventually expanded and blossomed into Visva-Bharati University in 1921. Conversely, Fort William College was founded by Lord Wellesley in 1800. Hindu College (later Presidency College) was established in 1817 by Raja Ram Mohan Roy and David Hare.

q: At which place was the Prarthana Samaj established in 1867?
exp: The Prarthana Samaj (Prayer Society) was historically and prominently established in the cosmopolitan city of Bombay (present-day Mumbai) in the year 1867 by Dr. Atmaram Pandurang. This progressive socio-religious reform movement was deeply inspired by the ideological visits of Keshab Chandra Sen to Maharashtra. It aggressively focused on crucial social reforms such as abolishing the rigid caste system, promoting widow remarriage, and strongly advocating for women's education. Calcutta was the foundational hub of the Brahmo Samaj.

q: In which of the following places was the first Singh Sabha formed?
exp: The very first and historically paramount Singh Sabha was officially formed in the sacred city of Amritsar, Punjab, in the year 1873. This highly influential socio-religious reform movement was urgently established by prominent Sikh leaders specifically to aggressively counter the rising proselytizing activities of Christian missionaries and Hindu reformists. Its core objective was to deeply restore the authentic purity of the Sikh faith, publish historical Sikh literature, and aggressively promote modern education among Sikh youth. It was decidedly not founded in Delhi, Karachi, or Hyderabad.

q: Who called the 'untouchables' Harijans or children of God?
exp: The great Mahatma Gandhi actively coined and heavily popularized the deeply compassionate term 'Harijan' (which literally translates to "Children of God") to respectfully refer to the severely oppressed 'untouchable' communities of India. In 1933, he aggressively started a highly influential weekly journal strictly named 'Harijan' and founded the Harijan Sevak Sangh to vehemently fight against the cruel social evil of untouchability. Conversely, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar generally preferred strictly using the term 'Depressed Classes' or 'Dalits' for political empowerment.

q: Who founded the reform organisation called Arya Samaj?
exp: The Arya Samaj was founded by the great Hindu ascetic and social reformer Swami Dayanand Saraswati in Bombay in the year 1875. The organisation promoted the infallibility of the Vedas (giving the famous call 'Go back to the Vedas') and condemned social evils like rigid casteism, untouchability, and idol worship. Raja Rammohun Roy established the Brahmo Samaj earlier, in 1828.

q: At which of the following places was the Hindu College established in 1791 to encourage the study of ancient Sanskrit texts?
exp: In 1791, the Sanskrit College (often referred to historically as the Hindu College in earlier texts) was formally established in the sacred city of Benaras (Varanasi) by Jonathan Duncan, the then British Resident. Its primary, explicit objective was to actively encourage the deep study of ancient Sanskrit texts, Hindu laws, and literature to assist the British East India Company in local administration. The other locations are incorrect: In Calcutta, the famous Hindu College was established much later in 1817 by Raja Rammohun Roy and David Hare. Poona and Mysore did not host this specific 1791 institution.

q: Khalsa College was founded by the leaders of which of the following movement?
exp: The historic and prestigious Khalsa College in Amritsar was monumentally established in the year 1892 explicitly by the visionary leaders of the Singh Sabha Movement. This highly influential reformist movement aimed actively to forcefully counter Christian missionary activities and Arya Samaj influence by deeply reviving authentic Sikh doctrines, promoting modern English education among the Sikh youth, and restoring the purity of the Khalsa identity. The Shuddhi movement was run by the Arya Samaj, the Aligarh movement by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, and the Swadeshi movement was a Bengal-led political boycott.

q: Who among the following was a prominent educational reformer and founder of Dayanand Anglo Vedic College?
exp: Lala Hansraj, deeply inspired by the progressive reformist ideals of Swami Dayanand Saraswati and the Arya Samaj, was a monumental educational reformer. He successfully founded the very first Dayanand Anglo Vedic (DAV) College in Lahore in 1886, dedicating his entire life to blending traditional Vedic values with modern Western scientific education. The other prominent figures listed are completely unrelated to the foundation of DAV institutions: Govind Ballabh Pant was a key political leader and the first Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh; Asaf Ali was a notable freedom fighter and diplomat; and Arun Chandra Guha was a respected Bengali nationalist and politician.

q: Who among the following played a significant role in establishing the Indian Women's Movement and All India Women's Conference?
exp: Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay was a highly influential social reformer, freedom fighter, and feminist who played a pivotal role in the Indian Women's Movement. She was instrumental in founding the All India Women's Conference (AIWC) in 1927, which focused on educational and legislative reforms for women. The other options represent important figures in different contexts: Sucheta Kriplani was a prominent freedom fighter and India's first female Chief Minister (UP), Rani Durgavati was a 16th-century warrior queen of Gondwana, and Tileswari Koch was a martyr of the Quit India Movement in Assam.

q: On 8th March 2025, the nation observed the Jayanti of which social reformer and founder of the Matua Sect, known for leading the Chandal movement against untouchability?
exp: Sri Sri Harichand Thakur was an incredibly revered social and religious reformer who founded the egalitarian Matua Mahasangha sect in undivided Bengal. Dedicated entirely to the upliftment of the oppressed Namasudra (Chandal) community, he fiercely fought against entrenched caste discrimination and untouchability through his profound teachings of love, equality, and devotion.

q: Who is associated with All India Scheduled Castes Federation, Mooknayak, Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha, and Bahishkrut Bharat?
exp: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, the principal visionary architect of the Indian Constitution, relentlessly dedicated his entire life to the massive social upliftment and fierce political empowerment of the brutally oppressed Dalit communities. To systematically organize and aggressively voice their struggles, he strategically founded formidable institutions like the 'Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha' (1924) and the 'All India Scheduled Castes Federation' (1942). He also published highly influential, revolutionary Marathi journals like 'Mooknayak' (1920) and 'Bahishkrut Bharat' (1927).

q: The 'Child Marriage Restraint Act of 1929', which fixed the marriage age for girls at 14 and boys at 18, is popularly known as the?
exp: Note: Missing correct option added to maintain historical accuracy. The landmark "Child Marriage Restraint Act of 1929" was a monumental piece of social reform legislation during British India. It is universally and popularly known as the 'Sarda Act', proudly named after its passionate sponsor, Harbilas Sarda. The act aggressively aimed to eradicate the devastating social evil of child marriage by legally establishing the absolute minimum marriageable age at 14 years for girls and 18 years for boys across all communities.

q: Who established the Ramakrishna Mission to promote spiritual upliftment, education, and service inspired by the teachings of Sri Ramakrishna, emphasizing humanitarian and educational work across India?
exp: The Ramakrishna Mission was founded in 1897 by Swami Vivekananda, the chief disciple of the 19th-century mystic Sri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa. Headquartered at Belur Math, its core philosophy revolves around the Vedanta doctrine and "Service to man is service to God" (Daridra Narayana Seva). Ramakrishna himself did not found the institutional mission. Dayanand Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj. Raja Rammohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj. Thus, Vivekananda is the correct founder.

q: Gulamgiri, a critical work on caste oppression and social justice, was authored by which social reformer advocating equality and the upliftment of marginalized communities?
exp: 'Gulamgiri' (Slavery), published in 1873, is a highly influential anti-caste book authored by the great social reformer Mahatma Jyotiba Phule. He dedicated the book to the good people of the United States who fought to abolish slavery, drawing a powerful parallel with the oppression of lower castes in India. He also founded the Satyashodhak Samaj. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar wrote 'Annihilation of Caste'. Periyar led the Self-Respect Movement. Therefore, Jyotiba Phule is the sole author.
