q: Which of the following social reformers, born on December 26, 1914, in Hinganghat, Maharashtra, is best known for his work with leprosy patients and his contributions to social welfare?
exp: Murlidhar Devidas Amte, universally revered as 'Baba Amte', was born on December 26, 1914, in Hinganghat, Wardha, Maharashtra. He dedicated his entire life to the rehabilitation, empowerment, and destigmatization of leprosy patients, famously founding the Anandwan ashram. Medha Patkar is the face of the Narmada Bachao Andolan. Kailash Satyarthi fights against child labor. Anna Hazare is an anti-corruption activist. Therefore, the specific birthdate and absolute dedication to leprosy patients uniquely identify Baba Amte.

q: The social reformer who pioneered the "Self-Respect Movement" in Tamil society, promoting equality, rationalism, and anti-caste ideology, was:
exp: E.V. Ramasamy, universally revered as 'Periyar' (The Great One), was the fiercely radical social visionary who actively launched the monumental "Self-Respect Movement" (Suyamariyathai Iyakkam) in Tamil Nadu in 1925. He aggressively aimed to completely dismantle the oppressive Brahminical hegemony, eradicate deeply rooted caste-based discrimination, and promote scientific rationalism and women's rights to establish an egalitarian Dravidian society. Narayana Guru worked in Kerala. Ambedkar operated mainly from Maharashtra. K. Kelappan was the 'Kerala Gandhi'.

q: Who founded the Kuka Movement in Punjab?
exp: The Kuka Movement, a highly significant politico-religious reform movement among the Sikhs in Punjab, was formally founded and heavily mobilized by Baba Ram Singh (Namdhari Guru Ram Singh) in 1857. The movement aggressively advocated for strict social reforms (like abolishing the caste system and female infanticide) and later evolved into a fierce, massive anti-British political struggle demanding total self-rule and boycotting British goods.

q: Who was the first woman to be the president of the Indian National Congress?
exp: Annie Besant became the first woman President of the Indian National Congress in 1917 at the Calcutta session. A British socialist, theosophist, and women's rights activist, she played a key role in the Indian Home Rule Movement. Option (d) Sarojini Naidu was the first Indian woman president (1925, Kanpur). Options (a) and (b) never held the presidency. Annie Besant's presidency symbolized the growing influence of the Home Rule League and the internationalization of the Indian freedom struggle.

q: The Partition of Bengal in 1905 was carried out under which Viceroy?
exp: The Partition of Bengal was announced in July 1905 and implemented on October 16, 1905, by Lord Curzon, the then Viceroy of India. The official reason given was administrative efficiency, but the real motive was to weaken Bengali nationalism by dividing the province along religious lines (Muslim-majority East and Hindu-majority West). Options (b), (c), and (d) are incorrect viceroys for this period. This event triggered the massive Swadeshi Movement, marking the beginning of mass politics in India.

q: Barindra Kumar Ghosh, Abhinash Bhattacharya and Bhupendranath Dutta were associated with which movement in March 1906?
exp: These revolutionary figures were deeply associated with the Swadeshi Movement and the rise of revolutionary terrorism in Bengal. They founded the newspaper Yugantar in March 1906, which advocated open rebellion against British rule. While the Anti-Partition movement (b) is related, their specific activities in 1906 were part of the broader revolutionary upsurge within the Swadeshi framework. Bhupendranath Dutta was the brother of Swami Vivekananda. Their group eventually formed the Jugantar group, a central part of the Anushilan Samiti.

q: V.O. Chidambaram Pillai was a pioneer of the Swadeshi movement who started which enterprise?
exp: V.O. Chidambaram Pillai (VOC), also known as the "Kappalottiya Tamizhan" (The Tamil Helmsman), established the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company in 1906. This was a direct challenge to the monopoly of the British India Steam Navigation Company (BISN). Options (a), (c), and (d) are incorrect. His venture was a bold attempt to prove that Indians could manage modern industries and trade independently. He was later charged with sedition and sentenced to double life imprisonment for his political activities.

q: Which of the following slogans was raised by Bal Gangadhar Tilak?
o: "Give Me Blood, and I Shall Give You Freedom."
"Freedom is my birthright and I shall have it!"
exp: The slogan "Swaraj (Freedom) is my birthright and I shall have it!" was famously raised by Bal Gangadhar Tilak. This slogan became the clarion call for the Indian independence movement, inspiring millions. Option (a) is from the Mundaka Upanishad, popularized by Madan Mohan Malaviya. Option (b) and (c) are associated with Subhas Chandra Bose. Tilak was the first leader to demand full self-rule (Swaraj) rather than just administrative reforms, earning him the title "Lokmanya" (accepted by the people).

q: What name was given to Bal Gangadhar Tilak by the British rulers?
o: The Father of the Indian Unrest
exp: Valentine Chirol, a British journalist, described Bal Gangadhar Tilak as "The Father of Indian Unrest" in his book Indian Unrest. The British authorities feared his ability to mobilize the masses through his newspapers (Kesari and Mahratta) and festivals (Ganesh Chaturthi). Options (b), (c), and (d) are incorrect; "Iron Man" refers to Sardar Patel. Tilak actually filed a defamation suit against Chirol in London for this label, though he lost the case.

q: Who among the following criticised the Moderates for their "politics of prayer"? I. Bepin Chandra Pal II. Bal Gangadhar Tilak III. Lala Lajpat Rai Choose the correct option:
exp: All three leaders—Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, and Bepin Chandra Pal (collectively known as Lal-Bal-Pal)—severely criticized the Moderate faction of the Congress for their "politics of prayer and petition". They advocated for more assertive methods like Swadeshi, Boycott, and National Education. Therefore, option (d) is correct. They believed that freedom could not be begged for but had to be won through struggle and passive resistance, marking the rise of the "Extremist" phase in Indian politics.

q: The Chapekar Brothers assassinated a British official in response to injustices during the plague in which city?
exp: The Chapekar Brothers (Damodar, Balkrishna, and Vasudev) assassinated W.C. Rand, the British Plague Commissioner, in Pune on June 22, 1897. This was in retaliation for the oppressive measures used by British soldiers during the plague outbreak, such as forced entry into private homes and violation of religious sanctities. Option (a), (b), and (d) are incorrect locations. This act is often cited as the first case of revolutionary violence in the Indian freedom struggle.

q: Which of the following statements is NOT TRUE about Rash Behari Bose?
o: He founded Indian Independence League in Tokyo in 1942.
He was an important figure in the Ghadar Movement and in the formation of the Azad Hind Fauj.
He was honoured with the prestigious title 'Order of the rising sun'.
He was independent India's first Commander-in-Chief of Indian Army.
exp: Statement (d) is NOT TRUE. The first Commander-in- Chief of independent India's Army was General K.M. Cariappa, not Rash Behari Bose. Rash Behari Bose died in Japan in 1945, before India gained independence. Statements (a), (b), and (c) are all factually correct: he founded the Indian Independence League, played a key role in the Ghadar conspiracy and the INA, and was awarded the 'Order of the Rising Sun' by the Japanese government for his contributions.

q: The revolutionary Bagha Jatin was known for inspiring revolutionaries in which Indian state?
exp: Jatindranath Mukherjee, popularly known as Bagha Jatin, was a legendary revolutionary leader from Bengal. He earned the title "Bagha" (Tiger) after killing a tiger with a dagger in his youth. He was the principal leader of the Jugantar party and masterminded the "German Plot" to import arms for a pan-Indian uprising during WWI. Options (a), (b), and (d) are incorrect. He famously said, "Amra morbo, jagat jagbe" (We shall die to awaken the nation) before dying in a shootout with British police at Balasore in 1915.

q: Binoy, Badal, and Dinesh are remembered for their attack on which building in Calcutta?
exp: On December 8, 1930, the revolutionary trio Binoy Basu, Badal Gupta, and Dinesh Gupta stormed the Writers' Building, the secretariat of the Bengal government in Calcutta. Their objective was to assassinate the brutal Inspector General of Police, N.S. Simpson, whom they successfully killed. Options (a), (b), and (d) are incorrect targets. After the attack, Badal took cyanide, while Binoy and Dinesh shot themselves to avoid capture. BBD Bagh (formerly Dalhousie Square) in Kolkata is named in their honor.

q: With whose participation did the Anushilan group join forces when the Bengal Congress broke up into two factions after the death of CR Das?
exp: After the death of C.R. Das in 1925, the Bengal Congress divided into two factions: one led by J.M. Sengupta and the other by Subhas Chandra Bose. The revolutionary Anushilan Samiti joined forces with J.M. Sengupta's faction, while the Jugantar group supported Subhas Chandra Bose. Therefore, option (c) is the correct answer. This alignment was significant as it brought revolutionary cadres into the mainstream Congress organizational politics of Bengal during the inter-war period.

q: During World War I the Defence of India Act 1915 empowered the executive to:
exp: The Defence of India Act 1915 was an emergency wartime measure that empowered the executive to detain people without trial (preventive detention), censor the press, and set up special tribunals. Option (a) is correct. It was enacted primarily to crush revolutionary activities like the Ghadar movement. Options (b), (c), and (d) were not its primary legal focus. This repressive act was the precursor to the hated Rowlatt Act of 1919, which extended these emergency powers into peacetime.

q: In which of the following years Mahatma Gandhi led the Champaran Movement?
exp: Mahatma Gandhi led the Champaran Satyagraha in 1917. This was his first major act of civil disobedience in India. He went to Champaran in Bihar to support indigo farmers who were being forced by British planters to grow indigo on 3/20th of their land (Tinkathia system) under exploitative conditions. Options (a), (c), and (d) are incorrect dates. 1918, established Gandhi as a major force in Indian politics.

q: Why did Mahatma Gandhi call for a campaign against the Rowlatt Act?
o: During the non-cooperation movement, thousands of Indians were kept in jail
British censorship of press and permitted detention without trial
Hundreds of people were killed in the Jallianwala Bagh massacre
Sir Sidney Rowlatt was a Britisher
exp: Gandhi called for a Satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act (Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act of 1919) because it gave the government enormous powers to repress political activities, including detention without trial for up to two years and stricter control over the press. Option (b) is the correct reason. This act was famously described as "No Dalil, No Vakil, No Appeal." Option (c) is incorrect as Jallianwala Bagh happened during the protests against this Act, not before it.

q: Which act introduced the system of dyarchy in the provinces of British India?
exp: The system of Dyarchy (double government) was introduced in the provinces by the Government of India Act 1919, also known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms. Under this system, provincial subjects were divided into "Reserved" (controlled by the Governor) and "Transferred" (controlled by Indian ministers). Option (d) is incorrect as the 1935 Act abolished provincial dyarchy and proposed it at the Centre. Options (a) and (b) did not introduce this structural change.

q: Consider the following statements comparing the Simon Commission (1927) and the Nehru Report (1928): 1. the Simon Commission was boycotted by Indian political parties primarily due to its all-Indian composition. 2. the Nehru Report proposed complete independence for India as its immediate objective. Choose the correct option:
exp: Both statements are incorrect. Statement 1 is false because the Simon Commission was boycotted due to its all-white composition (no Indian members), not an all-Indian one. Statement 2 is false because the Nehru Report (1928) proposed Dominion Status within the British Empire, not complete independence (Purna Swaraj), which was later demanded at the Lahore Session in 1929. Thus, option (a) is the correct answer.

q: The Simon Commission was boycotted by the Indian National Congress because:
o: It did not include any Indian members
exp: The primary reason for the boycott of the Simon Commission was that it did not include a single Indian member. The seven-member commission, led by Sir John Simon, was entirely British, which Indians felt was an insult to their right to self-determination. Option (c) is correct. This led to mass protests with slogans like "Simon Go Back." Lala Lajpat Rai was fatally injured during a lathi charge while protesting against this commission in Lahore.

q: Which freedom fighter was also known as 'Badshah Khan' or 'Frontier Gandhi'?
exp: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan was affectionately known as 'Frontier Gandhi' or 'Badshah Khan'. He was a Pashtun leader from the North-West Frontier Province (NWFP) who founded the Khudai Khidmatgar (Servants of God) movement. He was a staunch follower of Mahatma Gandhi's non-violence principles. Options (b), (c), and (d) refer to other prominent figures. He strongly opposed the partition of India and spent many years in jail in both British India and Pakistan.

q: The Salt Satyagraha of 1930 was a direct civil disobedience movement against which British policy?
exp: The Salt Satyagraha (Dandi March) was a direct challenge to the British government's monopoly on the manufacture and sale of salt and the heavy salt tax. Gandhi famously said, "Next to air and water, salt is perhaps the greatest necessity of life." By marching to Dandi and picking up a handful of salt, he broke the law symbolically. Option (b) is correct. While other issues existed, the salt tax was chosen because it affected every Indian, regardless of religion or class.

q: Who founded Harijan Sangh and contended that the Shastras did not approve untouchability; and if they did, they should be disregarded?
exp: Mahatma Gandhi founded the All India Harijan Sevak Sangh in 1932 to eradicate untouchability. He argued that true Hinduism (Shastras) did not sanction untouchability, and if any text did, it was an interpolation or should be rejected as contrary to reason and humanity. Option (d) is correct. He started the weekly journal Harijan and "Harijans" (Children of God).

q: Who was the prominent leader remembered for hoisting the Indian flag at Gowalia Tank Maidan in 1942?
exp: Aruna Asaf Ali is popularly remembered as the "Grand Old Lady of Indian Independence" for hoisting the Indian National Flag at the Gowalia Tank Maidan in Bombay on August 9, 1942. This occurred just after the arrest of senior Congress leaders at the launch of the Quit India Movement. Option (b) is correct. Her act of defiance signaled the start of the movement despite the leadership vacuum. She later went underground to direct the revolution.

q: Which of the following describes the role of Aruna Asaf Ali in Indian history?
exp: Aruna Asaf Ali's most defining role in Indian history was hoisting the tricolour flag at the Gowalia Tank ground in Mumbai during the Quit India Movement (1942). This act of bravery in the face of imminent police brutality galvanized the crowds. Option (b) is correct. She also edited the underground newspaper Inquilab along with Ram Manohar Lohia. Options (a), (c), and (d) are incorrect descriptions of her role.

q: Kanaklata Barua was shot dead while hoisting the national flag during "Quit India" in which state?
exp: Kanaklata Barua, a 17-year-old freedom fighter, was shot dead by the British police in Assam during the Quit India Movement. She was leading a procession of the Mrityu Bahini (Death Squad) to hoist the national flag at the Gohpur police station on September 20, 1942. Option (c) is correct. Despite being shot, she held onto the flag until another volunteer, Mukunda Kakati, took it from her. She is honoured as "Birbala" in Assam.

q: Baji Raut, a young boy from Odisha, became a martyr at what age?
exp: Baji Raut was the youngest martyr of the Indian freedom struggle, killed at the tender age of 12 years. He was a boatman from Dhenkanal, Odisha, who was shot by British police on October 11, 1938, for refusing to ferry them across the Brahmani river to chase freedom fighters. Option (c) is correct. His bravery serves as a poignant reminder of the sacrifices made by even children in the fight for independence.

q: Who among the following is related to the Parakram Diwas?
exp: Subhas Chandra Bose is the figure related to Parakram Diwas (Day of Valor). The Government of India declared his birth anniversary, January 23, as Parakram Diwas in 2021 to honor his indomitable spirit and selfless service to the nation. Option (a) is correct. Bose, affectionately called "Netaji", organized the Indian National Army (INA) and gave the slogan "Jai Hind".

q: Once the Time Magazine had mocked Gandhiji's physical size but to whom did it compare his martyrdom later on?
exp: Time Magazine, which had once mocked Gandhi's frail physique, compared his martyrdom to that of Abraham Lincoln. After his assassination in 1948, the magazine recognized the magnitude of his sacrifice and his role in unifying a divided nation, drawing a parallel to the American President who also died for his country's unity and freedom. Option (d) is correct. This reflects the global shift in perception regarding Gandhi's legacy.

q: Pingali Venkayya is widely credited for his significant contribution to the design of which national symbol?
exp: Pingali Venkayya was a freedom fighter and agriculturalist from Andhra Pradesh who is credited with designing the National Flag of India. He presented a design of the tricolour to Mahatma Gandhi at the Vijayawada session of the Congress in 1921. Option (c) is correct. While the flag underwent some changes (like replacing the Charkha with the Ashoka Chakra), his basic design remains the foundation of the Indian Tiranga.

q: In which year was the Revolutionary Socialist Party (RSP) established?
exp: The Revolutionary Socialist Party (RSP) was established in 1940. It was founded by Tridib Chaudhuri and other revolutionaries from the Anushilan Samiti who had embraced Marxism-Leninism but differed from the Communist Party of India (CPI) on the issue of supporting the British war effort during WWII. Option (c) is correct. The RSP has its roots in the Bengal liberation movement and remains a constituent of the Left Front.

q: Who is known as the "Father of the Nation" in India?
exp: Mahatma Gandhi is revered as the "Father of the Nation" in India for his pivotal role in the Indian independence movement using non- violent civil disobedience. Subhas Chandra Bose first used this title for Gandhi in a 1944 radio broadcast. Jawaharlal Nehru was India's first PM, Sardar Patel integrated the princely states, and Bhagat Singh was a prominent revolutionary martyr. Understanding these figures is essential for SSC exams as questions frequently target their distinct national contributions.

q: Which of the following movement was re-launched in 1932?
exp: The Civil Disobedience Movement, initially launched with the Dandi March in 1930, was temporarily suspended following the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 1931. However, upon returning empty-handed from the Second Round Table Conference in London, Mahatma Gandhi formally re-launched it in January 1932 due to renewed British repression. The Non-Cooperation and Khilafat movements were definitively launched and ended in the early 1920s. The Bardoli Satyagraha occurred under Sardar Patel in 1928. Timeline disruptions of major movements are core SSC topics.

q: Which of the following incidents took place on 13 April 1919?
exp: On 13 April 1919, General Reginald Dyer ordered troops to open fire on a peaceful gathering at Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, Punjab, killing hundreds of unarmed civilians — one of the most brutal acts of British colonial repression. The Ahmedabad Mill Strike was in March 1918. The Champaran Satyagraha was in 1917. The Chauri-Chaura incident occurred on 5 February 1922, after which Gandhi called off the Non-Cooperation Movement. April 13 also coincided with Baisakhi — many had gathered for the festival.

q: In which of the following year Gandhiji went to London for the Second Round Table conference?
exp: Following the successful signing of the historic Gandhi- Irwin Pact in March 1931, Mahatma Gandhi temporarily suspended the massive Civil Disobedience Movement. He subsequently agreed to travel to London in late 1931 to participate exclusively in the Second Round Table Conference, acting as the sole authorized representative of the Indian National Congress. The First Round Table Conference was held in 1930 (which Congress aggressively boycotted), and the Third was held in 1932. Knowing the exact sequencing of the Round Table conferences is an absolute must.

q: Which of the following acts gave the government enormous powers and allowed detention of political prisoners without trial for two years?
exp: The notorious Rowlatt Act (officially the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act of 1919) outrageously granted the British colonial government sweeping, unchecked powers to repress nationalist activities. It explicitly allowed the arbitrary arrest and strict detention of political prisoners without any trial or judicial review for up to two full years. This draconian law famously sparked the massive nationwide Satyagraha led by Gandhi and directly precipitated the tragic Jallianwala Bagh massacre. The Indian Councils Acts merely reformed administrative structures.

q: Which revolutionary freedom fighter is popularly remembered as "Shaheed-e-Azam"?
exp: The incredibly brave and iconic revolutionary Bhagat Singh is universally and affectionately honored with the prestigious title "Shaheed-e-Azam," which literally translates to "Great Martyr." He earned this ultimate reverence due to his fearless sacrifice and execution by the British in 1931 at the very young age of 23 for his involvement in the Lahore Conspiracy Case. Lala Lajpat Rai was known as "Punjab Kesari." Chandrashekhar Azad was simply known as "Azad." Matching historical freedom fighters with their popular monikers is an SSC staple.

q: Mahatma Gandhi organized a Satyagraha to support the peasants of Kheda. Kheda district is located in which of the following states?
exp: The historic Kheda Satyagraha of 1918 was an incredibly significant early movement organized by Mahatma Gandhi. It took place in the severely drought-stricken Kheda district, which is geographically located in the state of Gujarat. Gandhi, alongside Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, mobilized the highly distressed local peasants to firmly refuse the payment of oppressive land revenue taxes to the ruthless British administration following widespread crop failures. Maharashtra, West Bengal, and Uttar Pradesh are factually incorrect states for this specific seminal agrarian revolt.

q: Whom did Mahatma Gandhi regard as his mentor?
exp: Mahatma Gandhi deeply revered and officially regarded the moderate Indian National Congress leader, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, as his definitive political guru and guiding mentor. Upon Gandhi's historic return to India from South Africa in 1915, it was Gokhale who prudently advised him to extensively tour the nation for an entire year to genuinely understand the stark realities of the Indian masses before actively engaging in aggressive politics. Dadabhai Naoroji was the 'Grand Old Man', and Bose respectfully called Gandhi the 'Father of the Nation'.

q: Who among the following was the Viceroy of India when Simon Commission came to India?
exp: The highly controversial Simon Commission (officially the Indian Statutory Commission) arrived in British India in early 1928 to aggressively review the constitutional system. During this highly turbulent period of nationwide black-flag protests ("Simon Go Back"), the official Viceroy of India was Lord Irwin (who strictly served from 1926 to 1931). Lord Chelmsford was associated with the earlier 1919 reforms. Lord Willingdon and Lord Linlithgow were subsequent Viceroys serving in the 1930s and 40s. Aligning major historical events with the ruling Viceroys is essential.

q: Mahatma Gandhi started the famous Salt March accompanied by how many of his trusted volunteers?
exp: On March 12, 1930, Mahatma Gandhi boldly initiated the historic Dandi March (Salt Satyagraha) directly from his Sabarmati Ashram to fiercely defy the oppressive British salt tax. He explicitly began this gruelling 240-mile trek accompanied by exactly 78 of his most trusted and strictly disciplined volunteers (Satyagrahis). Along the arduous route, thousands more joined, but the initial core group size is a famous, rigidly verified historical fact of exactly 78. Minor factual details surrounding the Civil Disobedience movement are constantly tested.

q: Chittaranjan Das, fondly called 'Deshbandhu', was born on November 5, 1870, in which city?
exp: The highly revered nationalist leader, brilliant lawyer, and founder-leader of the Swaraj Party, Chittaranjan Das (universally honored with the title 'Deshbandhu' or Friend of the Nation), was proudly born into an upper-class Brahmo family in the historic city of Calcutta (now Kolkata), Bengal Presidency, in 1870. His political life and massive sacrifices were intrinsically tied to the revolutionary hotbed of Bengal. Delhi, Madras, and Bombay are entirely incorrect geographical origins for this iconic Bengali freedom fighter. Knowing birthplaces of top-tier leaders adds depth to historical preparation.

q: The Poona Pact is related to which of the following?
exp: The historic Poona Pact was crucially signed on September 24, 1932, strictly between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar at the Yerwada Central Jail in Pune. This highly significant agreement officially abandoned the controversial separate electorates for the depressed classes (Dalits) proposed by the British Communal Award. Instead, it successfully guaranteed reserved seats strictly within the general Hindu electorate, heavily securing political representation for them. Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das, and Shaukat Ali were deeply involved in other major freedom struggle movements, not this specific pact.

q: Which freedom fighter, popularly known as 'Punjab Kesari', played a key role in the Swadeshi Movement?
exp: The great Lala Lajpat Rai, fiercely revered and popularly hailed as 'Punjab Kesari' (The Lion of Punjab), was an aggressive and monumental Indian independence activist. As a crucial pillar of the famous 'Lal-Bal-Pal' radical trio, he played a massive, extremely vital role in fiercely promoting the anti-British Swadeshi Movement across the nation. He heavily advocated for absolute self-reliance. Rani Lakshmibai fought the 1857 revolt, Dayanand Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj, and Rabindranath Tagore was a legendary poet.

q: Womesh Chandra Banerjee was the first President of which political organization?
exp: Womesh Chandra Banerjee (W.C. Bonnerjee) was a highly prominent, deeply educated Indian barrister from Calcutta who proudly holds the monumental historical distinction of serving as the very first President of the Indian National Congress (INC). He masterfully presided over the incredibly historic inaugural session of the INC, which was grandly and formally held in Bombay (Mumbai) in December 1885. The Gadar Party, Swaraj Party, and Indian National Army were aggressively formed decades later during subsequent freedom struggle phases.

q: The Non-Cooperation-Khilafat Movement began in ______.
exp: Following the approval at the crucial Nagpur session of the Indian National Congress in December 1920, the Non-Cooperation- Khilafat Movement was officially launched nationwide in January 1921 under the unified leadership of Mahatma Gandhi and the Ali Brothers. It aimed to peacefully protest against the grave injustices of the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and the harsh treaty imposed on the Ottoman Caliph. The other options are historically incorrect: April 1919 marks the tragic Jallianwala Bagh massacre itself. February 1922 is famous for the violent Chauri Chaura incident, which abruptly ended the movement. December 1922 witnessed the formation of the Swaraj Party.

q: In which of the following year Simon Commission arrived in India?
exp: The Simon Commission, officially known as the Indian Statutory Commission, arrived in India in the year 1928 (specifically landing in Bombay on February 3, 1928). It was appointed by the British government strictly to review the constitutional reforms introduced by the Government of India Act 1919. Since the seven-member commission outrageously did not include a single Indian member, it was vehemently boycotted nationwide with massive protests and loud slogans of "Simon Go Back." The years 1909, 1919, and 1932 are related to the Morley- Minto reforms, Rowlatt Act, and Poona Pact respectively.

q: In which of the following movement was the Tricolour flag designed?
exp: The very first recognizable Indian national tricolour flag (composed of red, green, and yellow bands) was proudly designed and hoisted during the intense and historic Swadeshi Movement (which began in 1905) to passionately protest against Lord Curzon's cruel partition of Bengal. This flag uniquely featured eight lotuses representing British Indian provinces and a crescent moon. The other options are historically incorrect for this event: The Sanyasi movement was an early rebellion against British taxation, Champaran was Gandhi's first Satyagraha for indigo farmers, and Bardoli was a successful peasant tax revolt.

q: Which theory, proposed by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, did Maulana Azad strongly oppose?
exp: Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, a highly respected Indian nationalist leader and staunch advocate of Hindu-Muslim unity, adamantly and fiercely opposed the divisive 'Two-Nation Theory' aggressively proposed by Muhammad Ali Jinnah and the Muslim League. This deeply controversial theory argued that Hindus and Muslims were entirely separate nations requiring two distinct sovereign countries, which ultimately led to the tragic Partition of India. Azad firmly believed in a united, secular India. Satyagraha, Quit India, and Civil Disobedience were entirely separate Gandhian anti-colonial movements actively supported by Azad.

q: Who wrote 'Vande Mataram' as a hymn to the motherland in the 1870s?
exp: The incredibly stirring and patriotic national song of India, 'Vande Mataram', was brilliantly penned by the great Bengali writer Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay in the 1870s. Originally written in highly Sanskritized Bengali, it was later officially incorporated into his famous 1882 historical novel, 'Anandamath'. It subsequently became a massive, electrifying rallying cry during the passionate Indian freedom struggle, especially during the 1905 Swadeshi movement. The other options are incorrect: Devendranath Tagore was a Brahmo leader, Sri Aurobindo was a radical nationalist philosopher, and Shyamlal Gupta wrote the Jhanda Geet ("Vijayi Vishwa Tiranga Pyara").

q: Who wrote the book 'Unhappy India' as a reply to the biased views of journalist Katherine Mayo?
exp: The brilliant and highly patriotic book 'Unhappy India' was powerfully written and published in 1928 by the legendary freedom fighter Lala Lajpat Rai (the Lion of Punjab). He wrote this comprehensive masterpiece specifically as a direct, aggressive, and highly factual rebuttal to the deeply insulting and heavily biased colonial propaganda book 'Mother India', which was maliciously authored by the American journalist Katherine Mayo to publicly degrade Indian culture and society. The other great national leaders listed (Rajendra Prasad, B.C. Pal, B.G. Tilak) were not the authors of this specific counter-publication.

q: In March 1946, the British government sent a ______ Cabinet Mission to India to examine the demand for Pakistan.
exp: In the incredibly crucial political climate of March 1946, the British Government strategically dispatched a high-powered 'three- member' Cabinet Mission directly to India to negotiate the final, massive transfer of sovereign power to Indian leadership and to critically examine the Muslim League's aggressive demand for a separate Pakistan. The three prominent British cabinet ministers were Lord Pethick-Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps, and A.V. Alexander. They ultimately rejected the creation of Pakistan in favor of a united India with grouped provinces. The other numerical options provided are historically inaccurate.

q: Who composed the famous patriotic flag song 'Vijayi
exp: The deeply patriotic and inspiring flag song "Vijayi Vishwa Tiranga Pyara, Jhanda Ooncha Rahe Hamara" was composed by the prominent freedom fighter and poet Shyamlal Gupta 'Parshad' in 1924. This song became an anthem of the Indian independence movement and was officially adopted by the Indian National Congress in 1938. The other options are incorrect: Tileswari Koch was a young martyr of the Quit India movement, Sucheta Kriplani was a leading freedom fighter and the first woman Chief Minister of India, and Sukumar Sen was India's first Chief Election Commissioner.

q: On the occasion of his birth anniversary in July 2025, which contribution is Chandra Shekhar Azad most remembered for?
o: Promoting rural education and women's rights
Leading armed resistance against British colonial rule
exp: Chandra Shekhar Azad was a fearless and iconic Indian revolutionary who is universally remembered for fiercely leading the armed, militant resistance against the oppressive British colonial rule. He fundamentally reorganized the Hindustan Republican Association (HRA) into the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) alongside Bhagat Singh. He tragically achieved martyrdom during a fierce gunfight at Alfred Park in Allahabad, fulfilling his vow to never be captured alive. The other options are historically inaccurate: the drafting of the Indian Constitution was led by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar; the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) was founded by K.B. Hedgewar; and while Azad cared for the nation, his primary historical legacy lies strictly in armed revolution, not localized rural education campaigns.

q: What was the stated reason for the 1905 Partition of Bengal?
exp: In 1905, Lord Curzon controversially ordered the partition of the massive Bengal Presidency. The official "stated reason" provided by the British colonial administration was strictly "administrative convenience," arguing that the vast province, with a population of nearly 80 million, was far too large to govern effectively from a single center. However, the real underlying political motive was clearly to divide Bengal on communal lines (Hindu-majority West vs. Muslim-majority East) to systematically weaken the rapidly growing Bengali nationalism and anti- British sentiment. The question specifically asks for the "stated" public reason, rendering the other options incorrect in this context.

q: Which of the following accurately describes a key structural feature proposed by the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 for the future Indian Union?
o: It proposed the immediate creation of two independent states, India and Pakistan.
It advocated for a strong central government with extensive powers over provinces.
It included a provision for provincial groupings with a weak federal centre handling limited subjects.
It recommended that the Constituent Assembly be nominated by the Viceroy, without elections.
exp: The British Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 distinctly rejected the Muslim League's demand for a separate Pakistan. Instead, its key structural feature was proposing a united Indian Union with a notably weak federal center that would only handle Defence, Foreign Affairs, and Communications. To appease regional interests, it controversially introduced a complex system of grouping provinces into three sections (A, B, and C) possessing broad autonomy. The other options are factually incorrect: the Mountbatten Plan (1947) proposed partition, not the Cabinet Mission; the plan advocated for a weak center, not a strong one; and it explicitly mandated an elected Constituent Assembly, not viceroy nominations.

q: Which unsung hero composed patriotic poems and led the promotion of Indian national symbols during the freedom movement?
exp: Shyamlal Gupta 'Parshad' was an illustrious poet and an unsung hero of the Indian freedom struggle. He is most famous for composing the immortal patriotic song "Jhanda Ooncha Rahe Hamara" (Vijayi Vishwa Tiranga Pyara), which became the official flag song of the Indian National Congress in 1938 and deeply inspired millions to rally behind the national symbols. The other figures made different contributions. Pingali Venkayya designed the Indian National Flag. Makhanlal Chaturvedi was a renowned Hindi poet ("Pushp ki Abhilasha"), and Ram Prasad Bismil was a revolutionary freedom fighter famous for the Kakori conspiracy.

q: In 1916, two major political groups in India came together to present a united front to the British. Which organizations signed this historic agreement, known as the Lucknow Pact?
o: Indian National Congress and Swaraj Party
All-India Muslim League and Khilafat Committee
Indian National Congress and Muslim League
Hindu Mahasabha and Indian National Congress
exp: The Lucknow Pact was a landmark historic agreement reached in 1916 between the Indian National Congress (led by Bal Gangadhar Tilak) and the All-India Muslim League (led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah). It forged a united political front, demanding greater self- government from the British and bridging the gap between both communities.

q: Read the following statements and mark the correct option: Assertion (A): Subramaniya Siva edited the nationalist journal 'Gnanabhanu' in Tamil Nadu. Reason (R): He was the first Indian to be arrested under the Rowlatt Act.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
exp: The Assertion (A) is completely true; Subramaniya Siva was a fierce freedom fighter and writer from Tamil Nadu who courageously started and edited the nationalist journal 'Gnanabhanu' in 1915 to awaken the masses. However, Reason (R) is factually incorrect; he was primarily arrested multiple times for sedition long before the Rowlatt Act.

q: The Indian Independence Act of 1947 marked the end of British rule but also led to the partition of India. Critically evaluate the arguments for and against the partition, considering the political, social, and economic consequences that followed.
o: The partition was a universally welcomed decision that led to immediate peace and prosperity in both India and Pakistan.

While advocated by the Muslim League as the only way to secure Muslim interests, the partition resulted in widespread violence, displacement, and long-lasting socio-political tensions, with arguments against it focusing on the potential for a united India with adequate minority safeguards.
The British government unilaterally imposed the partition without any significant consultation with Indian leaders or consideration of its consequences.
The partition was solely driven by economic factors, with both sides seeking control over specific resources and territories.
exp: The tragic partition of 1947 was fiercely advocated by the Muslim League claiming it was vital to protect Muslim political rights. However, nationalists strongly opposed it, arguing a united, secular India with constitutional minority safeguards was viable. Ultimately, the partition triggered unprecedented communal violence, massive refugee displacement, and enduring geopolitical hostility.

q: Which of the following freedom fighters is also known as 'Mother Teresa of Western Odisha'?
exp: Parbati Giri, an incredibly courageous freedom fighter and dedicated social reformer from Odisha, is affectionately revered as the 'Mother Teresa of Western Odisha'. Heavily inspired by Mahatma Gandhi, she actively participated in the Quit India Movement, was imprisoned, and later devoted her entire life to uplifting orphans, women, and the destitute.

q: The primary reason for the British government's decision to partition Bengal in 1905 was:
o: To promote the educational development of the region.
To improve the administrative efficiency of the large province.
To foster greater unity between the Hindu and Muslim populations of Bengal.
To encourage the growth of industrialization in East Bengal.
exp: While the undeniable underlying political motive of Lord Curzon was to weaken the surging nationalist movement by dividing Hindus and Muslims (Divide and Rule), the official, primary administrative reason consistently presented by the British Government for partitioning Bengal in 1905 was to substantially improve the administrative efficiency of the unmanageably large province.

q: The "Indian Independence Act of 1947" outlined the terms for the transfer of power and the creation of independent India and Pakistan. Which of the following was a key provision of this Act regarding the princely states?
o: It mandated the immediate integration of all princely states into either India or Pakistan based on geographical contiguity.
It granted the princely states the freedom to choose whether to join India, Pakistan, or remain independent.
It stipulated that the British government would continue to exercise paramountcy over the princely states.
It ensured that the revenue sharing agreements between the princely states and the new dominions would remain unchanged.
exp: The Indian Independence Act of 1947 abruptly terminated British paramountcy over the 560-plus princely states. A crucial, yet highly contentious, provision of this Act granted these independent states the absolute legal freedom to freely decide their future: either to accede to the newly formed dominions of India or Pakistan, or to remain entirely independent.

q: Usha Mehta is famously known for which of the following contributions during the Quit India Movement?
o: Leading armed struggle against British forces
Organizing the underground radio to broadcast nationalist messages
Being the first woman to be executed by the British for revolutionary activities
exp: During the tumultuous 1942 Quit India Movement, when all top Congress leaders were abruptly arrested, the courageous 22-year-old student Usha Mehta ingeniously established "Secret Congress Radio." Operating underground in Bombay, this clandestine broadcasting station was instrumental in defying British censorship, disseminating crucial nationalist news, and sustaining the fierce momentum of the nationwide rebellion.

q: Rash Behari Bose was a key figure in forming the Indian Independence League and played a crucial role in the initial organization of which army?
exp: The veteran Indian revolutionary Rash Behari Bose, who had daringly escaped to Japan, was remarkably instrumental in founding the Indian Independence League. More importantly, he laid the incredibly vital initial organizational framework for the first Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj), which he subsequently and gracefully handed over to the dynamic leadership of Subhas Chandra Bose in 1943.

q: Read the following statements and mark the correct option: Assertion (A): Matangini Hazra died while participating in a Salt March in Odisha. Reason (R): She was shot by police while holding the national flag during the Quit India Movement.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are false.
exp: Assertion (A) is completely false; the incredibly heroic 73- year-old freedom fighter Matangini Hazra (Gandhi Buri) was not martyred in Odisha, nor during a Salt March. Reason (R) is perfectly true; she fearlessly laid down her life during the 1942 Quit India Movement when she was brutally shot by British police while valiantly leading a massive procession holding the tricolor in Tamluk, Bengal.

q: The "Simon Commission" of 1927 was intended to review the working of the Government of India Act of 1919. Why was it met with widespread protests and boycotts by Indian nationalist leaders?
o: It recommended the immediate granting of complete independence to India, which was deemed insufficient by some.
It proposed the complete dismantling of the existing legislative councils.
It did not include any Indian members in its composition, leading to accusations of being an imposition on India's future without Indian representation.
It advocated for the strengthening of the system of separate electorates.
exp: The Indian Statutory Commission, universally detested as the Simon Commission, was appointed by the British to strictly evaluate India's constitutional progress. However, it completely infuriated the entire nation because its seven-member panel consisted exclusively of white British parliamentarians. Indians fiercely boycotted it, raising the legendary slogan "Simon Go Back" for blatantly ignoring Indian representation.

q: The "Lahore Resolution" passed by the Muslim League in 1940 demanded:
o: Complete integration of all princely states with British India.
The creation of a separate state for Muslims in the northwestern and eastern parts of India.
Equal representation for Muslims in all legislative bodies.
The continuation of a united India with enhanced safeguards for minority rights.
exp: The highly historic Lahore Resolution (often called the Pakistan Resolution) was formally drafted and aggressively passed by the All-India Muslim League in March 1940. It marked a definitive political shift, decisively demanding the creation of independent, sovereign Muslim-majority states in the geographically contiguous northwestern and eastern zones of British India.

q: The "Rowlatt Acts" of 1919 faced intense opposition from Indian nationalists for undermining fundamental legal principles. What was the most objectionable aspect of these Acts?
o: They imposed heavy taxes on Indian businesses and traders.
They mandated the compulsory registration of all Indian citizens.
They allowed the government to detain individuals without trial based on suspicion of revolutionary activities.
They granted greater powers to local self-governing bodies.
exp: The draconian Rowlatt Act (Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act of 1919) outrageously authorized the British colonial government to arrest and imprison any Indian civilian for up to two years without a warrant or judicial trial. This blatant denial of basic civil liberties sparked nationwide fury, famously summarized as "No Dalil, No Vakil, No Appeal."

q: Which revolutionary was popularly known as "The Agni of India"?
exp: Durgawati Devi, affectionately and universally revered as "Durga Bhabhi" within revolutionary circles, was fiercely hailed as "The Agni of India" (The Fire of India). She was an extraordinarily fearless and highly active member of the armed freedom struggle. She famously and courageously assisted Bhagat Singh's dramatic escape from Lahore in disguise immediately following the high-profile assassination of the ruthless British police officer John P. Saunders in 1928.

q: Which revolutionary organization was Durga Bhabhi closely
exp: Durgawati Devi (Durga Bhabhi) was deeply and intrinsically associated with the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA), a formidable underground revolutionary organization aggressively led by iconic figures like Chandrashekhar Azad and Bhagat Singh. She played a highly instrumental, covert operational role by bravely running safe houses, discreetly transporting deadly ammunition, and heavily fundraising for the party's relentless armed anti-colonial activities across northern India.

q: Ram Prasad Bismil is best known for his role in which revolutionary event?
exp: Ram Prasad Bismil, an incredibly fearless, foundational pillar of the Hindustan Republican Association (HRA), is eternally immortalized for brilliantly masterminding and fiercely executing the audacious "Kakori Train Robbery (Conspiracy)" on August 9, 1925. In a highly coordinated, daring strike near Lucknow, he and his courageous revolutionary comrades forcibly halted a moving train and aggressively looted the British government's treasury strictly to fund their massive, desperately needed armed uprising against brutal colonial rule.

q: Durga Bhabhi had a strong influence on which revolutionaries?
o: Lala Lajpat Rai, Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal
Khudiram Bose, Surya Sen, Ganesh Ghosh
Bhagat Singh, Ashfaqullah Khan, Chandra Shekhar Azad
exp: Durgawati Devi, universally and affectionately revered as "Durga Bhabhi," was an incredibly fearless, hardcore revolutionary of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA). She wielded a massive, inspiring influence over top-tier armed revolutionaries, most notably Bhagat Singh, Ashfaqullah Khan, and Chandrashekhar Azad. She famously facilitated Bhagat Singh's daring escape from Lahore after the high-profile assassination of Saunders, heavily risking her own life for the nation.

q: Ram Prasad Bismil was associated with which freedom movement ideology?
exp: Ram Prasad Bismil was one of the most prominent, incredibly fearless leaders of the "Revolutionary Nationalism" movement in India. Fiercely rejecting Mahatma Gandhi's slow, non-violent methods, Bismil believed that true independence could only be violently snatched from the British through armed struggle. As a principal founding member of the Hindustan Republican Association (HRA), he boldly masterminded the historic Kakori Train Robbery (1925) to desperately fund their massive armed revolution.

q: Where did the Rowlatt Satyagraha begin in 1919?
exp: The nationwide Rowlatt Satyagraha was launched aggressively by Mahatma Gandhi against the intensely oppressive Rowlatt Act. To legally and systematically coordinate this massive anti-colonial strike, Gandhi specifically established the "Satyagraha Sabha" formally in Bombay (Mumbai) in early 1919. While brutal, historic, and tragic manifestations of the protest later exploded in Amritsar (leading to Jallianwala Bagh), the strategic organizational birthplace and initial epicentre of the Satyagraha movement was decidedly Bombay.

q: Who presided over the 'Allahabad Session' of the Muslim League that demanded Pakistan in 1930?
exp: The highly pivotal 1930 Allahabad Session of the All-India Muslim League was prominently presided over by the legendary poet, philosopher, and visionary politician Sir Muhammad Iqbal (Allama Iqbal). In his historic and intensely provocative presidential address, Iqbal forcefully articulated the ideological necessity of amalgamating the Muslim-majority provinces of North-Western India into a single, autonomous political entity. This powerful speech laid the very first foundational ideological groundwork for the eventual creation of Pakistan.

q: What did Mahatma Gandhi and his followers do at Dandi to break the salt law?
exp: Note: Missing option added based on historical facts. During the incredibly historic Salt March (Dandi March) of 1930, Mahatma Gandhi famously led thousands of followers on a grueling 240- mile trek to the coastal village of Dandi in Gujarat. Defying the highly oppressive, monopolistic British Salt Act, Gandhi boldly walked into the Arabian Sea, picked up a lump of natural salt mud, and symbolically "boiled seawater to manufacture salt," deliberately triggering the massive Civil Disobedience Movement nationwide.

q: The Indian revolutionary associated with the 'Berlin Committee' during World War I was:
exp: Note: Missing option Aurobindo Ghosh added. Virendranath Chattopadhyay (affectionately known as Chatto) was a profoundly influential, highly active radical Indian nationalist. During the chaos of World War I, he famously founded the Berlin Committee (officially the Indian Independence Committee) in Germany in 1915, heavily backed by the German Foreign Office. His brilliant, covert strategy was to aggressively incite a massive armed rebellion within British India by furiously smuggling German arms and funds to the Ghadarites.

q: The 'Dandi March' (Salt March) in 1930 was the beginning of which major movement?
exp: The historic Dandi March, courageously led by Mahatma Gandhi in March-April 1930, successfully triggered the monumental "Civil Disobedience Movement" nationwide. By marching 240 miles to the Arabian Sea and illegally producing salt from seawater, Gandhi aggressively shattered the highly oppressive British salt monopoly. The Non-Cooperation Movement happened earlier in 1920, the Swadeshi Movement in 1905, and the Quit India Movement occurred much later in 1942.

q: Why was the Lucknow Pact (1916) significant?
o: The Partition of Bengal was reversed.
Congress and the Muslim League formally cooperated.
exp: The historic Lucknow Pact of 1916 is incredibly significant because it marked a remarkably rare and powerful moment of absolute political unity in India. For the first time, the Indian National Congress and the All-India Muslim League "formally cooperated" and signed a joint agreement demanding comprehensive self-government from the British. Furthermore, the Congress controversially accepted the Muslim League's demand for separate electorates, temporarily bridging the bitter communal divide to strengthen the freedom movement.

q: Where was the first systematically organized act of mass civil disobedience in India, combining nonviolent protest with legal defiance against colonial policies launched?
exp: The Champaran Satyagraha of 1917 was Mahatma Gandhi’s first civil disobedience movement in India. In Bihar, British planters forced farmers to cultivate indigo on 15% of their land under the oppressive tinkathia system. When Gandhi arrived to investigate, the colonial authorities ordered him to leave. He openly defied the legal order, choosing jail over compliance. This peaceful resistance and refusal to obey unjust colonial laws marked India’s first organized act of nonviolent civil disobedience. It forced the British government to appoint an inquiry committee, eventually abolishing the exploitative system and proving the power of Satyagraha.

q: Who coined the term 'Pakistan' in 1933, envisioning a separate homeland for Muslims in British India during the struggle for independence?
exp: Choudhry Rahmat Ali, a Cambridge student, coined the term 'Pakistan' (meaning Land of the Pure) in his 1933 pamphlet titled "Now or Never". He envisioned it as an acronym for Punjab, Afghan (NWFP), Kashmir, Sindh, and BaluchisTAN. Muhammad Ali Jinnah later led the movement for its creation. Allama Iqbal first articulated the philosophical idea of a separate state in 1930, but he did not coin the name.

q: The 'Cripps Mission' of 1942 proposed 'Dominion status' after the war. Who famously called it 'a post-dated cheque'?
exp: Mahatma Gandhi famously rejected the proposals of the Cripps Mission (which offered Dominion Status to India only *after* WWII) by terming it "a post-dated cheque on a crashing bank." He believed the British Empire was collapsing and immediate independence was required, which led to the Quit India Movement. Nehru, Bose, and Azad also rejected the mission, but the specific iconic "post-dated cheque" quote is historically attributed to Gandhi.

q: Mahatma Gandhi attended which of the Round Table Conferences as the sole representative of the Congress?
exp: Mahatma Gandhi attended only the Second Round Table Conference held in London in 1931 as the sole official representative of the Indian National Congress. This was a direct result of the Gandhi- Irwin Pact. The Congress boycotted the First and Third Conferences due to civil disobedience and political differences. There was never a 'Fourth' conference. Therefore, the Second conference is the historically accurate choice.

q: Who was the first British person to become the President of the Indian National Congress?
exp: George Yule, a Scottish merchant, created history by becoming the very first British (and non-Indian) person to be elected as the President of the Indian National Congress during its fourth session held in Allahabad in 1888. A.O. Hume was the founder of the Congress but remarkably never served as its President. William Wedderburn and Alfred Webb served as Presidents in later years (1889 and 1894, respectively). Thus, George Yule holds the inaugural distinction.

q: In which session was the 'Quit India' resolution passed in 1942?
exp: The historic 'Quit India' resolution was formally passed by the All India Congress Committee (AICC) during its monumental session held at Gowalia Tank Maidan in Bombay on August 8, 1942. This session launched the mass civil disobedience movement under Mahatma Gandhi's "Do or Die" call. While the draft was prepared earlier in Wardha (July 1942), the official ratification and launch of the movement definitively occurred at the Bombay session.

q: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre, where General Dyer ordered troops to fire on a peaceful crowd, took place in which city?
exp: The horrific Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on April 13, 1919 (Baisakhi day), in the city of Amritsar, Punjab. Acting Brigadier- General Reginald Dyer ruthlessly ordered his Gurkha and Sikh troops to fire continuously without warning into a large, unarmed gathering of civilians trapped inside the walled garden. It became a profound turning point in the Indian freedom struggle. Lahore, Chandigarh, and Patiala were not the geographical locations of this brutal colonial atrocity.

q: After the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, the British government appointed which committee to investigate the incident?
exp: Following massive public outrage over the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919), the British Government appointed the Disorders Inquiry Committee, universally known as the 'Hunter Commission' (headed by Lord William Hunter). It investigated the disturbances in Punjab and mildly condemned General Dyer's actions, leading to his resignation. The Butler Committee (1927) looked into relations with Princely States. Muddiman (1924) reviewed the 1919 Act. Simon Commission (1927) proposed constitutional reforms.

q: After Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement, which party was formed by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru to advocate 'Council-entry'?
exp: Following the abrupt suspension of the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922 due to the Chauri Chaura incident, C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru broke away from the 'No-changers' in the Congress to form the 'Swaraj Party' (Congress-Khilafat Swarajya Party) in early 1923. Their primary strategy was to enter the legislative councils (Council-entry) to disrupt and oppose British policies from within. The Ghadar Party operated from abroad. The Justice Party was anti-Brahmin. The CSP formed much later in 1934.

q: The Indian nationalist leader who emphasized mass civil disobedience against British war efforts during World War II and launched the "Quit India Movement" in August 1942 was:
exp: Mahatma Gandhi was the preeminent nationalist leader who passionately opposed India's forced participation in World War II without the explicit guarantee of total independence. Consequently, on August 8, 1942, at the Gowalia Tank Maidan in Bombay, he launched the massive "Quit India Movement" (Bharat Chhedo Andolan), famously delivering his ultimate "Do or Die" speech. Subhas Chandra Bose chose armed struggle abroad (INA). Nehru and Patel strongly supported Gandhi but were not the chief architects of this specific final call.

q: Who was the editor of the revolutionary nationalist journal Bande Mataram, which promoted Indian independence and mobilized public opinion against colonial rule?
exp: The highly influential English-language nationalist newspaper 'Bande Mataram' was founded in 1905 by Bipin Chandra Pal, but it was brilliantly edited by Sri Aurobindo Ghosh. Under his intense editorship, it became a fierce, radical voice advocating for complete independence (Purna Swaraj) and aggressive boycott of British goods. Lala Lajpat Rai and Bal Gangadhar Tilak led other regional movements and publications (like Kesari). Hence, Aurobindo Ghosh was its defining editor.

q: The 'Bardoli Satyagraha' (1928), a major farmer's protest against tax hikes, was led by?
exp: The 'Bardoli Satyagraha' of 1928 was a highly successful, non-violent agrarian revolt situated in Gujarat against an unjust 22% tax hike imposed by the Bombay Presidency. It was brilliantly organized and led by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. His exceptional organizational skills during this intense protest earned him the prestigious title "Sardar" (Leader) from the women of Bardoli. Mahatma Gandhi provided moral support, but Patel was the undeniable ground commander.

q: On the recommendations of which committee was the Rowlatt Act passed?
exp: The draconian Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act of 1919, infamously known as the Rowlatt Act, was enacted primarily based on the strict recommendations of the Sedition Committee, which was chaired by British judge Sir Sidney Rowlatt in 1918. It allowed the colonial government to imprison suspects without trial. The Hunter Committee (1919) investigated the Jallianwala Bagh massacre. The Frazer Committee (1902) dealt with police reforms. The Minto-Morley reforms (1909) related to legislative councils.

q: The first session of the Indian National Congress (INC) was held in 1885 in which city?
exp: The inaugural and historic first session of the Indian National Congress (INC) was successfully convened in Bombay (Mumbai) from December 28 to 31, 1885. It was held at the Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College and attended by exactly 72 delegates from across India, presided over by Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee. While Calcutta and Madras hosted subsequent monumental sessions, the very first foundational meeting strictly took place in the city of Bombay.

q: What was the recommendation of the Nehru Report (1928)?
exp: The Nehru Report of 1928, drafted by a committee headed by Motilal Nehru, was a landmark framework for an Indian Constitution. Its primary recommendations explicitly included granting 'Dominion Status' to India (not complete independence or Purna Swaraj) and establishing 'Joint Electorates' with reservation of seats for minorities, thereby firmly rejecting the divisive system of separate electorates. Purna Swaraj was later demanded in the 1929 Lahore session under Jawaharlal Nehru after the British ignored the report.

q: From which of the following, the early 20th-century Home Rule Movement in India, which aimed at promoting self- government within the British Empire and mobilizing mass nationalist sentiment was inspired?
exp: The Indian Home Rule Movement, launched in 1916 by Annie Besant and Bal Gangadhar Tilak, was deeply and directly inspired by the 'Irish Home Rule movement'. Annie Besant, being of Irish descent, utilized the successful organizational template of Ireland to demand similar self-government (Dominion Status) for India within the British Empire. The American Civil War fought slavery, the French Revolution gave ideas of liberty and equality, and the Boer War was an imperial conflict in South Africa.

q: Which organization was formed after the Ilbert Bill controversy of 1883, which exposed racial tensions in colonial India by proposing that Indian judges could try European offenders?
exp: The 'European Defence Association' (initially formed as the European and Anglo-Indian Defence Association) was specifically established in 1883 by the British and Anglo-Indian community in India to violently oppose and successfully lobby against the Ilbert Bill. They fiercely resisted the idea that native Indian judges could preside over criminal cases involving Europeans. In response to this organized racism, educated Indians realized the need for their own national organization, leading to the creation of the Indian National Congress in 1885.

q: The first Indian woman to preside over an Indian National Congress Session:
exp: The distinguished poet and freedom fighter Sarojini Naidu made history by becoming the very first 'Indian' woman to be elected as the President of the Indian National Congress at the Kanpur session in 1925. Annie Besant was the first woman ever to preside over the Congress (in 1917), but she was British. Sucheta Kriplani was India's first female Chief Minister. Vijayalakshmi Pandit was the first female President of the UN General Assembly. Thus, Naidu is correct.

q: The jurist and statesman who became the first Indian member of the British Privy Council in 1928, reflecting both his legal eminence and the gradual inclusion of Indians in imperial governance was:
exp: Sir Satyendra Prasanna Sinha (Lord Sinha of Raipur) was a brilliant jurist who consistently broke racial barriers under British rule. He achieved the monumental distinction of becoming the first Indian member of the Viceroy's Executive Council, and later, the very first Indian to be appointed to the prestigious British Privy Council in 1926 (often cited around 1926-1928 in historical milestones). Dadabhai Naoroji was the first Indian MP in Britain. Gokhale and Banerjee were prominent moderate leaders.

q: Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia rose to prominence for his underground activities during which movement in India?
exp: Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia, a socialist and nationalist, shot to prominence for his courageous underground activities during the 'Quit India Movement' of 1942. He operated secret radio stations (Congress Radio) alongside Usha Mehta to coordinate resistance after major leaders were jailed. He was too young during the Swadeshi (1905), Champaran (1917), or Non-Cooperation (1920) movements to be a central leader.

q: In which year did the Indian National Congress split after witnessing a sharp ideological division between the Extremists and the Moderates?
exp: The Indian National Congress suffered a historic and highly damaging split during its annual session held at Surat in the year 1907 (infamously known as the 'Surat Split'). The severe ideological clash was between the Moderates (led by Gokhale, who preferred constitutional methods) and the Extremists (led by Lal-Bal-Pal, who demanded direct action and Swaraj). 1905 marked the partition of Bengal, which originally ignited the friction. The Congress eventually reunited in 1916.

q: Which of the following leaders, known for combining radical political agitation with mass mobilization, famously declared, "Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it," symbolizing the assertive demand for self-rule during the early 20th century?
exp: The legendary nationalist leader Bal Gangadhar Tilak (Lokmanya Tilak) was the fierce architect of the Extremist faction in the Congress. He fearlessly coined the immortal slogan, "Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it," effectively transforming the freedom struggle into a mass movement through festivals like Ganesh Chaturthi and Shivaji Jayanti. Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai were his close associates (the Lal-Bal-Pal trio), but Tilak alone authored this specific defining battle cry.

q: In which region of India did the Moplah Rebellion (1921) take place?
exp: The Moplah Rebellion (also known as the Malabar Rebellion) erupted violently in 1921 exclusively within the 'Malabar' region of northern Kerala. It started initially as a fierce resistance by Mappila (Muslim) tenant farmers against the oppressive British colonial administration and the extortionate Hindu landlords (Jenmis) aligned with them, heavily fueled by the broader Khilafat Movement. The uprising eventually took on a tragic communal color. It had no geographical connection to Bengal, Punjab, or Awadh.

q: The "Indian Sociologist", a revolutionary publication from London was established by:
exp: The "Indian Sociologist" was a highly influential, radical English-language monthly journal proudly established in London in 1905 by the visionary Indian revolutionary 'Shyamji Krishna Varma'. The publication served as a potent intellectual platform to vehemently criticize British imperial rule and promote the cause of Indian Home Rule abroad (alongside his 'India House' organization). Lala Hardayal was central to the Ghadar movement in the USA. Madame Cama published 'Bande Mataram' in Paris. V.D. Savarkar was a prominent contributor, but Varma was the sole founding editor.

q: The 'Partition of Bengal' (1905) was annulled (cancelled) in which year, following mass protests?
exp: The highly controversial 'Partition of Bengal', aggressively enacted by Lord Curzon in 1905 to divide the Hindu and Muslim populations, ignited the fierce, nationwide Swadeshi Movement. Overwhelmed by massive, unyielding political protests and radical unrest, the British Government was completely forced to capitulate. King George V officially announced the absolute annulment (cancellation) of the partition during the spectacular Delhi Durbar held in the year '1911', simultaneously moving the capital from Calcutta to Delhi to pacify Bengali sentiment.

q: The 'Kakori Conspiracy' (1925) was a train robbery near Lucknow, organized by which revolutionary group?
exp: The daring 'Kakori Train Action' of August 1925, wherein brave revolutionaries successfully halted a British government train to meticulously seize colonial treasury funds, was exclusively planned and executed by members of the 'Hindustan Republican Association' (HRA). Prominent heroic figures involved included Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan, and Chandrashekhar Azad. The Ghadar Party operated largely out of North America. Jugantar and Anushilan Samiti were fierce secret societies that functioned predominantly in the Bengal region.

q: The Indian National Congress (INC) was founded in 1885 by which retired British civil servant?
exp: The Indian National Congress (INC), which later spearheaded India's epic struggle for total independence, was fundamentally conceptualized and founded in 1885 by 'Allan Octavian Hume' (A.O. Hume), a highly sympathetic retired British member of the Indian Civil Service. He aimed to provide a political "safety valve" and a platform for educated Indians to voice grievances. Lord Dufferin was the serving Viceroy who permitted the gathering. William Wedderburn was a close British associate who later became Congress President.

q: Who is known as the "Frontier Gandhi" for his work in promoting non-violence and the rights of the people in the tribal areas of the North-West Frontier Province (now in Pakistan)?
exp: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, an exceptionally prominent Pashtun independence activist, is universally celebrated as "Frontier Gandhi" (Bacha Khan). He earned this highly revered title due to his deep, unwavering commitment to Mahatma Gandhi's principles of non-violence and secularism while leading the freedom struggle in the volatile North- West Frontier Province. He founded the peaceful 'Khudai Khidmatgar' (Servants of God) resistance movement. Option (c) is the definitively correct answer. Mahatma Gandhi (a) was the overarching national leader of the Indian independence movement. Jawaharlal Nehru (b) was India's first Prime Minister. Lal Bahadur Shastri (d) was India's second Prime Minister, famous for his "Jai Jawan Jai Kisan" slogan.

q: Who composed "Vande Mataram"?
exp: The incredibly stirring, deeply patriotic, and historically momentous national song of India, "Vande Mataram," was masterfully composed by the exceptionally brilliant Bengali literary giant, Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay (also spelled Chatterjee). He powerfully penned this magnificent, emotionally charged, and highly evocative hymn in highly Sanskritized Bengali during the 1870s, and later seamlessly embedded it directly into the core narrative of his incredibly famous and highly influential 1882 political novel, "Anandamath." This phenomenal song aggressively served as a massive, unparalleled source of immense spiritual inspiration and fierce motivation for brave revolutionaries during the brutal, decades-long Indian independence movement. Option (b) is definitively the accurate historical fact. The legendary Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore (a) proudly composed the official National Anthem, "Jana Gana Mana," but not this specific national song.

q: Who did Mahatma Gandhi praise with the words, "India would have attained independence long back if only it had a few stalwarts like him"?
exp: Potti Sriramulu was an incredibly dedicated, immensely selfless, and deeply passionate Indian revolutionary leader and an exceptionally devout follower of Mahatma Gandhi. He famously demonstrated an incredibly profound, unbelievable level of personal sacrifice and unshakeable inner conviction during the long, agonizing Indian freedom struggle, and later famously during the intense, highly volatile linguistic reorganization movement for a separate Andhra state. Witnessing his incredible, superhuman tenacity, unwavering deep devotion, and absolute, total commitment to the noble cause, Mahatma Gandhi famously, deeply, and generously praised him, stating emotionally that "India would have attained independence long back if only it had a few stalwarts like him." Therefore, option (a) is definitively the factually accurate historical quote attribution, highlighting Sriramulu's massive, often underappreciated legendary dedication.

q: Which statement about Rani Gaidinliu is correct?
o: Led the Naga tribal revolt against the British
exp: Rani Gaidinliu was a fearless Naga spiritual and political leader who bravely led a massive armed revolt against British colonial rule in India at a very young age. She joined the Heraka religious movement to establish self-rule for the Nagas. Jawaharlal Nehru gave her the title of "Rani" (Queen). She did not organize the Salt Satyagraha, nor did she found the Azad Hind Fauj (which was Bose). Acknowledging unsung tribal freedom fighters is highly emphasized in modern exams.

q: Consider the following statements about Potti Sriramulu: 1. He joined Gandhiji at the Sabarmati Ashram after enduring personal tragedies. 2. He refused to participate in the Salt Satyagraha. Which of the above statements is/are correct? Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Statement 1 is correct: After losing his wife and child, Potti Sriramulu dedicated his life to national service and joined Gandhi's Sabarmati Ashram. Statement 2 is entirely incorrect: He was an active, staunch participant in the Indian Independence movement, prominently taking part in the Salt Satyagraha (1930) and the Quit India Movement (1942), suffering imprisonment for his actions.

q: Khudiram Bose was executed by the British for his involvement in which revolutionary act?
exp: Khudiram Bose, along with Prafulla Chaki, orchestrated the Muzaffarpur bomb attack in 1908. Their target was Kingsford, an unpopular British magistrate known for harsh sentences against Indian nationalists. Unfortunately, the bomb hit a carriage carrying innocent British women. Prafulla Chaki died by suicide before capture, while Bose was arrested, tried, and subsequently hanged.

q: At what age did Khudiram Bose become a martyr, making him one of the youngest revolutionaries in India's freedom struggle?
exp: Khudiram Bose was hanged by the British authorities on August 11, 1908. Born on December 3, 1889, he was just 18 years, 8 months, and 8 days old at the time of his execution, forever cementing his legacy as one of the most prominent and youngest martyrs of the Indian independence movement.

q: Which popular Bengali song, written by poet Pitambar Das, immortalized Khudiram Bose's sacrifice?
exp: The highly emotional and patriotic Bengali folk song "Ek Baar Bidaye De Ma, Ghure Ashi" (Mother, bid me farewell once, I will return) was penned by Charan Kabi Pitambar Das. It poignantly captures the fearless, smiling face of the 18-year-old revolutionary Khudiram Bose as he willingly embraced the executioner's noose in 1908, forever immortalizing his youthful martyrdom in Bengali culture.

q: Surya Sen, an Indian revolutionary, popularly known as Master Da, was born in which place?
exp: Surya Sen, deeply revered by his followers as "Master Da" due to his profession as a schoolteacher, was a fiercely committed Indian revolutionary. He was born in the village of Noapara in Raozan upazila of Chittagong (in present-day Bangladesh). From this very region, he meticulously plotted the bold armed rebellion against British rule that would become his legacy.

q: Who led the Chittagong Armoury Raid on 18 April 1930?
exp: The incredibly audacious Chittagong Armoury Raid was masterminded and bravely led by Surya Sen (Master Da) on April 18, 1930. Leading a heavily organized group of young revolutionaries under the banner of the "Indian Republican Army," they successfully captured two main British armouries in Chittagong, completely severed communication lines, and momentarily hoisted the Indian national flag before British retaliation.

q: When and where did Nehru popularize the concept of Purna Swaraj?
exp: Jawaharlal Nehru popularized the concept of 'Purna Swaraj' (Complete Independence) during the historic Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress in December 1929, where he served as the President. This marked a major shift from the previous demand for dominion status. Following this, January 26, 1930, was observed as the first Independence Day. The other sessions mentioned correspond to different historical events or dates.

q: The Kuka Movement led by Guru Ram Singh coincided with which major event in Indian history?
exp: The inception of the Kuka (Namdhari) Movement under the dynamic leadership of Guru Ram Singh formally took place in 1857 in Bhaini Sahib (Punjab). This timeline perfectly coincides exactly with the monumental outbreak of the Revolt of 1857 (the First War of Indian Independence), sharing a parallel underlying sentiment of fierce resistance against the oppressive British colonial administration.

q: Who among the following established the Provincial Kisan Sabha in Bihar in 1929?
exp: Swami Sahajanand Saraswati formed the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha (BPKS) in 1929 to mobilize peasant grievances against zamindari attacks on their occupancy rights. This organization became the foundation for the All India Kisan Sabha (AIKS) formed in Lucknow in 1936. Options (b) and (c) were Congress leaders who worked with peasants but did not found the Sabha in 1929. Option (d) was a socialist leader. Swami Sahajanand is known as the "Peasant Leader of India" and dedicated his life to agrarian reforms.

q: After the indigo revolution in Bengal, where did the planters shift their operations?
exp: After the successful Indigo Revolt (Blue Rebellion) in Bengal (1859-60), the European planters shifted their operations to Bihar, particularly to districts like Champaran. In Bengal, the peasants' refusal to grow indigo and the subsequent Indigo Commission report (1860) made the business unprofitable there. Option (a) is correct.
