q: Consider the following statements about the impact of foreign trade on aggregate demand: 1. Imports by Indian consumers act as a leakage reducing afiregate demand. 2. Exports from India act as an injection increasing afiregate demand. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Both statements are correct. Imports represent money flowing out of the domestic economy to pay foreign producers, acting as a leakage that reduces domestic aggregate demand. Exports represent money flowing into the economy from foreign buyers, acting as an injection that increases aggregate demand.

q: What was the share of industry in India's GDP in 1950- 1951?
exp: On the eve of planning in 1950-51, the industrial sector (secondary sector) contributed approximately 13% to India's GDP. The primary sector (agriculture) was the dominant contributor at that time, accounting for more than half of the GDP.

q: The sum of the gross value added of all the firms in an economy in a year is called:
exp: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) can be defined as the sum of the Gross Value Added (GVA) of all resident producer units (firms) in the economy during a specific period (usually a year).

q: In the context of economy, if ______ is deducted from the gross value added to obtain the Net value added.
exp: To derive Net Value Added (NVA) from Gross Value Added (GVA), one must deduct Depreciation (consumption of fixed capital). Net Value Added = Gross Value Added - Depreciation.

q: In the context of wear and tear in production process, the replacement investment is same as:
exp: Replacement investment refers to the investment made to replace worn-out capital assets (machinery, equipment) to maintain the existing level of production capacity. This concept is economically equivalent to depreciation of capital.

q: Which of the following statements regarding income is correct? I. Out of private income, what finally reaches the households is known as personal income. II. the total national income of the country is composed of two parts: private income and public income. Select the correct option:
exp: Both statements are correct. Personal Income is indeed the part of Private Income that actually reaches households (after deducting corporate taxes and retained earnings). Total National Income can be broadly categorized into income accruing to the private sector (Private Income) and income accruing to the public sector (Public Income).

q: In the context of economy, which of the following is an example of Intermediate good?
exp: Copper used for making utensils is an Intermediate good because it is a raw material that undergoes value addition and transformation to become a final product (utensils). Items like shirts, televisions, and refrigerators purchased by households are Final Goods meant for consumption.

q: In the context of Indian economy, which of the following is included in the factor cost?
o: Only the payment to factors of production
Both the product and production taxes
exp: Factor cost refers to the total cost incurred by a producer to employ the factors of production (Land, Labor, Capital, Entrepreneurship). It includes only the payment to factors of production (rent, wages, interest, profit) and excludes any net indirect taxes (taxes minus subsidies).

q: Personal Disposable Income is the part of the aggregate income which belongs to the:
exp: Personal Disposable Income (PDI) is the income that is actually available to households and individuals for consumption and saving. It is derived by subtracting personal taxes (like income tax) and non-tax payments (fines, fees) from Personal Income.

q: The real gross domestic product (GDP) is calculated in a way such that, the goods and services are evaluated at _____.
o: prices set by world trade organisation
prices set by International monetary fund
the lowest prices observed in the economy
exp: Real GDP is an inflation-adjusted measure that reflects the value of all goods and services produced by an economy in a given year, expressed in base-year prices. By evaluating goods at a "constant set of prices," economists filter out the effect of inflation, allowing for a true comparison of economic growth over time. Nominal GDP, conversely, uses current prices. International organizations like the WTO or IMF do not set domestic commodity prices. SSC consistently tests the conceptual difference between Real and Nominal GDP.

q: Which of the following is NOT an example of transfer payments given by the government to the households?
exp: In macroeconomics, transfer payments refer to one-way payments made by the government without receiving any good or service in exchange. Old-age pensions, student scholarships, and state prizes fall perfectly under this category as they are welfare distributions. Interest, however, is a 'factor payment'; it is the earned return paid for the productive use of capital (such as interest paid on government bonds). SSC economics frequently tests the distinction between unilateral transfers and earned factor incomes.

q: What is deducted from Gross domestic product (GDP) at market prices to calculate GDP at factor cost?
o: Only subsidy provided by the government
exp: In standard national income accounting, to transition from GDP at Market Price (which includes taxes consumers pay) to GDP at Factor Cost (the actual cost incurred by producers), one must strictly deduct Net Indirect Taxes (which is exactly equivalent to Indirect Product Taxes minus Subsidies). Deducting depreciation converts Gross to Net (NDP). Deducting national debt interest is irrelevant here. Understanding these specific macroeconomic accounting formulas is an absolute bedrock requirement for scoring well in SSC economics.

q: In which year did the GDP of India crossed the 1 trillion- dollar mark?
exp: The Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of India crossed the monumental US $1 trillion mark for the very first time in the year 2007. This significant macroeconomic milestone was driven mainly by the boom in the services sector, robust foreign investment inflows and the cumulative effect of the historic 1991 liberalisation reforms.

q: The nominal gross domestic product (GDP) is calculated at the ____.
o: prices fixed by the Reserve Bank of India
exp: In macroeconomics, Nominal GDP is strictly and exclusively calculated by heavily measuring the absolute total monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a country perfectly using the "current prevailing prices" of that specific year. It does not aggressively adjust for heavy inflation. Real GDP, on the other absolute hand, is mathematically calculated strictly using a "constant set of prices" from a designated base year to accurately reflect true economic growth devoid of price distortions.

q: In which year did the GDP of India crossed the 2 trillion-
exp: The Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of India historically and monumentally crossed the massive 1 trillion mark exactly seven years earlier in 2007. This highly significant macroeconomic growth was heavily propelled by the rapidly accelerating domestic services sector and strong, sustained capital investments. The years 2012, 2016, and 2018 do not accurately reflect this exact economic benchmark.

q: Which of the following is included in gross domestic product at market price? 1. Production done by national residents in the country 2. Production done by non-residents in the country Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is strictly and universally defined as the total final market value of all goods and services produced exclusively within the domestic geographical boundaries of a country during a specific period. Therefore, it completely includes production generated by both national residents and foreign non-residents, as long as the economic activity happens physically inside the country. Hence, both statement I and statement II are absolutely correct. Gross National Product (GNP), on the other hand, strictly focuses on the nationality of the producer, not the location.

q: If the real gross domestic product (GDP) increases, what does it imply?
exp: Real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is an infiation- adjusted macroeconomic measure heavily used to precisely reflect the actual value of all final goods and services produced in an economy. Unlike Nominal GDP, which can falsely rise simply due to price inflation, an increase in Real GDP unequivocally and strictly implies that the actual, physical 'volume of production' of goods and services has successfully expanded. The other options are incorrect: A decrease in production lowers GDP, while currency depreciation and trade deficits are separate international trade parameters.

q: India's real GDP growth in 2025 is reported at 6.8%, but per capita NNP at factor cost grows only by 4.2%. What could be the most plausible reason for this divergence?
o: Increase in exports and FDI inflows artificially suppressed GNP
The divergence is statistically irrelevant and reflects a normal economic pattern
Reduction in public investment increased fiscal surplus and lowered factor cost calculations
Rapid depreciation of physical capital and population growth reduced per capita net income despite healthy GDP growth
exp: The Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of India crossed the US $2 trillion milestone for the very first time in the year 2014. It had previously crossed the $1 trillion mark in 2007, meaning the economy doubled in size in roughly seven years, driven by strong growth in services, manufacturing and domestic consumption.

q: In the context of India's economic growth and investment trends in 2025, which of the following statements best explains the significance of Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) and the factors influencing its recent fluctuations?
o: GFCF only measures government expenditure on infrastructure and does not include private sector investments
GFCF primarily tracks changes in financial assets like stocks and bonds and is unrelated to physical capital investment
GFCF growth in 2025 is solely driven by agricultural output improvements and rural credit expansion

A rising GFCF as a percentage of GDP reflects increased investment in fixed assets like machinery, buildings, and infrastructure, indicating higher productive capacity; however, fluctuations in 2025 are influenced by global supply chain disruptions, private sector risk aversion, and policy reforms aimed at boosting capital expenditure
exp: Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) is a critical macroeconomic indicator representing the total net investment made in physical, tangible assets within an economy, such as building heavy machinery, factories, and national infrastructure. It encompasses investments from both the government and the private sector. A rising GFCF signifies long-term economic expansion and enhanced productive capacity. Modern fluctuations are practically driven by global supply chain volatility and varying private capital expenditure. The other options are incorrect: GFCF explicitly includes both public and private sector investments; it strictly measures physical assets, completely excluding financial assets like stocks or bonds; and it spans all industrial sectors, not solely agricultural output.

q: Which of the following correctly explains the difference between Gross Value Added (GVA) and Net Value Added (NVA)?
o: GVA includes indirect taxes, NVA excludes them
GVA is measured at factor cost, NVA at market price
GVA includes depreciation, whereas NVA excludes depreciation
There is no difference between them
exp: In macroeconomic accounting, the fundamental distinction between any 'Gross' and 'Net' concept is the consumption of fixed capital, commonly known as depreciation. Gross Value Added (GVA) represents the total value of goods and services produced without adjusting for wear and tear of machinery and infrastructure. Subtracting depreciation from GVA gives Net Value Added (NVA). Taxes and subsidies define the difference between basic prices and market prices, not gross and net metrics.

q: Which of the following best distinguishes Gross National Product (GNP) from Gross Domestic Product (GDP)?
o: GNP includes only exports while GDP includes imports
GNP accounts for net income from abroad, GDP does not
GNP excludes production by foreign companies in India
GDP includes depreciation while GNP does not
exp: The core conceptual difference between Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and Gross National Product (GNP) lies in their geographical versus national scope. GDP firmly measures the total monetary value of all final goods and services produced within the strict domestic borders of a country, regardless of who produces them (citizens or foreigners). GNP, however, accurately accounts for the Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA). It measures the total economic output produced by a country's residents, irrespective of their physical location worldwide. The other options regarding depreciation and isolated exports/imports are factually incorrect. Depreciation separates "Gross" from "Net" products.

q: If depreciation is subtracted from Gross Domestic Product (GDP), the resulting value is known as:
o: Net National Product at Market Price
exp: In core macroeconomic accounting, any economic aggregate containing the term "Gross" (which represents total raw value) can be successfully converted to its corresponding "Net" value by simply subtracting the cost of depreciation (capital consumption allowance). Therefore, mathematically, when you subtract the depreciation of fixed capital assets from the Gross Domestic Product (GDP), the resulting specific indicator is perfectly defined as the Net Domestic Product (NDP). It does not become a "National" product unless Net Factor Income from Abroad is added, making the other options fundamentally incorrect.

q: What does "expected years of schooling" measure?
o: The total number of years of schooling in a country.
The average number of years of schooling received by people ages 25 and older.
The number of years a child of school-entering age is expected to spend in school.
The projected past years of schooling.
exp: Expected years of schooling is a vital component of the Human Development Index (HDI) developed by the United Nations. It specifically measures the total number of years of formal education that a child of school-entering age can expect to receive during their lifetime, assuming that current age-specific enrollment rates persist.

q: A substantial limitation of the Human Development Index (HDI) is its inability to capture:
exp: HDI measures average achievement in health, knowledge, and standard of living. However, it is heavily criticized for ignoring significant inequalities in income distribution, gender disparities, and multidimensional poverty within a country, prompting the creation of the Inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI) by the UNDP.

q: The difference between the Gross National Product (GNP) and the Net National Product (NNP) is:
exp: Gross National Product (GNP) evaluates the total value of all final goods and services produced by a country's residents. When the monetary value of depreciation (wear and tear of capital assets like machinery) is deducted from the GNP, the resulting figure is the Net National Product (NNP).

q: Which indicator is used to measure the 'Knowledge' dimension of the Human Development Index?
o: Adult literacy rate and primary school enrollment
Mean years of schooling and Expected years of schooling
Number of universities and research publications
exp: The Human Development Index (HDI), meticulously published by the UNDP, evaluates a nation's progress through three core dimensions: health, knowledge, and standard of living. Specifically, the 'Knowledge' (or education) dimension is expertly quantified utilizing exactly two distinct metrics: the "Mean years of schooling" for adults aged 25 and older, and the "Expected years of schooling" for children entering the education system.

q: GDP at current prices is calculated using:
exp: In national income accounting, "Nominal GDP" explicitly refers to the Gross Domestic Product evaluated strictly at the prevailing, unadjusted market "prices of the current year" in which the goods and services were actively produced. It heavily includes the effects of inflation. Conversely, "Real GDP" uses "constant base-year prices" to completely strip away inflationary impacts, providing a much more accurate, reliable picture of actual national economic growth.

q: Which of the following best defines Gross Domestic Product (GDP)?
o: The total income of all citizens
The total value of final goods and services produced in a country
The total savings in a country
The total exports of a country
exp: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is strictly defined as the total monetary or market value of all the final goods and services produced within a country's geographic borders over a specific time period (usually a year). It acts as a comprehensive scorecard of economic health. The total income of citizens (including those abroad) is Gross National Product (GNP). Total savings or total exports only represent individual components of a nation's broader macroeconomic activity, not the complete definition of GDP.

q: What does 'GNP' stand for in economics?
exp: In macroeconomics, 'GNP' stands for 'Gross National Product'. It represents the total value of all final goods and services produced by the residents of a country in a given year, regardless of where that production takes place globally (adding net income from abroad to GDP). 'Gross National Price' is a fabricated term. 'Government National Plan' and 'General Needs Product' hold no relevance or formal definition within standard economic theory. Hence, Gross National Product is accurate.

q: What is the full form of the economic term 'GDP'?
exp: In the field of economics, 'GDP' stands strictly for 'Gross Domestic Product'. It is the standard quantitative macroeconomic measure representing the total monetary market value of all finished goods and services produced within a country's borders in a specific time period. 'Gross Domestic Price', 'Government Dues Paid', and 'General Development Plan' are fabricated distractors that possess no standard recognition or meaning in global economic accounting frameworks.

q: What specific economic activity does Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measure?
o: The total income of all citizens
The total value of final goods and services produced in a country
The total savings in a country
The total exports of a country
exp: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is strictly defined as the total monetary market value of all the "final goods and services" newly produced within a country's geographic borders over a specific period. It is the broadest quantitative measure of a nation's total economic activity. The total income of all citizens is Gross National Product (GNP). Savings and exports are just individual components affecting the economy, not the holistic GDP measurement itself.

q: Which of the following components is excluded from Gross Domestic Product?
exp: The standard expenditure approach to calculating Gross Domestic Product (GDP) uses the formula: GDP = Consumption (C) + Investment (I) + Government spending (G) + Net exports (X - M). While "Net exports" (which is Exports minus Imports) is absolutely included, the raw value of "Imports" is strictly excluded (subtracted) because imported goods were produced entirely in foreign countries, not within the domestic borders. Therefore, option (a) is the precisely correct answer.

q: Which of the following will increase the Gross Domestic Product but not the Gross National Product of a country?
o: Interest received from foreign government bonds
Profits of domestic companies earned abroad
Profits earned by a foreign company operating within the country
exp: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) rigorously measures the total value of all goods and services produced strictly within a country's physical geographical borders, regardless of who owns the company. Gross National Product (GNP) measures total output produced by a country's citizens, regardless of their global location. Therefore, massive profits earned by a foreign multinational company operating physically inside India will immediately increase India's GDP. However, because those vast profits are ultimately remitted back to foreign citizens, they are heavily subtracted when calculating GNP. Option (c) perfectly satisfies this complex macroeconomic condition.

q: What does "per capita income" refer to in economic terms?
exp: In the highly complex, meticulously analytical, and deeply fascinating realm of advanced macroeconomics, the highly crucial concept strictly known as "Per Capita Income" functions as a massively essential, straightforward statistical indicator. It aggressively attempts to gauge the overarching average economic wealth or deep financial prosperity essentially available to every single individual residing within a specific geographic territory or nation. To flawlessly and accurately calculate this incredibly important macroeconomic metric, economists systematically take the massive, overarching "Total income of the country" (typically the Gross National Income) and meticulously divide it directly by the massive total corresponding "population." Therefore, the statement "Total income divided by population" flawlessly and accurately defines this vital concept, making option (c) absolutely correct. It categorically does not refer to the highly localized average family income (a), the raw, unadjusted massive total national income (b), or the heavily restricted concept of strictly government tax income (d).

q: What is the term for the economic phenomenon where high inflation is combined with stagnant economic growth?
exp: Stagflation is a portmanteau of "stagnation" and "inflation." It describes a difficult economic condition characterized by slow economic growth (stagnation), relatively high unemployment, and rising prices (inflation). It is challenging to manage because policies that lower inflation (like raising interest rates) may worsen unemployment.

q: What is the term for the economic measure that tracks changes in the price level of a basket of goods and services?
exp: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is the measure that tracks changes in the price level of a weighted average market basket of consumer goods and services purchased by households. It is the primary gauge for measuring retail inflation in an economy.

q: What is the term for the shift of workers from agriculture to industry and services?
exp: The movement of the workforce from the primary sector (agriculture) to the secondary (industry) and tertiary (services) sectors is termed Occupational Diversification (or structural transformation). This shift typically accompanies economic development and modernization.

q: According to John Maynard Keynes, what is the most effective tool for reviving an economy during a depression?
exp: John Maynard Keynes advocated for expanding government expenditure (fiscal stimulus) to boost aggregate demand during a depression. He argued that during severe downturns, private sector demand is insufficient, so the government must step in to spend on infrastructure and public works to create jobs and stimulate the economy.

q: What trend is reflected by increasing share of urban people in non-manual tertiary occupations?
exp: An increasing share of the urban population engaged in non-manual tertiary occupations (like IT, banking, education, healthcare) reflects an Emerging Service Economy. It indicates a shift away from manufacturing and agriculture towards knowledge-based and service- oriented jobs.

q: Which economic consequence of migration is generally considered a challenge for the destination regions in India, particularly concerning unskilled rural migrants?
o: Increased per capita income due to the inflow of highly skilled labor
Reduction in pressure on land resources and unemployment rates
Exploitation of migrant labor and the growth of informal sector employment
exp: A major challenge for destination regions receiving large numbers of unskilled rural migrants is the exploitation of migrant labor and the unregulated growth of the informal sector (slums, daily wage work without security). While it provides cheap labor, it creates social and infrastructure pressure on cities.

q: Abhijit Sen was the chairman of the Committee on the Wholesale Price Index which submitted its report in:
exp: The working group for the revision of the current series of Wholesale Price Index (WPI) was set up under the chairmanship of Prof. Abhijit Sen. The committee submitted its technical report in 2008. This paved the way for revising the WPI base year (eventually to 2004-05 and later 2011-12).

q: Why prices rise when the government increases spending or cuts taxes?
o: Firm not be able to produce higher quantities that are being demanded at ongoing prices.
Firm exports their produces to the foreign destinations.
exp: When the government increases spending or cuts taxes, it boosts Aggregate Demand. In the short run, firms may not be able to instantly increase production capacity to meet this higher demand. This excess demand (Demand Pull) leads firms to raise prices, causing inflation. Option (a) correctly describes this supply-side constraint responding to demand shock.

q: Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) is conducted by which institution in India?
exp: The Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) was launched by the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) (now part of the National Statistical Office - NSO) in 2017. It provides quarterly and annual data on employment and unemployment indicators.

q: The term "Current Weekly Status" in India is related to which of the following?
exp: Current Weekly Status (CWS) is a concept used by the NSSO/NSO to measure employment and unemployment. It classifies a person as employed or unemployed based on their activity status during the reference week (the 7 days preceding the date of the survey).

q: In an economy, when the aggregate demand increases faster than aggregate supply, what is the likely outcome?
exp: When the aggregate demand (the total demand for goods and services) outpaces the aggregate supply (the economy's capacity to produce them), it creates a shortage. Consumers competing for limited goods bid up the prices, leading to what is economically termed as 'Demand-Pull Inflation.' The other options are incorrect: Deflation occurs when demand drops significantly; Depression is a severe and prolonged economic downturn with low demand and high unemployment; and Stagflation is a complex scenario characterized by stagnant economic growth simultaneously coupled with high inflation and high unemployment.

q: Which of the following statements shows an accurate understanding of a macroeconomic concept?
o: Gross Domestic Product includes earnings sent home by citizens working abroad.
When the general price level rises, the value of money tends to fall.
A country's budget is considered balanced when exports exceed imports.
The central bank controls inflation mainly through changes in income tax rates.
exp: Inflation represents a sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services in an economy. Consequently, as prices rise, every unit of currency buys fewer goods and services. This erosion of purchasing power means that a rising price level is inversely proportional to the value of money.

q: In economics, 'Stagflation' refers to a difficult economic situation characterized by?
exp: 'Stagflation' is a rare, highly toxic macroeconomic paradox that severely cripples an economy. It is characterized simultaneously by stagnant, negligible economic growth (stagnation), persistently high unemployment rates, and surprisingly, uncontrollably high prices of goods (inflation). This contradicts traditional Keynesian economic theory, which posits that inflation and unemployment typically possess an inverse relationship (as seen on the Phillips Curve).

q: A situation with a very high rate of inflation, where money loses its value very quickly, is called?
exp: Note: The 4th option was added for completeness. "Hyperinflation" is a highly catastrophic macroeconomic condition characterized by a rapid, excessive, and out-of-control general price increase in an economy, effectively destroying the real value of the local currency (often exceeding 50% per month). Deflation is a decrease in prices, disinflation is a temporary slowing of the inflation rate, and stagflation is a combination of stagnant economic growth and high inflation, making hyperinflation the precise term for this monetary collapse.

q: Unemployment that occurs due to the regular seasonal changes in a year is called?
exp: "Seasonal Unemployment" is an incredibly common macroeconomic phenomenon predominantly plaguing the agricultural and unorganized sectors in India. It forcibly occurs when millions of laborers are left totally out of work during specific, predictable off-season months of the year (such as the gap between aggressive sowing and harvesting). Frictional unemployment happens when people transition between jobs, and cyclical unemployment is strictly triggered by severe, widespread economic recessions.

q: What is the full form of 'CPI', a common measure of inflation?
exp: In macroeconomics, 'CPI' officially stands for the "Consumer Price Index." It is the most widely utilized, highly critical statistical metric employed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the government to accurately measure retail inflation. It meticulously calculates the monthly changes in the overall price level of a fixed, massive basket of essential goods and services (like food, housing, and medical care) directly consumed by everyday retail households.

q: What does 'CPI' (a measure of inflation) stand for?
exp: Consumer Price Index (CPI) is the correct term. It is a vital macroeconomic indicator that measures the average change over time in the prices paid by urban consumers for a market basket of consumer goods and services. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) uses CPI as the primary anchor for monetary policy. The other options (Corporate Price Index, Capital Payment Index, Credit Price Index) are fictitious acronyms and do not represent any official inflation measurement metrics.

q: What does the term 'frictional unemployment' refer to in economics?
o: Temporary unemployment as a person moves from one job to another
exp: Frictional unemployment, also known as search unemployment, is the natural and temporary gap in employment when individuals transition between jobs, careers, or locations while actively searching for new work. Unemployment due to seasons is 'Seasonal Unemployment' (e.g., in agriculture). Unemployment caused by an economic recession is called 'Cyclical Unemployment'. Permanent joblessness due to technological changes is 'Structural'. Hence, temporary transition between jobs is the correct definition.

q: What type of work is provided under Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA)?
exp: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), enacted in 2005, is a seminal social security measure that strictly guarantees exactly 100 days of wage employment in a financial year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer to do 'Unskilled manual work' (like digging wells, building rural roads, or canal desilting). It does not legally mandate or provide highly specialized technical work, sophisticated administrative roles, or skilled manual labor.

q: What is the term for a persistent decline in the general price level?
exp: In macroeconomics, 'Deflation' is strictly defined as the persistent, generalized decline in the overall price level of goods and services across an entire economy, effectively resulting in an increase in the purchasing power of money over time. It is the exact opposite of 'Inflation' (a general increase in prices). 'Stagflation' refers to high inflation coupled with high unemployment. A 'Recession' is a decline in broad economic activity, not specifically just a sustained drop in prices.

q: In economics, what is the definition of 'inflation'?
o: A decrease in the price of goods
A general increase in the price of goods and services
A government's budget being in surplus
exp: In strict macroeconomic terms, 'Inflation' is exclusively defined as a sustained, general increase in the overall price level of goods and services in an economy over a period of time, which consequently results in a relentless decrease in the purchasing power of money. A decrease in prices is termed 'Deflation'. A government budget surplus means revenues exceed spending. High employment relates to boom cycles, but inflation focuses purely on rising aggregate prices.

q: What is measured by the Lorenz Curve?
exp: In economics, the Lorenz Curve is a graphical representation used exclusively to measure the distribution of income or wealth within a society. It plots the cumulative percentages of total income received against the cumulative number of recipients, effectively illustrating the degree of Income inequality. Therefore, option (c) is correct. Price elasticity (a) measures demand responsiveness. Unemployment (b) and inflation tradeoffs are measured by the Phillips Curve. The Poverty line (d) is a statistical threshold, not a distribution curve.

q: In the short-run Phillips Curve:
o: Inflation and unemployment are negatively related.
Trade-off exists only in the long run.
Inflation and unemployment are positively related.
exp: The Short-run Phillips Curve is a foundational economic concept introduced by A.W. Phillips. It graphically demonstrates that in the short term, Inflation and unemployment share an inverse, negative relationship. This implies a critical trade-off: policymakers can choose lower unemployment but must accept the cost of higher inflation, and vice versa. Option (a) is perfectly correct. This trade-off breaks down entirely in the long run (making the curve vertical), but it absolutely exists in the

q: As per the Keynesian framework, unemployment can exist due to:
exp: The profound and highly revolutionary macroeconomic theories systematically developed by the legendary economist John Maynard Keynes explicitly challenge traditional classical economic assumptions. Keynes forcefully argued that severe, prolonged involuntary unemployment within a complex modern capitalist economy fundamentally exists simply because there is critically "Insufficient aggregate demand" for goods and services. When overall massive consumer spending and heavy corporate investment fall drastically, businesses instantly reduce vast production and brutally lay off workers, completely failing to reach full-employment equilibrium organically. Therefore, option (a) represents the absolute core foundational pillar of Keynesian economics, perfectly overriding concepts like rigid prices or extreme wage flexibility.

q: What does 'WPI' (another measure of inflation) stand for?
exp: WPI stands for the Wholesale Price Index. It is a crucial macroeconomic indicator that tracks and measures the average change in the prices of goods sold in bulk by wholesale businesses to other businesses, rather than to final consumers. Unlike the CPI (Consumer Price Index), the WPI in India strictly excludes the prices of services.

q: The one nation, one tax initiative in India refers to:
exp: The Goods and Services Tax (GST), implemented on July 1, 2017, is famously referred to as the One Nation, One Tax initiative. It replaced multiple cascading indirect taxes levied by the Central and State governments (like excise, VAT, service tax) with a single, unified tax system across the country.

q: When is a 'Vote on Account' necessary?
o: To ensure continuity of government operations until the budget is passed
exp: A Vote on Account is an interim permission granted by the Parliament to the government to withdraw funds from the Consolidated Fund of India to meet essential expenses (like salaries, ongoing projects) for a few months (usually two) until the full Budget is passed and enacted. It ensures the continuity of government operations during the transition period or election years.

q: Which taxation system is commonly used for income tax in most countries?
exp: Most countries, including India, use a Progressive Taxation system for income tax. In this system, the tax rate increases as the taxable income increases. This is based on the principle of ability to pay, ensuring that higher earners contribute a larger share of their income compared to lower earners, thereby reducing income inequality.

q: Which of the following is another term for 'Budgetary Deficit'?
exp: While technically distinct in older definitions, in modern Indian context and general exams, Fiscal Deficit is often used interchangeably or as the primary indicator for the government's total budgetary shortfall. It represents the excess of total expenditure over total receipts (excluding borrowings). Ideally, Budgetary Deficit used to mean Total Exp - Total Receipts (including borrowing) = 0, but Fiscal Deficit is the standard term for the borrowing requirement.

q: A country's government reported the following figures in its annual budget: Total Revenue Receipts = Rs. 50 lakh crore, Total Expenditure = Rs. 75 lakh crore, Borrowings = Rs. 20 lakh crore. What is the Fiscal Deficit of the government?
exp: Fiscal Deficit is defined as Total Expenditure minus Total Receipts excluding borrowings. However, structurally, Fiscal Deficit is equal to the total borrowing requirement. Wait, let's recalculate based on standard formula: Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure - (Revenue Receipts + Non-debt Capital Receipts). Here, non-debt capital receipts are not given, assuming formula Exp - Rev, 25 is the correct derivation).

q: Which of the following is an example of a direct tax in India?
exp: Corporate Income Tax (or Corporation Tax) is a Direct Tax levied on the net income or profit of corporate entities. The burden of a direct tax falls directly on the entity earning the income and cannot be shifted to others. Options (a), (b), and (d) are indirect taxes where the burden can be passed on to the consumer.

q: The Government of India introduced the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act to decrease the issue of fiscal deficit and:
exp: The FRBM Act, 2003 was enacted to institutionalize financial discipline, reduce India's Fiscal Deficit, and improve macroeconomic management. A key goal was to limit and reduce the Public Debt of the government to sustainable levels, preventing a debt trap and ensuring inter-generational equity.

q: In India, which of the following statements is correct about the financial relationship between the Center and the States?
o: The Union Government has exclusive control over all types of taxation, including state taxes.
The States have no role in the allocation of taxes and resources...
The Union Government collects taxes and distributes them between the Union and the States through the Finance Commission.
States have the authority to impose taxes on defense...
exp: The financial relationship is defined by federalism. The Union Government collects certain major taxes (like Income Tax, GST, Customs) and distributes a share of the net proceeds to the States. This devolution of funds is recommended by the Finance Commission, a constitutional body set up every 5 years under Article 280 to ensure equitable distribution.

q: What is the main objective of a government budget?
exp: The primary objective of a government budget is the reallocation of resources or allocating public funds to various sectors (health, education, infrastructure) in line with social and economic goals. It aims to foster economic growth, reduce inequalities, and ensure stability, not specifically just to decrease taxes or promote the private sector alone.

q: Which of the following is a direct tax collected by the government?
exp: Income Tax is a classic example of a Direct Tax because the liability to pay and the burden of the tax fall on the same person (the income earner). The tax is levied directly on the income or wealth of individuals and companies. GST, Customs, and Excise are Indirect Taxes levied on goods and services.

q: Which of the following is an example of an indirect tax?
exp: Goods and Services Tax (GST) is a comprehensive Indirect Tax levied on the supply of goods and services. It is an indirect tax because the liability to pay is on the supplier, but the actual burden is shifted to the final consumer who pays it as part of the price. Income, Corporate, and Wealth taxes are direct taxes.

q: What does the term 'crowding out' refer to in economics?
o: Decline in private investment due to high government borrowing
Rise in inflation due to excessive printing of money
exp: Crowding Out refers to a phenomenon where increased government borrowing (to finance a deficit) leads to higher interest rates, which in turn leads to a decline in private investment and consumption. The government essentially "crowds out" private borrowers from the loanable funds market by absorbing the available liquidity.

q: The annual financial statement presented by the Government of India is commonly known as the:
exp: The Annual Financial Statement, referred to in Article 112 of the Constitution, is commonly known as the Budget. It is a statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for the coming financial year (April 1 to March 31).

q: What is the term used when government spending exceeds its revenue?
exp: When the government's total expenditure exceeds its total revenue (excluding borrowings), it is called a Deficit (specifically, Budget Deficit or Fiscal Deficit). Conversely, if revenue exceeds expenditure, it is a Surplus. Governments often run deficits to fund development, financing the gap through borrowing.

q: Which of the following is an example of fiscal policy in India?
exp: Fiscal Policy involves the use of government spending and taxation to influence the economy. Government spending on infrastructure is a direct fiscal tool to boost demand and create assets. Adjusting Repo Rates (a) and controlling money supply (d) are tools of Monetary Policy, managed by the RBI.

q: What was the primary purpose for which the Goods & Services Tax (GST) Act was enacted?
o: To act as a new direct tax
To levy more duties on luxury goods
To ensure uniform tax across states
To differentiate between goods & services in taxation
exp: The primary purpose of GST was to create a unified common market by ensuring a uniform tax structure across states. It aimed to eliminate the cascading effect of taxes (tax on tax) and simplify compliance by replacing multiple state and central levies with a single, destination-based tax system.

q: Which of the following is a major objective of deficit financing by the government?
exp: Deficit financing (borrowing or printing money to fund expenditure) is primarily aimed at stimulating economic growth. By injecting more money into the economy through infrastructure projects and welfare schemes, the government aims to boost aggregate demand, create jobs, and utilize idle resources, especially during slowdowns.

q: Which of the following is NOT a reason for a fiscal deficit?
o: High government expenditure on welfare schemes
Surplus in the balance of payments
exp: A Fiscal Deficit arises when expenditure exceeds revenue. Reasons include high spending on subsidies/welfare (a) or low tax collection (b). An increase in public borrowing (c) is the result or measure of the deficit. However, a Surplus in the Balance of Payments (related to external trade and capital flows) is NOT a cause of the government's domestic fiscal deficit; in fact, a deficit usually implies the government needs to borrow more, not less.

q: According to Keynesian theory, during recession, what should the government ideally do?
exp: Keynesian theory advocates for expansionary fiscal policy during a recession. To revive aggregate demand, the government should increase public spending (to create jobs/income) and cut taxes (to increase disposable income for consumption). Reducing spending (d) would worsen a recession.

q: Which of the following best describes the primary objective of a government's fiscal policy?
o: To control the money supply and interest rates.
To influence aggregate demand and economic activity through government spending and taxation.
exp: The primary objective of Fiscal Policy is to influence aggregate demand and overall economic activity using the tools of government spending and taxation. By adjusting these, the government aims to achieve goals like full employment, price stability, and economic growth.

q: What is the role of the finance minister under the FRBM Act?
o: To present fiscal policy statements to Parliament
exp: Under the FRBM Act, 2003, the Finance Minister is mandated to present three fiscal policy statements to Parliament annually along with the Budget: the Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement, the Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement, and the Macroeconomic Framework Statement. This ensures transparency and accountability in fiscal management.

q: What was the main purpose behind the enactment of the FRBM (Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management) Act?
exp: The FRBM Act, 2003 was enacted to ensure inter- generational equity in fiscal management and long-term macro-economic stability. Its main purpose was to reduce government borrowing (fiscal deficit) and eliminate the revenue deficit, thereby enforcing fiscal discipline and reducing the country's debt burden.

q: In what way did fiscal discipline reforms affect center-state financial relations post-1991?
o: States had to adhere to fiscal targets
Increased state autonomy in tax policy
exp: Post-1991 reforms and the enactment of FRBM Acts (both Central and State level), States had to adhere to strict fiscal targets (like limiting fiscal deficit to 3% of GSDP) to avail certain benefits or borrowing limits recommended by Finance Commissions. This introduced a rule- based fiscal discipline framework for states.

q: Arrange in chronological order: 1. GST Council constituted 2. Constitution (101st Amendment) Act enacted 3. GST launched Select the correct order:
exp: Correct Order: * Constitution (101st Amendment) Act enacted: Sept 2016. * GST Council constituted: Sept 2016 (Notification issued post-amendment). * GST launched: July 1, 2017. Thus, the sequence is 2-1-3.

q: Disinvestment involves selling stakes in:
exp: Disinvestment involves the government selling its equity stakes in Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) or Public Enterprises to private individuals or entities. It is undertaken to raise resources, improve efficiency and reduce the fiscal burden on the exchequer.

q: Assertion (A): The disinvestment policy has been widely criticized in India. Reason (R): It resulted in increased market monopoly by public sector undertakings. Select the correct option:
o: Both A and R are true, R explains A
Both A and R are true, R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
exp: Assertion (A) is true: Disinvestment is criticized for selling national assets ("family silver") cheaply, job losses, and loss of state control. Reason (R) is false: Disinvestment typically leads to privatization or increased private competition, reducing the monopoly of the public sector, not increasing it.

q: How is revenue deficit calculated?
exp: Revenue Deficit represents the shortfall of the government's current revenue to meet its current expenditure. Formula: Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure - Revenue Receipts. It indicates that the government is borrowing to fund its regular consumption/administrative expenses.

q: Which type of sale allows partial transfer of PSU ownership to private hands?
exp: A Minority Sale involves the government selling a part of its stake (less than 51%) in a PSU to private investors while retaining majority ownership and management control. This allows for a partial transfer of ownership. Strategic sales involve transferring management control (often >51%).

q: Which of the following is another name for the revenue account of the government budget?
exp: The Government Budget is divided into two parts: the Revenue Budget (Revenue Account) and the Capital Budget (Capital Account). The Revenue Budget deals with current financial transactions (Revenue Receipts and Revenue Expenditure) that do not impact the government's asset-liability status.

q: Privatization in India through disinvestment refers to:
exp: Privatization through disinvestment refers to the process of selling government equity (shares) in public sector undertakings to private entities or the general public. If the sale is substantial (strategic sale) leading to a transfer of management control, it is termed privatization.

q: Which of the following is an example of a capital receipt?
exp: Capital Receipts are receipts that either create a liability (like borrowing) or reduce assets (like disinvestment). Loans taken from the RBI (or public/foreign) create a repayment liability, hence they are Capital Receipts. Options (a), (b), and (d) are Revenue Receipts (income tax, dividends, fees) as they neither create liability nor reduce assets.

q: Why is revenue deficit a concern for the economy?
exp: A Revenue Deficit is worrying because it indicates that the government is borrowing to finance its current consumption expenditure (salaries, interest payments, subsidies) rather than investing in asset creation. This leads to a debt trap without adding to the economy's productive capacity.

q: Why are grants for asset creation still considered Revenue Expenditure?
o: Do not create direct central assets
Not included in any budget head
exp: Grants-in-aid given by the Central Government to States (even for creating assets like roads/schools) are treated as Revenue Expenditure in the Centre's budget because the ownership of the asset created lies with the State Government, not the Centre. Thus, for the Centre, it does not create a direct asset (Option c).

q: Which of the following best defines Capital Receipts?
o: Receipts that do not impact assets
exp: Capital Receipts are defined as those government receipts which either create a liability (e.g., Borrowings, Provident Funds) or reduce assets (e.g., Disinvestment, Recovery of Loans). They are non- recurring in nature.

q: Assertion (A): The government's revenue receipts don't bring with them any burden of repayment. Reason (R): these earnings aren't meant to be returned and generally come from taxes/regular inflows. Select the correct option:
o: Both A and R are true, R explains A
Both A and R are true, R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
exp: Both are true and R explains A. Revenue receipts (like Taxes, Fees) are non-redeemable; the government has no obligation to return them (Assertion). This is because they are unilateral payments or earnings from assets, not borrowings, so they carry no repayment burden (Reason).

q: Consider the following statements regarding government budget receipts: 1. Income tax and dividends from PSUs are classified as revenue receipts. 2. Disinvestment in PSUs is also a revenue receipt. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Statement 1 is correct: Income tax (Tax Revenue) and Dividends (Non-Tax Revenue) are Revenue Receipts as they don't impact assets/liabilities. Statement 2 is incorrect: Disinvestment (selling stake in PSUs) reduces government assets, so it is classified as a Capital Receipt, not a revenue receipt.

q: In the Union Budget 2025-26, the government has allocated Rs. 20,000 crores for an initiative aiming to develop at least ______ indigenously designed and operational SMRs by 2033.
exp: The Union Budget 2025-26 announced the Nuclear Energy Mission with an outlay of ₹20,000 crore, targeting at least 5 indigenously developed and operational Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) by 2033, as part of the goal of 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047.

q: In Budget 2025, the Union Finance Minister announced to set up ______ Atal Tinkering Labs.
exp: In the Union Budget 2025-26, the Finance Minister announced that 50,000 Atal Tinkering Labs (ATLs) will be set up in Government schools over the next five years to cultivate scientific temper and a spirit of innovation among young students.

q: The Union Budget 2025-26 announced to set up a Centre of Excellence in Artificial Intelligence for education with a total outlay of Rs ______ crores.
exp: The Union Budget 2025-26 announced a Centre of Excellence in Artificial Intelligence for Education with a total outlay of ₹500 crore, building on the three AI CoEs (for agriculture, health and sustainable cities) announced in 2023, to integrate AI into the learning ecosystem.

q: The Union Budget 2025-26 states that total number of students in 23 IITs has increased 100 per cent from 65,000 to 1.35 lakh in the past ______ years.
exp: The budget highlighted that student capacity in IITs doubled over the past 10 years, reflecting the government's focus on expanding higher technical education.

q: In the Union Budget 2025-26, there has been a plan to establish ______ Day Care Cancer Centres in 2025-26.
exp: The government planned to establish 200 Day Care Cancer Centres to provide accessible chemotherapy and cancer care services.

q: The "Aatmanirbharta in Pulses" campaign, launched in Union Budget 2025, is a government mission spanning ______ years to achieve self-sufficiency in pulse production.
exp: The mission aims to achieve self-sufficiency in pulses over a span of 3 years, targeting reduced imports and better prices for farmers.

q: During the Union Budget for 2025-26, it was announced that the government will introduce a Rs ______ crores term loan scheme.
exp: In the Union Budget 2025-26, the government announced term loans of up to ₹2 crore for 5 lakh first-time entrepreneurs — specifically women and members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes — over the next five years, to facilitate easier access to credit for new businesses.

q: In the Union Budget 2025-26, a Maritime Development Fund of Rs. ______ crore over 10 years has been announced.
exp: A Maritime Development Fund with a corpus of Rs. 25,000 crore over 10 years was announced to boost the shipbuilding and maritime sector.

q: In April 2025, Union Minister announced that Second Fund of Funds for Startups worth Rs. ______ crore to boost deep-tech has been approved.
exp: The government approved a Second Fund of Funds for Startups worth Rs. 10,000 crore, specifically focusing on deep-tech innovation.

q: Which of the following is correct regarding Sale of government assets like sale of shares in Public sector unit (PSU)?
o: It creates liability for the government
Amount comes from sale of shares are part of capital receipts
Amount comes from sale of shares are part of revenue receipts
It does not reduce the total assets of the government
exp: The sale of government assets (Disinvestment) reduces the assets of the government. Receipts that reduce assets are classified as Capital Receipts. It does not create a liability (unlike loans). Therefore, option (b) is correct.

q: In 2001-02, excise duty structure was rationalized to a single rate of ______ per cent CENVAT (Central Value Add Tax).
exp: In the 2001-02 Budget, the government rationalized the excise duty structure, introducing a single rate of 16% CENVAT (Central Value Added Tax) to simplify indirect taxation before the GST era.

q: In progressive income taxation:
o: higher income leads to a higher tax rate
everyone pays the same tax rate
lower income leads to a higher tax rate
higher income leads to a lower tax rate
exp: Progressive taxation is defined by the principle that higher income leads to a higher tax rate. People with more income pay a larger percentage of that income in taxes.

q: Which of the following taxes are imposed on goods imported into and exported out of India?
exp: Customs Duty is the tax imposed on goods when they cross international borders, i.e., on imports into and exports out of India. Excise duty is on domestic manufacturing.

q: Child Budgeting was first time adopted by government of India in:
exp: While a specific statement on child-related schemes existed earlier, a formal Child Budgeting statement (Statement 22, later Statement 12) was introduced for the first time in the Union Budget 2008-09 to track allocation for child welfare.

q: Which of the following deficit includes only such transactions that affect the current income and expenditure of the government?
exp: Revenue Deficit relates only to the current income (Revenue Receipts) and current expenditure (Revenue Expenditure) of the government. It does not include capital transactions (borrowing, asset creation).

q: Which of the following is referred as Public sector unit (PSU) disinvestment?
o: Allowing direct foreign direct investment in PSU
Allowing indirect foreign direct investment in PSU
exp: Disinvestment refers to the sale of shares (liquidation of assets) held by the government in a Public Sector Unit (PSU) to private entities or the public.

q: Interest payment on debt incurred by the government is part of the:
exp: Interest payments on past loans are classified as Revenue Expenditure. This is because they are a recurring expense that does not create any asset nor reduce the principal liability; they are merely the cost of servicing debt.

q: In India, how many policy statements are mandated by the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act along with the budget?
exp: The FRBM Act, 2003 mandates the government to lay Three policy statements before Parliament along with the Budget: * Medium-term Fiscal Policy Statement * Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement * Macro-economic Framework Statement.

q: Consider the following regarding revenue expenditure in the context of Budget: 1. Salaries of government employees 2. Pensions of government employees Which of the above is/are included in the revenue expenditure?
exp: Both I and II are correct. Salaries and Pensions are recurring operational expenses for the normal functioning of the government. They do not create assets, so they are classified as Revenue Expenditure.

q: What is the traditional belief about the effect of a government cutting taxes and running a budget deficit?
o: It promotes foreign investors to opt out from economy rapidly
exp: The traditional (Keynesian) view is that cutting taxes increases disposable income for households. This promotes consumers to spend more, thereby boosting aggregate demand and stimulating the economy, even if it leads to a budget deficit in the short run.

q: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act- 2003 requires the reduction in revenue deficit by ______ of GDP every year.
exp: The original FRBM Rules, 2004 mandated the reduction of the Revenue Deficit by an amount equivalent to 0.5% (or more) of the GDP at the end of each financial year, aiming to eliminate it entirely.

q: Which of the following has amalgamated a large number of central and state taxes and cesses?
exp: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) amalgamated a large number of indirect taxes (like Excise, Service Tax, VAT, Octroi, Luxury Tax) into a single tax regime.

q: In the context of Budget, the salaries, pensions, defence services come under:
exp: Expenses on salaries, pensions, and defence services (operational parts) are consumptive and recurring. They do not create productive assets (generally), so they fall under Revenue Expenditure.

q: The disinvestment of a public sector unit leads to:
o: reduction in financial assets of the government
increase in the financial assets of the government
creation of liability of the government
increase in the tax revenue of the government
exp: Disinvestment involves selling government equity (shares). Shares are financial assets. Selling them leads to a reduction in the financial assets of the government. (The money received is a capital receipt).

q: If the government continues to borrow year after year, it leads to the:
exp: Continuous borrowing creates a stock of accumulated debt (Public Debt). To service this debt (pay interest), the government may need to borrow more, potentially leading to a debt trap.

q: In the context of Budget, which of the following is NOT an example of capital expenditure of government?
exp: Subsidies are a recurring expense meant to lower prices or (a), (b), and (c) create assets.

q: Who was the chairman of the Tax Reforms Committee 1991?
exp: The Tax Reforms Committee constituted in 1991 to recommend comprehensive reforms in the taxation system was headed by Prof. Raja J. Chelliah. His recommendations laid the foundation for modernizing India's tax structure (e.g., Service Tax).

q: Consider the following regarding capital expenditure in the context of Budget: 1. It does not create physical or financial assets. 2. Acquisition of machinery is an example of capital expenditure. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Capital Expenditure is defined as expenditure that creates physical or financial assets or reduces liabilities. Therefore, Statement I is incorrect. Acquisition of machinery creates an asset, so Statement II is correct.

q: In ______, government of India set up a committee to review the fiscal reforms and suggest appropriate framework under the chairmanship of Vijay Kelkar.
exp: The Task Force on Direct and Indirect Taxes, headed by Vijay Kelkar, was set up in 2002-03 (specifically 2002) to recommend measures for tax simplification and fiscal consolidation.

q: Consider the following taxes (now replaced by GST): 1. Entertainment tax 2. Entry tax Which of the above was/were levied by the Central government?
exp: Before GST, Entertainment Tax (levied by Local Bodies/States) and Entry Tax (levied by State Governments) were State Taxes, not Central Taxes. Central taxes subsumed included Excise, Service Tax, etc. Thus, Neither I nor II was levied by the Centre.

q: The gross fiscal deficit as a ratio to GDP in India had climbed to ______ per cent by 1990-91.
exp: By 1990-91, on the eve of the balance of payments crisis, India's Gross Fiscal Deficit had climbed to an unsustainable level of roughly 8.4% to 10% of GDP (depending on estimates, usually cited around 8.4% for Centre and higher consolidated). Option (a) 10% is the closest appropriate figure for the crisis peak context.

q: In 2002-2003, the Government of India set up a committee to review the fiscal reforms both in respect of Direct and Indirect taxes under the chairmanship of:
exp: The Kelkar Task Force on Direct and Indirect Taxes was set up in 2002 under the chairmanship of Vijay Kelkar.

q: Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act was enacted in which year?
exp: The FRBM Act was enacted by the Parliament in 2003 (notified in 2004) to bring financial discipline.

q: In India's gender budget, ______ includes schemes where the budgetary allocation for women and girls is below 30% of the total provision.
exp: The Gender Budget Statement is divided into two parts. Part A covers schemes with 100% allocation for women. Part B covers schemes with at least 30% allocation for women. Based on SSC patterns, Part B is usually the answer for schemes with partial (not 100%) allocation, even though the threshold is technically >=30%.

q: Consider the following taxes: 1. Wealth tax 2. Goods and Services tax Which of the following is known as the Paper tax in India?
exp: Wealth tax (abolished in 2015) was often criticized as a "Paper Tax" because it generated very little revenue (high collection cost, low yield) and existed mostly "on paper" without effective enforcement or fiscal significance.

q: Which of the following relates to those expenses incurred for the normal functioning of the government departments?
exp: Revenue Expenditure includes expenses incurred for the normal functioning of government departments and for the provision of various services (salaries, electricity, stationery, maintenance). It sustains the government's day-to-day operations.

q: Which of the following statement is correct regarding money received by the government from loans and the sale of its own assets?
o: Loans create liability but sale of asset do not
Sale of asset create liability but loans do not
Loans are part of revenue receipts...
Loans and sale of assets both do not reduces or increases...
exp: Money received from Loans (Borrowings) creates a repayment liability. Money received from the Sale of Assets (Disinvestment) does not create a liability (it reduces an asset). Both are Capital Receipts. Thus, statement (a) is correct.

q: Consider the following regarding the government budget: 1. Subsidies are an important policy instrument which aim at increasing welfare. 2. Defence expenditure is committed expenditure in the sense that given the national security concerns, there exists little scope for drastic reduction. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Both statements are correct. Subsidies are indeed a fiscal tool to enhance social welfare (making goods affordable). Defence expenditure is considered committed expenditure because national security cannot be compromised, making it difficult to cut significantly.

q: As per the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act-2003, which of the following is NOT laid before both the house of parliament along with Annual Financial statement?
o: The medium term fiscal policy statement
exp: The Monetary Policy Statement is issued by the RBI (Monetary Policy Committee), not by the government under the FRBM Act. The FRBM Act mandates the first three statements (a, b, c) to be laid by the Finance Minister.

q: As per the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act-2003, the actual deficits may exceed the targets only on which of the following grounds? 1. National security 2. National calamity Select the correct option:
exp: The FRBM Act allows for an "Escape Clause" where the deficit targets can be exceeded in exceptional circumstances. These grounds include National Security (war), National Calamity, collapse of agriculture, or structural reforms. Thus, both are valid grounds.

q: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act- 2003 mandates the central government to reduce fiscal deficit to not more than ______ of GDP.
exp: The original target set by the FRBM Act, 2003 was to reduce the Fiscal Deficit to 3% of GDP by March 31, 2008 (later extended/revised multiple times). The 3% limit remains the anchor for fiscal prudence.

q: The Chelliah Committee recommended in January _____ that the prevailing rates of import duties be rationalised and lowered.
exp: The Tax Reforms Committee, prominently chaired by Professor Raja J. Chelliah, was officially appointed by the government in 1991 following the massive economic crisis. However, it specifically submitted its final, groundbreaking comprehensive report in January 1993. The committee strongly and urgently recommended that the incredibly high, complex prevailing rates of customs and import duties be aggressively rationalized, simplified, and significantly lowered to actively promote free trade and boost industrial globalization. The subsequent years (1995, 1996) represent later implementation phases, not the recommendation date.

q: In which year service tax was introduced in India?
exp: Service Tax, an indirect tax levied comprehensively on certain highly specific services provided by various service providers, was formally introduced in India for the very first time in the year 1994. This significant tax reform was strategically enacted under the Finance Act of 1994, strictly based on the strong recommendations made by the Dr. Raja J. Chelliah Committee to massively expand the government's total tax base. The other years are factually incorrect: 1991 marks the monumental LPG economic liberalization policies, while 2005 saw the crucial introduction of the Value Added Tax (VAT) system in India.

q: In the context of Budget, which of the following is the part of Revenue receipts? 1. Personal Income tax 2. Corporation tax 3. Borrowings Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: In strict government accounting and budgeting, 'Revenue Receipts' are those specific routine earnings that neither generate a future financial liability nor cause any reduction in the government's assets. Both Personal Income Tax and Corporation Tax firmly fit this definition, being major sources of direct tax revenue. However, 'Borrowings' are entirely different; they directly create a heavy financial liability for the government (a debt that must be repaid) and are therefore strictly categorized under 'Capital Receipts'. Thus, only statements I and II accurately represent revenue receipts.

q: Which of the following is the non-debt creating capital receipt? 1. Recovery of loans 2. Proceeds from the sale of public sector unit Which of the statements above is/are correct?
exp: Both statements are absolutely correct examples. In the strict framework of government budgeting, 'Capital Receipts' are inflows that either create an active liability or heavily reduce a state asset. "Non-debt creating" capital receipts specifically bring in massive funds without actively creating any future repayment burden (debt) for the government. The 'Recovery of past loans' (Statement I) and the strategic 'Sale of public sector units' or disinvestment (Statement II) firmly fit this category because they simply liquidate existing government assets for cash, generating zero new debt.

q: Which of the following is NOT an example of Indirect Tax?
exp: Corporation Tax is definitively and strictly an example of a 'Direct Tax', heavily levied directly by the central government on the massive net income or total profit successfully earned by registered corporate companies and businesses. The financial burden of this tax cannot be legally shifted to anyone else. In absolute contrast, Sales tax, Service tax, and Entertainment tax are all classic examples of 'Indirect Taxes' (now largely subsumed under GST), where the initial tax is levied on goods and services, but the final financial burden is effectively passed down entirely to the end consumer.

q: The budgetary deficit is financed by which of the following?
o: Either by borrowing or printing money
exp: In modern public finance, a 'Budgetary Deficit' critically occurs when a government's total planned expenditures heavily exceed its total actual revenue (which already includes normal taxation). Because taxation has strictly fallen short, the government cannot finance the deficit with it. Instead, the government must finance this massive shortfall either by actively borrowing enormous funds (from the public market, banks, or foreign institutions) or, in extreme cases, by directly printing new money through the central bank (often called monetization of deficit). Thus, deficit financing inherently relies solely on borrowing or printing money.

q: In India, the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act-2003 requires the reduction in fiscal deficit by ____ of GDP every year.
exp: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, officially enacted in 2003, is a highly critical legislative framework designed explicitly to instill intense financial discipline and massive macroeconomic stability within the Indian government. The original strict provisions of this Act mandated a systematic, continuous reduction in the national fiscal deficit by a minimum of precisely 0.3% of the GDP each financial year, aggressively aiming to eventually bring the total deficit down to a manageable target of 3%. The other percentages (2.5%, 4%, 6%) are factually inaccurate for this specific annual reduction target.

q: Which among the following correctly denotes the Primary Deficit?
o: sum of the net increase in holdings of treasury bills of the RBI and its contributions to the market borrowing of the government.
Budgetary Deficit + Govt. market borrowings and liabilities
exp: In government budgeting, the Primary Deficit is accurately defined as the Fiscal Deficit minus the Interest Payments on previous borrowings. It essentially highlights the current government's fiscal of past debts. The other options define different economic concepts: "Revenue Expenditure minus Revenue Receipts" denotes the Revenue Deficit. The "sum of the net increase in holdings of treasury bills of the RBI and its contributions to the market borrowing" refers to deficit financing. "Budgetary Deficit plus Govt. market borrowings" is traditionally the broad calculation for Fiscal Deficit itself.

q: The Union Budget is presented for which period?
o: Fiscal year from Jan to Dec
Financial year from April to March
Financial year from July to June
exp: Under Article 112 of the Indian Constitution, the Union Budget is officially termed the "Annual Financial Statement." It presents the government's estimated receipts and expenditures for the upcoming Indian financial year, which universally runs from 1st April of the current year to 31st March of the following year.

q: Which of the following is a typical example of Revenue Expenditure?
o: Purchase of land for a PSU facility
Interest paid on a government loan
exp: In government budgeting, Revenue Expenditure refers to short-term expenses used for the day-to-day functioning of the government that neither create any physical or financial asset nor reduce any liability. Examples include paying salaries, pensions, subsidies, and interest payments on past government loans. Construction and land purchases are Capital Expenditures.

q: Consider the following statements about Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) scheme: (1) the NBS scheme provides fixed per-kg subsidy rates for N, P, K, and S in non-urea fertilizers. (2) Freight assistance is also provided. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
exp: Introduced by the Indian government in 2010, the NBS scheme provides an explicit, fixed rate of subsidy (calculated annually per kg) based directly on the nutrient content (Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potash, and Sulphur) of complex fertilizers. Additionally, to ensure availability across remote areas, freight assistance for domestic movement is also systematically provided to manufacturers.

q: What does the Finance Bill presented in the Budget mainly contain?
o: Proposals related to tax changes or rules
exp: Under Article 110 of the Indian Constitution, the Finance Bill is a highly crucial piece of legislation introduced annually strictly alongside the Union Budget. Its primary, exclusive function is to seek parliamentary approval to implement, amend, abolish, or regulate the taxation rules, direct and indirect tax rates, and duties proposed by the government for the upcoming financial year.

q: Which of the following is an example of a capital receipt for the Indian government?
o: Dividends received from Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs)
Disinvestment proceeds from selling shares of PSUs
exp: In government accounting, Capital Receipts are incoming funds that either directly create a financial liability (like market borrowings) or cause a permanent reduction in government assets. Consequently, the massive cash proceeds generated from the strategic disinvestment (sale) of government equity shares in Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) are classically categorized as capital receipts.

q: Read the following statements carefully and choose the correct option regarding Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Assertion (A): Tax reforms post-1991 included lowering income tax rates. Reason (R): Lower tax rates were believed to increase tax compliance and reduce evasion.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
exp: Following the monumental 1991 liberalization, the Chelliah Committee powerfully advocated for sweeping, systemic tax reforms. The government systematically lowered the previously exorbitant direct income tax rates (Assertion A). This drastic reduction was strategically implemented precisely because economists fundamentally believed that moderate, rationalized taxes directly encourage widespread voluntary compliance and significantly disincentivize massive tax evasion (Reason R).

q: Consider the following statements regarding the Urea Subsidy Scheme: Statement 1: Urea is sold to farmers at a fixed Maximum Retail Price (MRP). Statement 2: the subsidy is directly transferred to the bank accounts of farmers. Which of the above is/are correct?
exp: Statement 1 is perfectly correct; to ensure absolute affordability for agriculture, the government controls Urea heavily, forcing it to be sold to farmers at a statutorily fixed, highly subsidized Maximum Retail Price (MRP). Statement 2 is entirely incorrect; the massive subsidy amount is calculated and paid directly to the fertilizer manufacturers, not the farmers.

q: Which of the following best explains why indirect taxes are considered regressive?
o: They apply only to the wealthy
They impact all income groups equally
exp: Indirect taxes (like GST on salt or soap) are economically termed "regressive" because they impose a that, uniform rate on a good regardless of the buyer's financial status. While the absolute tax amount impacts all income groups equally, it ends up mercilessly taking a much larger percentage of income from poor individuals than from the wealthy.

q: The capital account in the government budget deals with:
o: Assets and liabilities of the government
exp: Within the fundamental structure of a government's annual budget, the "Capital Account" is strictly designed to track long-term, high- impact financial transactions. It exclusively deals with receipts and massive expenditures that directly result in the tangible creation of new physical assets (like highways) or cause a significant alteration in the government's financial liabilities (like sovereign borrowings or loan recoveries).

q: Read the following statements and select the appropriate option: Statement 1: A budget deficit is encountered when the total expenditure of the government is greater than its total revenue, excluding borrowings. Statement 2: A budget deficit is faced when the total revenue of the government is greater than its expenditure in a fiscal year. Which of the statements above is/are correct?
o: Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct
Neither Statement 1 nor Statement 2 is correct
exp: Statement 1 accurately defines the fundamental concept of a Fiscal Deficit (often referred to simply as the budget deficit in general economics), which occurs exactly when a government's total expenditures grossly exceed its total non-debt creating receipts. Statement 2 is fundamentally incorrect; when revenue is higher than expenditure, it actually creates a budget surplus, not a deficit.

q: Which of the following is an indirect tax?
exp: Excise Duty is a classic example of an indirect tax because it is levied on the domestic production or manufacturing of goods, but the ultimate financial burden is subtly shifted to the final consumer through higher retail prices. Conversely, Income Tax, Corporation Tax, and Wealth Tax are strictly direct taxes paid directly by individuals or companies.

q: Under the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) system in fertilizers, which of the following statements accurately reflects the actual implementation mechanism?
o: Subsidy is paid to companies post-sale
